I OF A PILGRIMAGE
THE SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD

Knowledge of Saint Augustine in our time is a duty of Christian and humanistic culture, because Christianity and Humanity have in him a typical representative, an index of their greatness, vigor and power. Saint Augustine is the contemporary of all generations, the eternal man, endowed with extraordinary sympathy and human warmth for all who approach him and receive the breath of his spirit and his word. It is certainly not an easy task to encompass the fullness of his thought and work, and our glass will be small to pour into it the copious flow, the tremulous immensity of his oceanic spirit. However, he himself has facilitated the task of understanding and has left open the path that leads us to his intimacy, to vast horizons that open to heaven, earth and the abyss. The Confessions are the indispensable source to know Saint Augustine and the wonderful and divine book, because it does not conceal what is human, rather it describes it with a penetration and success that few geniuses have achieved. Humanity finds in it one of its best portraits, its own crystal palace, wide and hospitable, where souls can know each other and, above all, find the path to their own knowledge and redemption. Here we are interested in the Augustinian autobiography to draw up the profile and itinerary towards the truth. Aurelius Augustine was born on November 13, 354 in Tagaste, a small town in Numidia, in Proconsular Africa. His parents were Patricio and Mónica; He a pagan, she a fervent Christian. Three fronds grew on the tree of that marriage: two sons, Navigio and Agustín, and a daughter, named Perpetua. Agustín was a larger leaf than the native garden, and he introduced, without a doubt, a new bubbling and movement of sap into the house. Compared to the docile Navigio and the sweet Perpetua, Agustín was the most lively, the most boisterous and torrential. It has been said that the child's soul is like a blackboard clean of all writing, like a virgin land in which nothing is planted. Two hands passed over the satin wax of the soul of Saint

Augustine: that of Monica, who recorded with firm strokes the name of Christ and some truths of the Christian faith, and the hand of paganism, embodied in Patrick and in the public life of that time. Patrick did not leave any deep and lasting mark on his son's soul, judging by the silence of the author of the Confessions. Monica, on the contrary, is the type of Christian motherhood in the double corporeal and spiritual ministry. She fulfilled the highest mission that belongs to the authors of our existence: what Saint Augustine calls suscitare semen Christi (raising the germ of Christ), multiplying his spiritual descendants. She was, as R. Guardini says, "the living incarnation of the Church", and always influenced Augustine with doctrine, example and prayer. The affectionate presence of that chaste woman, collected, withdrawn into a painful intimacy, left a healthy mark on the son. The portrait that the Confessions have preserved for us, and that Saint Augustine had sculpted in the living flesh of his heart, leaves no room for doubt on this point: "I will not silence any of the feelings that spring up in my soul inspired by that servant of yours, who gave birth to me in the flesh so that I would be born to temporal life and gave birth to me in her heart so that I would be born to eternal life." \ No more beautiful praise can be given of Christian motherhood. Augustine and Monica are inseparably united in spirit and blood, just as Ary Schefer sensed in the painting of the Vision of Ostia. He is the son of prayer and tears: "To you, source of mercy, I offered prayers and tears, denser and more continuous so that you would accelerate your help and illuminate my darkness. And I ran with greater zeal to the Church, and hung from the mouth of Saint Ambrose, fountain of water flowing to eternal life" a. "Such was my mother, You being her intimate teacher in the secret school of her breast. Finally, already at the end of her temporal life, she won her husband for You, and in him, now faithful, she did not have to mourn what she had had to tolerate when she was unfaithful. She was the servant of your servants. Likewise, paganism and its culture left deep traces in Augustine's soul. Education in the 4th century included three grades: the first, school and elementary training, in which children learned to read, write, and count; The second, from twelve to sixteen years old, included the study of the Latin language, with a grammar teacher who made them read and analyze, above all, historians and poets; The third, from the ages of sixteen to twenty, covered rhetoric and philosophy. Augustine went through the three scholastic degrees in Tagaste, Madaura and Carthage. His cultural training was complete, according to the studies of that time, to which he brought his "celeritas intelligendi et disputandi aaimen". At the Tagaste elementary school he learned to read and count, getting used to the annoying chant: one and one, two; two and two, four. straps for punishment. primary school, Agustín manifested himself as a child with great intellectual hopes, and that is why his family decided to make him continue his studies, sending him to Madaura, a city about 30 kilometers away from Tagaste. Grammar, history, geography, metric art for Latin versification, music, mythology, were part of the studies of this period. One of the favorite authors was the poet Virgil. The Virgilian Aeneid was always an exquisite treat for Augustine's taste even as a boy and it exalted his imagination and creative faculties. At the same time, his sensitivity was awakened by the episodes of the great heroic poem. Especially the fourth book, which narrates the tragic passion of Dido and her death on the African coast, motivated by the escape of Aeneas, moved our young man to tears. When the teacher forced the students to reconstruct a psychological situation and improvise the words of a character, for example, Juno, angry at the arrival of the Trojans in Italy, Agustín received the most enthusiastic applause for his interpretation. The creative power of the greatest genius of the Christian West was already evident in him. The esteem that he always gave to the highest Latin poet contributed not a little to his appreciation, particularly in the Middle Ages, which considered the Aeneid, with all its fables, as an allegory of man's pilgrimage on earth, as John of Salisbury maintained in his Polycraticus. It is not easy to specify the entire contour of the classical culture of Saint Augustine. Without a doubt he read everything that passed through his hands, mostly the Latin classics, whose traces are recognized in his books: Virgil, Cicero, Sallust, Horace, Varro, Apuleius, Terence, Quintilian. In Madaura, the stories of Apuleius that bear the title of Golden Donkey were undoubtedly the object of particular preference. "They were for him what the novels of Jules Verne are for young French people" J1. From the Greek authors he knew Homer, although the difficulty of understanding his language sprinkled the softness of the Greek fables like gall, according to the Saint. He read very little of Aristotle, perhaps the Perihermeneias and the Topics, and he knew Plato through his disciples, the Neoplatonists. But this knowledge of the classics of literature and philosophy was progressive, and should not be placed precisely in the period of time just indicated. P. GOILLOÜX, The soul of S. After completing his secondary studies in Madaura, and after a year's vacation in Tagaste, in 370 or at the beginning of 371 he was sent to Carthage to study eloquence, a profitable career at that time in the Roman Empire and its colonies, because it was the best path to fortune and glory. In Africa, "nursery of lawyers," according to Juvenal, the art of well-speaking was ardently cultivated, and Augustine was endowed with wonderful dispositions for that profession. Carthage was then a great capital—splendidissima Cartilago—, proud of its history, its monuments, its luxury and commerce, its power and pleasures. Paganism had its headquarters with a fervent cult of the celestial goddess Tanit or Carthaginian Venus. The young provincials went there to follow the higher course of rhetoric and obtain the title of professors and teachers 12. The great city, saturated with a lascivious and tempting perfume, soon seduced the stranger. A love of theater was awakened in him, which was one of the favorite entertainments of the Carthaginians. On the contrary, the bloody scenes of the circus disgusted him. During his four years in Carthage, Agustín took advantage of the time to continue his intellectual training. He was, above all, a self-taught person who by himself assimilated the science of his time. He read a lot not only in books, but in the great school of life and his own heart. Then, when he was about twenty years old, he read Aristotle's Categories, and understood them perfectly without the help of teaching 13. He aspired not only to the mastery of the external and elegant word in saying, but also to the nourishing substance of ideas, because he never paid for verbal vanity, delving into the knowledge of the liberal arts, later included in a vast encyclopedic plan of Christian culture, which he began to develop in the retreat of Casiciaco. Classical culture imprinted its mentis form on Augustine, it opened his eyes to the vision of what was real and objective, at the same time that it put in his hands the instrument of an imperial and Catholic language. However, he laments that period of forgetfulness of God, because "what good did it do me if I, evil and slave of my evil appetites, had read for myself and understood all the books I could on the so-called liberal arts? And I took pleasure in them and did not know where everything that was true and true came from.

TWO CITIES AND TWO LOVES

Carthage and Milan are the two most intimate cities of the Augustinian soul. If we reduce the substance of Augustine's pilgrimage to a double experience and discovery of love and charity—eros and agape—, as Milan was the city of the encounter with the redeeming charity of God, Carthage means in his life the encounter with human love, double-edged and aspiration: towards the earthly and the heavenly, or the ideal of wisdom, with which reading the Hortensius inflamed him. This is what some call the first Augustinian conversion. "I had an endearing hunger for the inner maintenance that is You, my God" ls. With the tremor of puberty, Agustín felt a new fervor of the intimate being, which struggled to overflow from its own glass. Young, ardent and communicative, he needed to unite with another soul to pour into her all the treasure of his youth and the deep, sweet tenderness of his soul. To love and be loved was his aspiration. Love was presented as an urgent imperative of donation and enjoyment, without the scrupulous discrimination of higher motives, which give enhancement and decorum to human friendship. And so he fell into the soft captivity of feminine beauty. But in the vital drive of that fiery, first-time love there was perhaps as much spirit as flesh. Augustine did not lose the elasticity for other delicate experiences, nor the virile strength of the spirit, nor a certain dark virginal longing, which made him sigh for a life of greater cleanliness and decorum: "Give me chastity and continence, but not now," he used to say to God 1G. But until we get here, how much fatigue and feverish agitation, how many deceptions and disappointments! After a failed attempt to read the holy books, whose humble style struck him in the face, he fell into the snare of some superbly delirious men, in whose mouths were traps of the devil and a malicious and sticky sweetness, made with the words of the name of Christ. The promise of a rational conception of the world was the bait with which they caught Augustine, who did not want to submit to any creed, but rather sought a rational system of certainties, of clear truths, supported by reason. "Oh truth, truth! How deeply did the core of my soul sigh for You then when those men made Your name resonate in my ears, frequently and in many ways, with only their voice and with many and great books!" 21 "And they continually said: "Truth, truth! "; and without ceasing they spoke to me about her; and the truth was never in them" 2! Yo. The promise of a sincere and naked truth seen with the eyes of reason; the apparent contradictions, which they gloried in finding in the Holy Scripture, for example, in the genealogies of Christ according to Saint Matthew and Saint Luke; the hope and the rush to reach a scientific vision of nature, its phenomena and laws; the origin of evil, explained with the metaphysics of the two principles; the hypocritical austerity of the sect's teachers; Ethical fatalism, which annulled all human responsibility, relieving the moral weight of guilty conscience and legitimizing all movements of sensuality, were part of winning over Monica's son, impatient and eager for the truth. But at the bottom of this adhesion there was, above all, a deep need, a vital vehemence, a dull restlessness, which at all costs aspired to the harmony of a solution. Agustín was thirsty, and he had to quench his thirst in the first stream that came into view. He himself compares the artifice of the Manichaeans with that used by hunters to catch unsuspecting birds: they cover the course of the mountain streams, and, leaving some small pool free, they place branches around it.

fallen, so that the birds, drinking there, remain trapped in the league: ut non electione, sed inopia decidant s\ Such was the tactic of the Manichaeans: they covered the pure spring of Catholic Truth with their slander, presenting it as superstitious, full of contradictions, lacking reason. Scared from drinking at the fountain, Augustine's soul threw itself into the murky Manichean backwater, remaining imprisoned in his dualistic conception of the universe. The problem of evil found an easy and apparently satisfactory solution in the doctrine of Manes. All beings in the world offer an identical structure in their composition: matter, the plant and animal kingdom, man, are composed of a double divine and substantial element, one coming from the principle of good and the other from the principle of evil. God is a Corpus lucidum et immensum, et ego frustum de tilo corpore: God is an immense and luminous body, and man is a portion of it. Souls are also composed of luminous and dark particles, to which are attributed, respectively, clear ideas, noble feelings, clear reflections or dark thoughts, cloudy passions, irritation, envy, anger, lust. In the autumn of the year 383, Augustine crossed the Mediterranean Sea for the first time to settle in Rome with a more peaceful exercise of his profession. But shortly after arriving he fell seriously ill, and, convalescing, he began his teaching to reap a new disappointment, because if the students of Carthage were too rowdy, those of Rome did not pay; and, when the time came to do so, they passed on to other teachers. Augustine, then, having achieved the official title of Prefect, which was Symmachus, in the autumn of the year 384, began his new teaching period in Milan. Thus begins the period of religious metaphysics and inner experience. Augustine glimpses the peak of Platonic idealism, "a fundamental truth that can never be extinguished. It is the conviction that there is a kingdom of truth beyond the whims of men, that truths have a value independent of our consent, that their empire is at a heavenly height above human opinion and desires. Egoism, in its double form of sensuality and pride, was the dead weight with which his spirit braced itself to rise from the state of abjection in which it groaned. And through a healthy experience he knew how much goes from presumption to confession, and the misery "of those who see where they should go, but do not see where", and the path that leads to the beatific homeland, which must not only be from the naked eye, but also inhabited from within. Neoplatonism proposed union with God as a condition of perfect happiness, and Augustine had to wrestle with this active and contemplative problem. But there are only two ways of union with God: either by raising the lower to the higher and embracing it, or by descending the higher to man to embrace him and lift him up with himself. Neoplatonism proposes the first solution, appealing to man's effort to detach himself from the sensible and unite with his principle. Christianity teaches the second: the descent of God to the creature; that is, humility or divine humanity is the principle of human ascension or deification. Because God has descended to the depths of man's misery, he can ascend to the palace of divine happiness. And the humility of God is what Saint Augustine did not find in the books of the Neoplatonists nor will ever be found in the books of pure reason. And she was the path of new life. Augustine wanted to move and ascend to God, but the heaviness of his pride and sensuality immobilized him in the mire of selfishness.
Only the eyes—two eyes like two suns—, transcending the sensible, could weakly follow the distant glimpse of infinite beauty.

In the Dialogues there is hardly any Christianity; everything is art and philosophy, with a mystical tinge derived from Neoplatonism. Augustine in Cassiciacus is not simply a neophyte of Neoplatonic philosophy, but also a Christian, a convert in the religious and biblical sense of the word. But conversion entails a profound psychological change, the discovery of a new realm of values, the passage from an inferior state to a more perfect one, the regression to the principle of whoever It has separated the rational creature by a guilty deviation, the renewal of the internal being, which becomes broader and more solid. It is not mere contemplation, but action and contemplation at the same time. To describe the Augustinian conversion, these words seem written: "A conversion involves three stages: first, a previous state of dispersion and grace. disorder; second, an intermediate state of crisis; third, a state of order and unity in the soul" GS. The three stages have an extraordinary highlight in the conversion of Saint Augustine. The psychology of intimate dispersion, the crisis and the solution, as well as the state of spiritual balance, achieved by union with God, find in the Confessions the most picturesque formulas of expression and content. What partly gives the conversion of Saint Augustine an aspect of homogeneous evolution is the multitude of ancient elements incorporated into the synthesis of life Thus, in Casiciaco the ideal of the ancient wise man remains tense and the central knot of Platonic thought perseveres. That is, in conversion there is a phenomenon of continuity and another of rupture, noticed by those favored with the grace of God. Thus Theodore de la Rive writes: "By entering the Church I did not break with my ancient faith, but I completed it, I perfected it, giving it what it always lacked: a solid foundation and a superior sanction. He rejected the Protestant part of Protestant Christianity and retained the Christian part, which is the true part" 6 • Conversion does not mean, therefore, an absolute void of the old and the beginning of a new plenitude.

Human Augustine does not disappear under Christian Augustine. Augustine, loaded with the best treasures of ancient wisdom, does not have to shed them when passing through the door of the Catholic Church. The old gold will come in handy for the chalices and candelabra of the new temple of the Lord. But from this fact it does not follow that there has not been a radical change in the aspirant to the new faith, as if the scene in the Milan garden had not occurred. A profound change has been made in Augustine, and that is why we can speak of true conversion. Firstly, a change in ideas, because he has adhered to Christianity in what he found most repugnant when he was a disciple of Plato: the Incarnation of the Son of God. Dialogues and Confessions agree on this point. Neoplatonism did not teach him the humility of the Word of God, and for the same reason it was powerless to cure him of his pride. The change of ideas was slow and progressive. It cannot be specified when he discarded the error or heresy of Photinus on the Incarnation and embraced the Catholic truth™. Without a doubt, this was a reason for the delay in the conversion. Secondly, there was a change of affections, of the general estimation of life, previously directed to the earthly and now moved by a force superior to the celestial and eternal. In many cases the two changes are distinguished: a religious conviction can be anticipated without the will immediately following it, because affect—tardus affectus n, Saint Augustine would say—does not have the same lightness as thought. In our convert, the change of will consisted in the conquest of "a strong and entire will", that is, in a phenomenon of unification of what was previously dispersed. The various tendencies were reduced to unity by a superior power.

Saint Augustine is a great mixed genius of action and contemplation, burned by the supreme interest of saving souls. Contemplation is married in him with a vigilant love in the service of the Christian community. Such is the fundamental law of Christianity. His geniuses and his religious heroes, dedicated to probing the world of the spirit, are those who have worked the most for the brothers to improve and exalt their earthly existence, because holiness engenders a double bond of union with God and men. The Saint is not antisocial, but rather the most cordial and human of men, the one who wants to transform and deify them to offer them to Christ as trophies of his power. This law regulated the life of Saint Augustine. Incorporated into the Church by baptism, he knew how to be, like few others, universal and Catholic for his thought, for his love and his action for the Christian and human community. Having received baptism, the Saint began his return to his homeland, stopping in Ostia Tiberina to embark. And there Saint Monica separated from her beloved son. Once her wishes were fulfilled, no ties held her on earth, and she could easily soar into eternity. Separated from the noise of the world, they were one day looking out of a window that overlooked a garden, conversing with each other with great sweetness about the Light of truth present in their souls, and they had the joy of drinking in the streams of the divine spring, because, gradually ascending the ladder of creatures, they arrived at that region of abundance where the Lord feeds his people with the pabulum of truth. And in that tasty conversation, the mother said to the fruit of her tears: "As for me, nothing delights me in this world; there was only one thing for which I wanted to linger a little in it, and that was to see you a Catholic Christian before I died. God has more than crowned this desire of mine, for I see you as his servant, with absolute disdain for earthly happiness. What am I doing here?" \ A few days later he was attacked by fever and fell ill. laid down;

Augustine gave a Christian burial to his mortal remains, and after a return and not a very long stay in Rome, he sailed towards his country with Adeodatus and Alypius. Alii ivimus, et alii redivimus, the Saint would later say: He returned completely changed, that is, converted. In Tagaste, one of the first cares was to organize monastic life. The visit to the monasteries of Milan and Rome and the knowledge of ancient monasticism served as his orientation and guide. His monastic ideal, as P. de Monceaux well notes, comprised three elements: an ideal element, or the memory of the primitive community of Jerusalem, as described in the Acts of the Apostles; a network element, the memory of the monasteries visited in Italy; a persond element, his ancient ideal of asceticism and common life, associated with retirement and study in the company of other lovers of wisdom. From the combination of the three elements, the ascetic program of Saint Augustine was born. Alienated from the small patrimony, with some of his old friends and recent postulants, he formed the first monastery in Tagaste with a life of prayer, study, penance and good works. Living for God: such was the ideal of Saint Augustine and his companions. The asceticism of the ancient monks was softened with a program of culture and apostolate, and the great Augustinian candelabra began to shine for the benefit of souls. LEGACY OF THE POOR A most pleasant task for Saint Augustine was attention and mercy towards the poor. He has been one of the most ardent propagandists of the evangelical and supernatural theology of the poor, a patient member of Christ on earth. "Give, therefore, to the poor, he says in a sermon; I beseech you, I admonish you, I order you, I command you. I do not want to hide from you the reason for this exhortation. At the church door, as I enter and leave, the poor assail me, begging me to preach on alms. And they have begged me to tell you about this; and when they are disappointed and do not receive what they expect, they say that I work in vain. They also receive something from me. I give them what I have, I help them as I can; but not enough to remedy their needs. And because my assets are short for this, I speak to you, my brothers, as a legacy of the poor. You already know it, then; I see signs of approval; thanks be to God; The seed has fallen on good soil, your gestures say it." 2S. "The central idea, the key that opens the intelligence of thought, of the vision of the world and of the philosophy of the Middle Ages, is the belief that the world is a cosmos, a whole ordered according to a plan, a whole that moves calmly according to eternal laws and arrangements, which, born with the first principle of God, also have their final reference in God. Saint Thomas Aquinas, the greatest spirit of those who shaped the medieval idea of the world, considers that the purpose of philosophy consists of in anima describatur totus ordo universi et causarum eius: in impressing on the soul the total order of the universe and its causes... The a priori confidence that in the world, everywhere limited, order reigns, constitutes the grandiose metaphysical optimism of the medieval world, against whose background moral pessimism stands out equally. This metaphysical optimism, this vision of universal order, also qualifies Augustinian thought, which contemplates the universe above all in its metaphysical connections. It is not hidden from me that there has been talk of the poverty of Augustinian ontology as a subsidiary of the Platonic one. But note that true ontology owes its most powerful lights to Christianity, which has illuminated Being by essence. Saint Augustine draws on Platonic thought, but also on the sovereign ontology of the Ego sum qui sum. He has rested his eyes on this definition of God with slow delight, and it has served him to draw the dividing line between the being of the creature and the Creator. positive of his own, the universe shone in his eyes with a new clarity and beauty, rescued from the ghost of the evil principle, which clouded his right understanding. The world was reintegrated into the sovereignty of a single principle, essentially good and creator of all goodness. All beings could now breathe a purer and freer atmosphere, because they were in the hands of God and not of a tyrant. Thus, the goodness of the universe is the fundamental and first truth of Augustinian thought, and rests on a vestigial or trinitarian structure, since every creature is a vestige of God, a trace of omnipotence, wisdom and infinite love. The fundamental principle of Augustinian ontology can, then, be stated in this way: "We Catholic Christians worship God, from whom come all good things, great and small; from Him comes every manner, whether great or small; from Him, every form or species, whether great or small; from Him, every order, whether small or great. For all things contain the greater good the more moderate, beautiful and ordered; and the less moderate, beautiful and ordered. These three things, I say, should be known: mode, form and order, as general goods, are found in all things made by God, both in the spiritual and in the corporeal. form and all order. Where these things are lavishly poured out, there are great goods; where they are scarce, goods are also diminished; where they are lacking, there is no good. Likewise, where these things shine, there are great natures; where they are bargained, natures are also poor, and where they do not exist, there is no nature. Here is a fundamental principle of Saint Augustine's ontology, which admits a general structure for all sec-

res, both spiritual and material, showing a predilection for the ternary—modus, species, ordo—, because he contemplates the universe as a vestige of God, revealer of eternal and absolute values. His religious genius is never satisfied with the relative and seeks the sphere of the absolute even in the created. The mode, then, the species and the order are constitutive categories, that is, ontological. As one ascends the scale of beings, these elements are enriched with new content and excellence. Thus, the species in the soul is the idea, the art, the doctrine, the illumination, and the order or weight means the love of delight, the appetite for good, the moral order. The entire bundle of ontological properties of beings is thus enclosed in the vestigial ternary: being, unity, form, distinction, beauty, variety, truth, limitation, ordering to a purpose.

Creatures, with their incessant changes, imitate, in a certain way, the richness of the divine Being. Their intrinsic purpose is their own perfection and that of the universe, of which they are a part: ut perficiantur. Achieving a degree of excellence and perfection through the development of all its powers, so that the Creator is glorified in them: such is the meaning of everything created. Once this goal is achieved, they grow old and die, because they no longer have interest: intereunt. That is why the modus implies a certain idea of perfection and plenitude: "The excessive and the scarce are things contrary to each other. The scarce has less than what is convenient; the excessive supposes more than what is convenient. In the middle of the extremes is the mode, that is, what is sufficient: horum in medio modus est, quod dicitur sat est" 14. Every being, then, entails within itself a certain autarky or sufficiency, or if you want, a plenitude of qualities that adapt it to its end or destiny. A tree, because it is made in the right way, has nothing more or less, neither lacks nor excess; what is convenient for his birth, development and maturity he has received from his Principle. Everything conforms to a wise and diligent plan. The way, like the measure, leads to order, since only a perfect intelligence can adjust so many elements to a complex plan, without anything being missing or superfluous. The last words of Saint Augustine relate the modus with the measurement, which is the first ontological pair of the constitution of beings.

In the order of Nature, Saint Augustine contemplates three things: the series of causes concatenated among themselves, the work and reflection of reason and the kingdom of ends. In the book On Order he pursues these ideas and the philosophical conviction that nothing is done without cause, without order and without end in the universe, because divine Providence subjects everything to a necessary order of things: necessario rerum ordine includitw ", even moral evil. He was already familiar with this thought in the first philosophical and religious reflections, which is well condensed in the following passage: In everything that exists, one thing is that of which it consists, another is what discriminates it from the rest, and another is what makes it convenient. Saint Augustine has not maintained an occasionalist or romantic ideology of Nature, because there is room for secondary causality in his conception of the world. The first Principle works in natural things in three ways: creating, preserving and concurring with second causes to bring them to the perfection of their development. And the Saint clearly excludes the two extremes, which must be avoided in this matter: one, which diminishes the rights of God, and another, which diminishes those of the creature. There are those who believe that the universe was created by God, and then, left to itself, it produces all things, without Him acting in anything. To such we must remember—says the Saint—what is said in the Gospel: Pater meus usque moda operatur, et ego operor. Let us believe, then, and understand that God still works, so that if He subtracted His operation from things, they would crumble into nothingness." The opposite extreme consists in maintaining that God formed creatures in such a way that He in no way included in their original condition the constitutive elements of their nature, and this also contradicts the scriptural passage where it is said that God finished His works on the sixth day. IS IT ME, MY GOD?

In the eyes of Saint Augustine, man has always been presented as an enigma and great miracle: magnum miraculum. His anthropology is permeated with admiration, with self-strangeness. When in the Confessions he asks this passionate question: What am I, then, my God, and what is my nature?, he does so moved by an urgency and thirst for knowledge of the human mystery. The central questions of Augustinian philosophy are intertwined with that of man. What, then, is man, in his essence and process? Two great currents of ideas, but influenced by his own experience, influence the anthropology of Saint Augustine, as well as that of Western culture: the biblical and Pauline current of man, the image of God and being fallen into guilt, and the Greek current of homo rationalis, or animal moved by an interior verb, in which all his highness and dignity are encrypted. Following the logical direction of the vestigial ternary pointed out in the previous article, the mode, the species and the order illuminate the human being and its ontological position and relationship with creatures. The mode expresses its dualistic composition, the unity of the compound, the contingency of its being, its finitude, its relative perfection; The species includes its entire rational or cognitive life, for which it is not only a human species, but also a species of species or form of forms, insofar as they are all entailed and stored in memory. Order and weight prioritize its multiple elements through love or gravitation to the center, which is God. The three general goods, distributed in the universe, enhance the very external fabric of man, in whose body there is a certain mass of flesh and beauty of form, and the order and distinction of members and moderation of health: quaedam moles carnis, et formae species, et ordo distinctionis et temperatio valetudinis'.

Here Augustinian optimism shines again against the pessimistic conception of the Gnostics and Manichaeans: the body does not have a diabolical origin nor is it a mass of corruption. "It is false, it is heretical, it is blasphemous to say that: because of the body and the soul there is only one Artificer. I want everything to be healthy, because I am everything. I do not want my flesh, as a strange thing, to be separated from me forever, but for everything to be healed with me: ut mecum tota sanetur." "Not even the body is a prison, in which the soul has been confined to purge ancient sins, as the Platonic myth supposed. Augustine, commenting on biblical passages, uses the word prison, not in an ontological sense, but in a moral one, or as equivalent to corruption: Ergo si caro carcer est, non corpus est carcer tuus, sed corruptio corporis tui. Corpus enim tuum fecit Deus bonum, quia bonus est4. This is the privileged situation of man, due to the excellence of his soul; It is found between the abysses: the infinite abyss of God and that of formless matter, which is almost nothing: prope nihil. Its greatness and excellence lies in proximity to God; its misery, in its connection with matter. The distance between matter and spirit is hierarchically bridged. That is to say, Saint Augustine, without admitting the Platonic trichotomy or splitting the personal unity of man, intercalates, between the upper portion and the lower portion, connecting powers, whose purpose is to establish contact between the two. The senses, both external and internal, and the appetites, or consequent tendencies, belong to the lower part, of which man is composed. There is no dualism, but an order of hierarchy, although in the current state of fallen man the relationships are disturbed, as we will see. That is why man is subject to a double law of polarity, since he obeys natural and psychophysical laws, and as a spiritual subject or mind, to laws of reason. Both portions are two windows or openings that tear the hermeticism of the human being and give it a double orientation: one towards the sensible and temporal, the other towards the invisible and eternal. Through the lower senses and appetites he relates to the natural world, and through the mind and will, to the invisible and superior, being a citizen of two worlds and occupying a middle point, a horizon between eternity and time. Saint Augustine has defended the value of the testimony of the senses and sensible experience, without which man would be a larva of spirit with no natural possibility of growth. The spiritual pilgrimage of Saint Augustine can be summarized in these words of his great disciple Saint Bonaventure: Domine, exivi a te summo, et venio ad te summum per te summum,... Et sic eris verus metaphysicus: Lord, I came from you supreme, I come to you supreme and for you supreme... This is all our metaphysics: of emanation, of exemplarity, of consummation, that is, being illuminated by spiritual rays and reduced to the supreme. And thus you will be a true metaphysician \ The divine is the atmosphere of the genius of Saint Augustine, because in the created universe he only sees vestiges, shadows, winks of infinite Wisdom, which make him return and ascend to the supreme and exemplary Cause of all that exists. The idea of ​​God illuminates the Augustinian conception of the world. Knowing God is the most joyful and profitable occupation of the spirit, because He is the value of values, the supreme Good, in whom the human heart is stilled. The dialectic of Augustinian culture is moved internally by this impulse of knowledge of God, which is a soteriological impulse or the salvation of the soul, that is, the deepest impulse that submoves man. These passages have served as the basis for the proof of the existence of God, based on the degrees of beings. But Saint Augustine, more than to prove existence, strives for the conquest of a concept as far as possible adequate to divine greatness and supereminence. It is an analytical process that, starting from the contemplation of the various degrees of good, distributed among beings, ends in an absolute good without limit or measure. Because each created good contains a positive and a negative aspect in its being, a sum of utilities or excellences, but mixed with imperfections. By affirming God's pure essence of good and removing all limits and imperfections, we will forge a concept of God that is more or less close, but always very distant from divine reality. The immaculate cognition, which Nietzsche postulated, does not belong to this world. God always escapes from our hands and from the most complicated network of our concepts. That is why thought must transcend itself in the search for God. There is no idea adequate to the divine Being, because all our funds come to us on loan from the world of the senses or the spirit. He did not want a religion of authority, but of reason, because he was attracted to üuminism. The disillusionment caused by the interview with Fausto and, as a consequence, the failure of the dualist system, began to cure him of rationalism. But his ideal of truth subsisted; He aspired to wisdom, to a totally rational understanding of things, and mathematical certainty presented itself to his spirit as the perfect type of knowledge. Knowing everything that two and two make four and that the radii of a circle are all equal: here is true science. But the rationalist illusions gave way little by little, and with a more serene vision of human life, all supported by faith and tradition, he recognized the primacy of belief, whose value he ponders in the booklet De utilitate credendi. Pure reason is not enough to live rationally, because authority is also a form of reason that must be attended to. Saint Augustine made his way through the tangle of errors and difficulties until he discovered the church of Christ, the domestic refuge of his spirit, eager for eternal truth. He started from a point different from that of the Greek Fathers, insisting in particular on the intimacy and immanence of divine processions and ruining subordinationism on its basis. At the same time, it avoided all modalism and the explanation of the real plurality of the divine persons was made clearer by the doctrine of relations. By illuminating the inner life of God, it also provided a deep look at the being of the human spirit, an analogical bridge that comes closest to the unity mystery of God. The psychological trinity - mens, notitia, love - introduces the rational creature to the glimpse of the secret infinite life of God. To complete the theological features of Saint Augustine I will briefly refer to his "kerygmatic" or preaching theology. H. Rahner has attempted to give it its own organization and consistency, as a diverse scientific branch of theology born from the priestly impulse of our time: that of applying dogmatics to Christian life, disseminating it among the faithful. Experience has shown that scholastic theology is poorly adapted for this purpose, because it is inaccessible to the majority of Christians. "Kerygmatic" theology seeks a way to communicate and extend the content of theological speculation in preaching 66. Preaching, "kerygma", is a theological moment of primary importance, as is hearing. Until the divine word becomes theology, in the systematic sense, it goes through various stages. In its first moment it is verbum Dei, a word, revelation or locution of God, who manifests himself to man as if removing a veil that hides him from mortal eyes.

He conceives the pastoral teaching as a paternal and vital function of the ecclesiastical body. Dogmas are milk and bread for the faithful, and he is in charge of distributing those provisions to the members that make up the mystical body. There is no Christian life without dogma and no dogma that does not respond to two vital needs of the human spirit: one for usefulness, the other for beauty. Dogma is a living force and matter of contemplation. The Trinity, the elevation of the creature to the state of grace and friendship with God, original sin, the Incarnate Word, the magnificence of the Redemption, the deification of men, the beauty of the mystical body, the sacraments, the very new: everything in the hands of Saint Augustine is transmuted into soft and hot bread, into pure milk to be given to the little ones of Christ. The theology of preaching needs, above all, two things: the strength of the spirit and the strength of the word. The word of God without the spirit of God loses its supernatural courage and becomes the cold tinkling of the human voice. Likewise, the word of God without the faithful consortium of the human word, its artistic resources, its expressive power, becomes dull and useless. Saint Augustine, as a saint and extremely skilled rhetorician, has combined the two forces with an inimitable technique. Only a genius of "kerygmatic" theology can say to his listeners after having preached so much: Fatigatos vos nunquam sentio. I never notice tiredness in you; Despite that, God knows that I fear being burdensome to you. Fill me with joy to see you receive the divine word with such pleasure that your enthusiasm in coming to hear me surpasses the passion that drives fools to the theater. Because the transition from one to the other is easy, its use in religious and popular propaganda enjoys so much value. It is therefore convenient to know the great spiritual Master of Europe. Let us first eliminate certain interpretations that disfigure their spirituality, which has been branded, for example, as being excessively selfish. The same reproach is repeated in the Protestant camp against Catholic piety. Saint Augustine is moved by the force of eros more than agape. Eros and agape mean two tendencies rooted in love. Eros, according to the Platonic myth, is the son of poverty and need, and moves man to look for what he lacks, to satisfy his desires, his hunger and restlessness. The erotic is considered as an interested impulse that harms the purity of the spirit. Agape is the complete opposite; not an acquisitive movement, like that of eros, but a donation. He does not seek his own interest, but that of others; He does not want to receive, but rather offer what he has. Agape means oblation, descent into the realm of misery to alleviate it selflessly, without any selfish goal. It is the generous affection of the rich towards the poor, of God towards men, without any advantage of its own. It does not set any limit between the worthy and the unworthy, between the just and the sinners 7. According to some, Augustinian spirituality is essentially motivated by eros, by the pure interest of subjective satisfactions. Saint Augustine seeks the complete harmony of his being, enriching himself internally to enjoy himself. Above all, he intends to build a wide and rich house to live and enjoy. This concept of Augustinian spirituality is one-sided and wrong. In a spirit as complex as that of Saint Augustine, "the richest soul of the Christian West", according to T. Haecker, one cannot go to a brief discrimination of elements. His soul cannot be dissected. Augustinian and Christian spirituality are internally animated by eros and agape together. It is neither pure interest nor pure disinterest, but disinterested interest and interested disinterest. He is not formulaic like Kant or utilitarian like Spencer. Agape—says Nygren—ist die originóle Gmndkonzeption des Christenturnss. It is the fundamental conception of Christianity, which reads like this: God is charity. Not eros, but charity, agape. The love of God is sovereign, independent of all external motives. For a profound qualification of these two impulses, see A. NYGREN, uros8 und Ágape (Gütersloli 1930). O. c, p.31. This psychology says the following: there are only three human opinions in which fundamental attitudes towards God, man and the world are really manifested. Pascal indicates Epictetus, Montaigne and the Church as their representatives. Here is also a profound psychology of human spirituality in its essential aspects. Life can only be lived in three ways: as an Epicurean, as a Stoic or as a Christian. Materialism, idealism, Christianity embody three ways of life, whose ideals are pleasure, virtue of the soul and God. Saint Augustine lived all three solutions. He was active in the school of Epicurus, seeking happiness in delight, in comfort, in the joys of human friendship and the plastic and literary arts. Neoplatonism separated him from materialism, by opening his eyes to a higher world of beauty, but it filled him with pride, which is the attitude of the Stoic, of the man who places beatitude aspiring in the perfect calm of his desires. They believe, says Saint Augustine, that the sick soul can heal itself: aegrotum animum a seipsis sanari nosse crediderunt1. Man is a doctor and savior of himself. Both solutions are contrary to the spirit of Christianity. On this point, Saint Augustine delivered a sermon in Carthage where he confronted the Epicurean, the Stoic and the Christian with his diverse spirituality. The speaker starts from a universal fact: the desire for happiness: appetitío beatae vkae. The important thing is to know what makes a man blessed. And here the trivia of philosophers and even of men is presented: happiness is constituted by either material pleasure, or the virtue of the soul, or the gift of God. The materialistic solution ultimately leads to despair. It is a fundamental law of the spirit that the disordered spirit is the executioner of itself I9. Pleasures sprinkle life with the most bitter wormwood, as the great disillusionment of Taso Gaste says. The Stoic solution cannot be accepted either. "You are among those who desire virtue, among those who place hope in man. Virtue delights you; you put your happiness in good things. I know it very well: you are thirsty; but virtue cannot flow from yourself. You are a dry well. If I point out the source to you, perhaps you will burst out laughing and say: - Shall I drink from that Rock?

But the rod came near to the Rock, and the living spring sprung up. The Jews ask for miracles, but you, Stoic, are not a Jew; I know, you are Greek, and Greeks seek wisdom. You no longer mock; You recognize the cross in the wand, the fountain in Christ, and if you thirst, drink virtue. Be satisfied at the fountain of Christ. Weren't you looking for virtue? Cry out, then: You are my virtue, Lord. Didn't you want the blessed life? For blessed is he whom you teach. Blessed are the people who do not put their end in the delight of the senses or in the virtue achieved with their strength, but blessed are the people whose Lord is. WOOL AND LINEN DRESS

The unbreakable connection of Augustinian spirituality with Christ supposes another that is derived from it: the union with the Church. The Christian spirit is born, develops and perfects in the maternal womb of the mystical Body. The spirituality of Saint Augustine is ecclesial and overcomes all contradiction between the internal and external elements of Christian life, which is nourished by two vegetative poles: one intimate, in contact and immediate relationship with God, and another external, linked to a visible, hierarchical organization, vicarious of Christ and continuator of his work of salvation. Saint Augustine is, without a doubt, one of the great architects of interiority in the Christian soil of the West; but it has not prevented him from submitting to external and organized discipline. I will say with his allegorical language that he wears a woolen dress and a linen dress. He says when explaining the passage of the strong woman in Proverbs: "You ask me what wool means and what linen means. The first means something carnal and external; the second, the intimate part of our life. I adopt this explanation because woolen dresses are worn on the outside; linen ones are worn on the inside. Everything we do with the body is visible; what is done with the spirit remains hidden. Working with the flesh and not with the spirit is of no use; just as working with the spirit and not with the body is typical of lazy people. Saint Augustine, with his word and his pen, has been one of the greatest propagandists of religious culture in Europe. With this heading, then, we point, above all, to his catechetical work. The spread of the Gospel is based on the communication of some souls with others. The coals must not be separated from the central fire that burns in the hearth of the Church through the hearts of its apostles and priests. Communicative art has achieved great splendor and effectiveness in San Agustín. It was a vital necessity for him to expand with his parishioners with a cordial outpouring, into which he poured out the treasures of his soul. The inhabitants of Hippo, Carthage, Constantine, Caesarea, Hippo Dyarrhytus, Sinitum and Tagaste were the main witnesses of the eloquence and apostolic activity of the Saint. Veritas pañis est, he said '; The truth is the delicacy of the souls. It is a synthesis of science and wisdom. The Form, jormarum or the Word preserves its ontological and moral purity by embracing the corporeal or sensible world. Here Saint Augustine is very far from Plato, like a Christian from a pagan. The sensible world is sanctified and consecrated in Christ and becomes the object of a culture. And "if intellectual knowledge of eternal things belongs to wisdom, rational knowledge of temporal things belongs to science" 2S. The deepest reason for the existence of Christ and Christianity is to serve as a link to the eternal and temporal, because the temporal can only be illuminated with an eternal light. That is why Christ is the sum of science and wisdom. In it we touch the Word of life in an exchange of divine and human, eternal and historical clemencies. Saint Augustine is a valiant champion and defender of Humanity and Christian humanism, undermined by a system of ideas for which austere monks were spokespersons who boasted of going out under the jurisdiction of human rights. "The meeting of Saint Augustine with Pelagius," says J. Guitton, "begins a new epoch in his life. And a new epoch also for the religious thought of the West." As in the books on the Trinity, delving into one's own conscience, he outlined the metaphysics of personality, so in the anti-Pelagian polemic the anthropology of the Saint was rounded out with ideas that brought to the foreground of consciousness the relationships that bind man to Christ. Anthropology and Christology attract and complete each other in Augustinian thought. The Pelagians propagated an autonomous conception of the spirit and the world. God is not only a spectator, but an actor in the conscience of man. The fundamental support of the Pelagian system was stoicism, the morality of effort and tension to achieve the supreme good—ataraxia—in a purely natural order. GRACE AND HUMAN VALUES

But the action of grace also extends to a sphere of natural goods, rooted in the human being. It does not destroy, but perfects nature. The Augustinian doctrine is equidistant from the two extremes that can occur at this point: Manichaeism and Pelagianism. Extremely pessimistic, the first admits a substantial corruption of nature, where the action of the good and redeeming principle is not possible. The infected area of ​​evil cannot be touched by the grace of God. But Saint Augustine does not admit a total devastation of nature due to sin, but the real estate, which is man's heritage, continues to stand. Such are, for example, the powers that preserve their natural strength, the desire for happiness, the love of truth and goodness, the natural capacity to know God. Being capax Dei is also a radical good that has preserved the soul as the image of God. Grace is inserted into these goods to heal man and improve him internally. Pelagianism, essentially optimistic, sees everything rosy in the universe and in man. But it coincides with Manichaeism by denying the possibility of a saving influence on man through grace. Catholic and Augustinian doctrine, on the other hand, confesses the possibility, convenience and reality of divine action in fallen man. That the infinite Spirit enters the most intimate part of the finite person to awaken him, move him, elevate him and improve him is the most blessed and rational of all possibilities and realities. The entire nature is improved with this action and contact with the divine in man. Even natural values ​​are profitable. Grace saves nature. Grace and nature relate to each other, seek and complete each other. They are not destroyed, like two explosive forces, when they join, but rather they are solidly united with a bond that is beneficial for both parties. Medicine is not repugnant to nature: Medicina autem ideo inventa est ut pellatur vitium et sanetur natura. Ideo magnus Medicas venit5". Vice is the enemy and destroyer of nature, not the grace of medicine. The Christian does not repugn the human, but heals, completes and perfects it. Grace, according to Saint Augustine, not only brings a new excellence and way of being—filiation of God—with which the human being stands above the purely natural being.

X THE MYSTIC BODY OF CHRIST
THE DONATIST PARTY

Saint Augustine is the great teacher of Catholic ecclesiology, because he has taught us to understand Christianity and to live in intimacy with the mystical Body of Jesus. "The glory that we want to vindicate for Saint Augustine," says Batiffol, "is that of having made Catholicism not only an intelligence and a unity, but a mysticism, because no doctor like him had the affectionate intuition of the active presence of God in the Church." When he was consecrated bishop he found an Africa torn by schism, by the "pars Donati." Donatism had its sacraments, its cult, its hierarchical organization, its brave and dynamic body of supporters, who had fortified themselves against the true Church with a defensive system of apologetics and theology. The Church of Christ, according to them, had become temporary, surrendering itself into the hands of the public Power. His ministers became corrupt, becoming unclean vessels that could neither contain nor distribute the grace of God. Only a select minority was saved: Africa sola bene olet, totus mundus putet. The whole world is a sewer of corruption; Only in a small African corner does the garden of Christ flourish 2. The campaign against this error and in defense of the immaculate Bride of Christ occupied a large part of the literary activity of the great Doctor. He refined all the arts of persuasion and catechesis against schism: the doctrinal treatise, the tract, the dialogue, the poem with popular rhythm and chorus, the manifesto, correspondence of all kinds, the sermon, the conference and public discussion with stenographically reproduced verbal processes. He spread the epithet of Mater Ecclesia, which so often flows from his lips with a musical and tender lullaby. Defending the Church, he defended the spiritual Mother of man and the civilization of Europe. Donatism was a terrorist system that sought to dominate with violence. Their bosses professed subversive theories about the abolition of property and distribution

Supporting their ideas with evangelical passages, they appealed to looting, arson, and popular unrest, to the point of forcing the authorities to take repressive measures by force. In Hippo, the Donatist clergy forbade the sect's bakers from baking Catholic bread. A particular target of their viciousness was the Bishop of Hippo, who raised the flag of religious unity and civil order. More than once they shouted at him in the street: "Down with the traitor!" His violence and excesses forced the emperors to take part in the fight for the common good and security of public order. In the year 411, Catholics and Donatists met in Carthage, under the presidency of the tribune Marcellinus. The doctrinal program was summarized in these points, presented by Catholics: 1. The Church of God, announced by the prophets and preached by Christ, is universal, therefore the Catholic Church is the true one. 2.° She is made up of righteous and sinners, of good and bad, of grain and chaff. 3. The Donatists cannot prove that the Church, corrupted everywhere, is only preserved pure in the party of Donatus, because even assuming the unworthiness of Caecilian—a fact that cannot be demonstrated—he would not be enough to corrupt the Church or invalidate his baptism. With these points of extraordinary dogmatic importance the nature of the true Church was defined. Without speaking a word when it came to minutiae of procedures, since he reserved his performance for the nerve of the cause, incapable of being defeated by all the interruptions, upright, luminous, strong, endowed with an overflowing anointing, Augustine can be called without hyperbole the true winner of the conference" 3. There the Donatists were doctrinally and legally defeated.

As the Body of Christ, the Church displays certain divine traits that distinguish it from all false imitations. The true Bride enjoys an original and her own beauty, with which she leaves all claimants to the hand of Christ far behind. Saint Augustine has carefully studied the beauty and features of the Church in three portraits that we have of her: prophecy, the word of Christ and the doctrine of the apostles. In the book De imitate Ecclesiae the characters of the Bride of Christ are drawn as they are contained in the Old Testament, in the testimony of the Savior and the apostles. We have the divine books, whose authority is recognized on both sides; Let us look for the Church there, let us investigate our cause there. XI THE "CONFESSIONS" OR THE RELIGIOUS GENIUS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE
BOOK OF THE EPIPHANIES OF THE LORD

The Confessions are, without a doubt, the great definition of the soul of Saint Augustine, those that best adapt to his religious genius, as a fruit on par with understanding, heart and fantasy. They spread a fragrance of intimacy throughout Europe that had not been known until then. Classical antiquity remained sparing in declarations of individual conscience. Only Christianity, elevating the individual to a new category of excellence, made possible the literary flowering of the Confessions and Revelations. Ancient man lived subject to the rules of social coexistence, to the spirit of the polis. Christianity did not deny the social fact, but rather strengthened it from within, from the central core of the spirit, demanding a new man much richer and more interior, because the relationships with God were more cordial and intimate than in the ancient religious. This new man, trembling with passion and pathetic sincerity, stirs and moves in the Confessions. He can display his soul very well, like a romantic museum and like a hall of God, embellished with the beauty of all natural and supernatural gifts. Because that is what Confessions are: a prodigious exhibition of one of the most prodigious souls that the Creator has given to the world to show off his mercy and greatness. That small and worthy book, by illuminating the personal conscience of Saint Augustine, has illuminated the enigmas of God and man, since the Confessions are in the individual order what the City of God is in the collective and universal: a brilliant effort to clarify in the light of God the depths of one's own conscience and life. Both are books of the Lord's epiphanies. The City of God introduces order and meaning into the shapeless mass of the events of universal history. Where chaos reigned, a cosmos emerges, an organic whole in which the highest divine pedagogy shines, aimed at the salvation of man. The fatalistic conception of historical cycles is corrected, because the spirit, in contact with God, has been elevated to a new

form of existence, which produces original and very varied movements in the course of History. The human family moves toward a great destiny with the direction of divine Providence. But the land of one's own chaotic individuality was still unexplored, until Saint Augustine placed the ember of the fire of his genius there. Like universal history, each person's personal history is the theater of mysterious theophanies and, therefore, a sacred history with deep roots in the divine plan. What for others was a dry, cramped and sterile land, has become in the hands of Saint Augustine a perennial orchard, moist with penitential dew. The Augustinian genius sniffs out the footprints of the Lord, follows the trail and breathes the scent of Providence to discover his plans and clarify individual movements with the light of a general sense, with which they acquire unity and higher order. Individual consciousness has become an ordered universe, the small being geared to the whole of which it is a part through communication with God, who governs and gives meaning to all individual and collective processes. Such is one of the greatest merits of the author of the Confessions: having incorporated a dark zone into the cosmos, which is the life of an ineffabile individuum. The Saint has projected two lights upon it: that of God and that of his own soul. They are two enigmas that tire the great genius from the first to the last page. Already in the first chapter he opens our eyes to the double interior and superior panorama. "You are great, Lord, and praiseworthy beyond measure; your strength is great and your wisdom is without number. And a man, a vile part of your creation, presumes to praise you; a man who carries around him the rags of his mortality, who carries upon him the stigma of his sin and even the testimony that you resist the proud. And with all this a man, a vile part of your creation, presumes to praise you. You awaken him so that he may delight in praising you, for you made us for yourself and our heart is restless as long as it does not find rest in you." \ They strive here to bring to the surface a new theodicy and anthropology unknown to the ancients. That is why it is difficult to classify this book. It is certainly one of the most beautiful of the spiritual sciences, a sui generis type of religious philosophy.

The Augustinian conversion is also an internal conflict that reveals the depths of God and Satan. There is an impressive sensation of fallen man, that is, of man chained, servant of the power of passions. To feel this chain is to sense a bitter and elemental reality and at the same time feel the need and desire for redemption or form of a free and harmonious existence. The experiences of both events, chaining and thirst for redemption, form the primordial strata of the human being or the religious subject of the Concessions. The spiritual chain is expressed in them as a tearing apart of the being, as rebellion and automatism of the lower psyche. The indocility of the beastly herd of appetites is offered to the eyes by Saint Augustine with ruthless sincerity and nakedness. Because he had seen the servitude of captivity so face to face, it was easy for him to measure the depth of the Lord's grace, that is, the fact of redemption. Thus, the Augustinian man, moved by restlessness and passing through the region of misery and helplessness—regio egestatis—, through a very difficult conflict, reaches the last stages of his religious process: redemption and holiness. The true eigentliche Existenz, the existence that has found itself, is illuminated with the light of redemption. The history of man receives a consecration when he is rescued and united to the Savior. TWO MODERN ERRORS

In Augustinian speculation on the psychological trinity, two serious teachings shine, which contain the medicine for the errors of our time. I am referring to two antitrinitarian heresies, let's put it that way, a consequence of having destroyed the order of the internal hierarchy of the faculties. The one denies the excellence and value of the human word, the other the strength and dignity of the caritas. The one is a sin against the word, the other a sin against love. The first consists of a kind of psychological Arianism, which postpones and diminishes the logos with respect to the irrational elements of life. The human mind, as we have seen, generates its verb, its concept of itself, of God and of things, reproducing them in itself with an objective similarity, in which its truth consists. The human spirit has its prolific fertility, which makes it an image of the divine. These prerogatives are not recognized in much of modern philosophy. The question posed by Nietzsche: Should life dominate over science or knowledge over life? has been resolved by modern man, giving supremacy to life and origin to the vitalist, pragmatic, positivist and agnostic philosophies of our time. Life itself is considered the supreme development and perfection of intimate forces, at the service of ideals. The understanding, which works through abstract concepts, should not assume the direction of life, but rather the heart, the feeling, the instinctive impulses, the intuition of the concrete. Cold, analytical thinking has blocked the sources of life, ending in pure denial and stagnation. The new organ of intellection is not thought, but the heart, the feeling, the control of the appetites. Intelligence is sterile for truth and for life "\ This great philosophical heresy endangers life itself, because it immerses it in the blind current of instincts, it ignores the value of the hierarchy of faculties and their operations. It gives primacy to will and practice, postponing the faculty of forms and norms that is intelligence. The psychological organism is ordered in its faculties; the three terms of the trinity, analyzed by Saint Augustine in his books De Trinitate, are they state according to a law of priority and origin, the same as in the mystery they reflect. From what has been said, an important law is derived, which can be called the circularity of the spirit. The mind, as if fertilized by the very being of things, generates the word, and this produces love; but love, in turn, flows over the verb, over the amata notitia, and the charge of impulse towards the object it loves. Love wants to make its way and get involved with what it loves: Quanto quisque minus diligit, mucho pigrius movetur in via. The less one loves, the more lazily one travels the path of pilgrimage. The dialectical movement is animated by love. It is a current that circulates from the object to the thought, from the thought to the will. By virtue of the circuminsession that we have pointed out, each of the correlative terms is armed with an impetus of invasion over the other two, to which they essentially refer. The mind that knows and loves itself, by its own internal constitution, is constantly transported towards others. The knowable and lovable object communicates its substance to the concept, and the concept passes it on to the will, which is the organ of love; This is launched and bursts upon the object and its verb with an affectionate movement, in which the entire being vibrates with new longing for truth, light and joy. That is why an endless movement qualifies the religious dialectic of the spirit.

XIII THE CITY OF GOD OR THE DIALECTIC OF HISTORY

Saint Augustine is the creator of the City of God: this is an unmistakable feature of his genius. He was profound and original in the way he embraced History, ordering it in a unique plan, modeled by the thought of God. The City of God has not only been a hilltop for contemplation of History, but also a model for the organization of society. "After the Old and New Testaments, it is difficult to find a book whose influence on the development of the West has been greater than that of the City of God. It took part in the education of statesmen and thinkers of the Middle Ages from Charlemagne to Dante. By no theologian of antiquity was the Church studied with more penetration" \ That is why he has been called "the greatest theologian and sociologist of the Middle Ages" 2. It is also an encyclopedic book, "a librofloresta, since it contains an apologetics, a theology, a philosophy of History and a morality" 3. The medieval vision of History is determined by the City of God. Orosius, Otto" of Freising (De duabus civitatibus, 1158), Dante (De monarchia, 1321), Rupert of Deutz (1135) and Joachim of Fiore (1202) collect the speculative heritage of Saint Augustine to interpret historical events. In the Modern Age, Bossuet, with his discourse on universal history; the Count of Maistre, F. Schlegel and W. Soloviev will follow the inspiration and the Augustinian spirit. To these and other names can be added that of Vito Fornari, not as appreciated as it deserves. His voluminous Life of Jesus is a true philosophy of History, penetrated by a high Augustinian spirit. Vito Fornari sees the entire process of events in a Christological framework, and human culture offers what he calls preludes to Christ.

From what has been said, we can glimpse the vitality of the great work of Saint Augustine, one of the chapters of the philosophia perennis of Christianity and also of human culture. It does not matter that it contains many deciduous and withered elements, leaf litter due to the state of the historical culture of the 5th century. The City of God is an evergreen book of unfading greenery. "The philosophy of History," says Leo XIII, "was first devised and perfected by this great Doctor of the Church. Those who have come after him and have left traces worthy of memory in this field of study took Saint Augustine himself as their teacher and guide, drawing as much as they could from his speculation and writings. On the contrary, those who separated themselves from the footsteps of this great man fell into many errors, because in the investigation of the course and development of states they did not have the true understanding of the causes that moderate human events." 4. Such a categorical statement refers to the essential content of the doctrine of the City of God rather than to the support of evidence with which he supports his thesis, taken from the defective encyclopedia of his time. 2.

Saint Augustine, "prophet and philosopher of intuition", as H. Scholz calls him, applied for the first time to historical events the fundamental principles and truths of Christian metaphysics, introducing order and harmony into the chaos of human events, so disjointed, it seems, from a living organism. And the illumination of chaos, as always, comes from the Word from above, from a theological and teleological conception of the universe, of which History is an integral part. Saint Augustine does not illuminate the higher through the lower, as evolutionists do, for example, but rather the lower with the higher. The material world receives its light and meaning from the rational soul, and this from the Spirit of God. This is why the most fundamental thesis that circulates throughout the City of God is called providentialism. But the word providence and providentialism is a complex of ideas that offer various aspects, or if you want, moments of eternal and temporal order. God's exemplary causality encompasses everything, ab angelo ad vermiculum, from the highest seraph to the most insignificant worm on earth. His providence also extends usque ad passerum administrationem*. To the immutable plenitude of the divine Being belongs the eternal vision of the temporal, that is, the infinite science, in which all present times are found in a marvelous way. Foreknowledge does not impose any needs on free wills, as fate (fatum) did in pagan religion. The Gentiles could not conceive or harmonize divine foreknowledge with human free will. On this topic, the author of the City of God polemicizes with Cicero, whose reasoning sounds like this: "If there is foreknowledge of everything future, things must happen in the order in which they are known: if in such an order they are to be verified, it is certain for God that he knows the order of things, and since the order of things is certain, the order of causes is equally true, because nothing can be verified without a sufficient cause preceding it, and assuming a certain causal order to which everything that happens, all things, is due. They are subject to fate. There is, therefore, no place left for our power nor is there human free will. Cicero finds himself caught between the horns of the dilemma. To admit a God who is aware of the future is to mutilate man and society of a necessary organ: freedom, without which there is no morality or legal order. Consciousness did not allow him to make this painful amputation to the human organism. On the other hand, to admit the undeniable fact of human freedom, the postulate of all justice, is to deprive God of all knowledge of free futures, to mutilate him in his absolute science. But between a one-armed God or a one-armed man, he preferred the former. The Ciceronian God is a diminished god, that is, an idol. "But we, against these impious assertions, maintain both things, and say that God foresees everything, before it happens, and that we freely act everything that we know and feel to do as voluntary beings. We do not admit a fate that does everything, but rather we confess that nothing is the effect of fate. And the order of causes, where the will of God can greatly influence, we neither deny nor designate with the name of fate.
Nor is there any consequence in this reasoning: If the causal order is true for God, the action of our free will is nullified. For our very wills are in the order of causes, which

It is true for God and encompasses it with his foreknowledge, because human wills are the cause of human works: quoniam et humanoe voluntates humanorum operum causae sunt'. Therefore, both facts must be agreed upon: divine foreknowledge and free will. A God ignorant of the future is not God: qui enim non est praescius omnium juturorum, non est uttque Deus \ The foresight of a free fact does not diminish the freedom of the one who performs it, nor is a memory an efficient cause of what is remembered. With providence and free will, the double causal order that originates the course of human events is enthroned in History. Two errors must therefore be avoided in the interpretation of Augustinian thought: on the one hand, what I. Gentile calls "il fatalismo theologico providenziale" \ The Christian concept of God excludes fatum, submission to a causal order independent of divine sovereignty itself. Saint Augustine is neither a fatalist nor a determinist, but a Christian providentialist whose theological sense is repugnant to any mutilation in the supreme Being. Another extreme of false interpretation consists of denying the intervention of free will or secondary causes in the development of history. L. Dempf admits such a strange exegesis: "God's monergism, his absolute and exclusive intervention in the salvation of man, is so unlimited that man's cooperation is reduced to a mere "as if" of his freedom" 10. But this interpretation is unfair to Saint Augustine, mirror of Christian orthodoxy, and to the many Roman Pontiffs who have exalted his doctrine. Saint Augustine never attributes to God a unique and absorbing causality in the government and administration of the world. Humanae voluntates humanorum operum causae sunt, the Saint has told us little. The Augustinian historical universe is the joint work of God and man, without denying the influence of other mundane or extramundane agents.
