The three aspects correspond to the Christian concept of God, infinitely just, infinitely wise, infinitely beautiful. Thus, History is a reverberation of the divine attributes, because it has a justification in itself, an order to good and a splendor of beauty. Firstly, in the City of God there is a Theodicy or justification of God, particularly in the problem of the permission of evil. This, the result of the ontological limitation of rational creatures and the misuse of free will, belongs to the current dialectic of History, now in its form of physical and moral suffering, now in that of voluntary malice. The existence of evil comes from the abuse of free will, from its conditioned autonomy in the face of the sovereign will of God, with which it sometimes presents itself in a titanic struggle. But this postulate is the very condition of the good. Moral values ​​come from the spiritual freedom of man, whose existence justify the movement and drama of History, which does not mean that the course of the world is reducible to clear causes or reasons or that superrational elements do not abound. History unfolds in time, which is divided into past, present and future. We owe to Saint Augustine one of the most interesting studies in European philosophy on the metaphysics of time. THE LONGING FOR PEACE

Men have a temporal and eternal end, but both merge in a single sweet word: pax. Saint Augustine dedicates perennial pages like bronze to peace. All things aspire to peace, and this is the tranquility of order: pax omnium rerum tranquillitas ordinis Yes. As the rest and tranquility of being in all its manifestations, peace was studied by ancient philosophers, whose opinions it reviews, establishing the doctrine of the supreme Good and the end of man. The universal desire and tendency for peace can be considered the deepest substratum of History, both in the City of God and on earth. Peace with God, with men among themselves, domestic peace, civic peace, the peace of all things, are celebrated by Saint Augustine with enthusiasm. It is seen that he is on a battlefield, on the dangerous border of many enemies. Particularly delighting is the last chapter on eternal rest, so admired by the great Italian historian L. Among all the Augustinian books, the City of God has had a privilege: that of having been illustrated by artists, especially medieval ones. Commentators, pendolists and miniaturists have made it the subject of their meditation, study and art. With what sumptuous ornaments and decorations, with what magnificent borders and foliage, with what wise illuminations did the artists of the Middle Ages know how to enhance the controversies and ideas of the great Doctor! Purple and gold, with the most delicious mix of colors and fantasies, have paid tribute to the truly royal thought, with which so many kings since Charlemagne were nourished by reading the great book. The French aristocrat, Count A. de Laborde, in a truly monumental work, illustrated with more than one hundred plates or reproductions of miniatures, gives us news of some two hundred and fifty miniaturized manuscripts of the City of God. A WHIMOUS EQUATION

Saint Augustine is one of the greatest geniuses of Europe, as he has collected the aspirations and concentrated the best of the spirit of the West. The history of European culture bears the traces of his thought everywhere. To measure the width and depth of the epithet stated, it is advisable to first go to a consistent definition of Europe. With an equation perhaps a little capricious, but one that helps me to organize the ideas of this article, the following equivalence could be formulated: EUROPE = E" + R° + P a The abbreviated signs are equivalent to Evangelium, Ratio and Homeland. Gospel, Reason and Homeland form the plastic principles of Europe, or if you want, the Christian Religion, Reason or Science and the principle of nationalities. The three elements are encrypted in three great towns: in Jerusalem, Greece and Rome. The Gospel, with the supernatural vision of the world, has come to us from Jerusalem; the Fatherland or nation in its most perfect form, from Rome. in the eternal law and in the order of conscience; the credere, intelligere and agere, or faith, intelligence and action; here is the wonderful creative trinity of the culture and spirit of the West. The Gospel was the supernatural leaven that transformed the face of Europe. Ancient man had a myopic and fragmentary vision of humanity, which Christianity corrected with three catholicities: that of grace and redemption, that of the Logos that enlightens every man who comes to earth. this world and that of the politics and government of souls. When Saint John said that the Word illuminates every man who comes into this world, he canonized the as-

pirations and suspicions of a perennial philosophy, latent in the highest spirits of Antiquity. The light and intimate warmth of Christ reaches everyone, head and germ of a new type of humanity, far superior to the old. Verbum Dei omnes compluit, the Saint would say. The Word of God bathes everyone with its dew. The conception that had been slowly developing in the thoughts of some Jews, spread throughout the Greek world, strengthened by faith, made possible the consecration and baptism of Greek culture, which was sponsored by some Fathers of the Church. This episode, very interesting in the history of European culture, could be defined as the marriage of reason with the Gospel in the mind of Europe. The third catholicity that brought the Gospel prepared its espousal with Rome or the Roman order. It entailed dogmatic and soteriological principles, that is, the doctrine of the unity of the human race, the equality of men before God, the universality of salvation. New ideas-forces, they contributed to the consecration of the imperialist effort of the queen of the West. Rome aspired to a universalist plan, but it lacked spiritual strength and unifying elements for the formation of a true society of souls. Christianity, then, entailed a double impulse of conservation and acquisition or creation. For the first, he respected and vivified everything he found healthy in human nature in Greeks, Latins or barbarians; He converted the basilicas into churches, assimilated languages ​​and customs, customs, costumes, etc., and infused a new spirit into the created organisms. He showed himself to be the repository of tradition, in the noble sense of this word. But, at the same time, the zeal of souls forced her to preach the Gospel to every creature, developing an unparalleled expansive force and putting into practice the universalist plan, with a Roman spirit. The progress of the kingdom of God, while uniting the most antagonistic peoples in the unity of Christ, head of the human race rescued with the same faith, baptism and sacraments, developed the qualitative differences of the European nations, created languages, interpreted and assimilated their art, forging a new individual physiognomy and literature; and this fusion of individual and universal traits was the beginning of European nationalities, whose physiognomy would be indefinable without Christianity.

If we move from the Middle Ages to the Modern Age, we will also find Augustinian traces everywhere, because the great Doctor is linked to the profound transformations of the human spirit. The Reformation and the Renaissance are based on Saint Augustine. Luther disjoints the wonderful synthesis of his genius, giving powerful force to half-truths, disjointed from the total organism. Reason and faith, linked in the crede ut intelligas, are dissociated, each one going its own way. The first is mutilated, reviled and diminished in its power by Luther. Faith looks at and dismisses reason as a fornicator who dishonors the house. The flight from God begins, a characteristic hallmark of modern man, because fear is a fugitive movement from God," said the great carver of Latin prose. The fear of God is perhaps the most profound spiritual fact of the entire modern era. Atheistic humanism has strived to free humanity from the idea of ​​God as a burden and oppression imposed by the Middle Ages. The consequence is the disappearance of God and the secularization of the spirit and culture, separated from their divine foundation, with the consequent breaking of the links and connections, which give such an architectural and monumental aspect to the thought of the Middle Ages. The internal and the external, the inferior and the superior, the divine and the human, the natural and the supernatural are separated, melting their wonderful welds. The secure Augustinian order, based on the intimate interconnection of its component parts, where everything moves according to an eternal plan conceived by the divine mind, decomposes, and the modern order is born, the pure connection of realities among themselves, without relation to an intelligible realm, which contains its entire reason for being. The new order rests on itself. The history of the modern spirit is defined by its cen18 force

And in this process of breakage and disintegration, Saint Augustine is present in two ways: by presence and by absence. By absence, because the modern means, as a flight from God, the anti-Augustinian in its healthiest elements: theological idealism, image of God, order, hierarchy, faith, reason, sacraments, grace, liturgy, Church, authority, etc. At the same time, Saint Augustine has given an apparent pretext to the separatist movements of modern times. He is at the crossroads of innumerable paths, because he is complexio oppositoram. He deeply accentuated the contrasts of reality, but subjecting them to a heroic balance. Thus, the tension between the flesh and the spirit acquires a relative balance in him through grace. Both extremes—spirit and concupiscence—offer a singular and dangerous relief. One can go towards an exaggerated spiritualism or an instinctive fatalism of the servum arbitrium. The Reformation, by disfiguring the concept of grace, instead of taking the living unity of the being renewed and penetrated by the force of God, isolates concupiscence, disintegrating it from the purifying process of grace, and considers it in all its tyrannical and dispersive force of despotic instinct. Man is a dissonant being, irreducible to harmony, because grace cannot reach the substantial and corrupt core of his being or the bottom of his animality. He is a servant, a slave to his passions, which he fatally serves. Through this slope we can eventually reach the Freudian conception of man, moved by the mechanism of libido. Saint Augustine is not a Freudian, but Freud could find useful elements in his doctrine of concupiscence. The reinforced libido, deprived of the elements of contrast—grace—becomes the center of gravity of the spirit. According to the Viennese psychiatrist, it is the very form of the spirit, where an ordo amoris does not properly fit, because it is dominated by monism and sexual fatalism or amor concupiscentiae. In this way, by weighing certain extremes we can lose the sense of balance and fair means in which the truth is found. Saint Augustine, as a difficult synthesis of strong contrasts, can favor and has favored their exaggeration, and what is said about concupiscence can be extended to other extremes.
But limiting ourselves here to philosophical thought and considering Hegel's Insichsein des Geistes as a defining element of the Reformation and the modern spirit, we can point out in it

two intuitions: the Cartesian, oriented towards pure thought, as the origin of all certainty and principle of all science, and the ancient and medieval, Platonic and metaphysical, represented by the Platonic Academy of Florence. Antiquity, particularly in Plato, aspires to absolute truth, to the contemplation of archetypal ideas, the root of everything intelligible and real. The Middle Ages will be platonic and metaphysical. But in Descartes we already notice a shift in thought towards the state of subjective rest in the possession of the truth, which we call certainty. The objective orientation, without being annulled, is noticeably diminished. The spirit itself becomes a source of truth. Man becomes accustomed to looking at himself and gradually loses his contemplative strength, his grasp of heights and distances. The self gradually supplants the object and becomes the sole subject of contemplation. In Saint Augustine the two intuitions coexist: the Platonic and the Cartesian. He knows and loves interiority, the Insichsein des Geistes. By seeking the epistemological foundations of truth, like Descartes, he affirms his footing in the living and thinking subject, the indestructible core of eternal truths. But he does not stagnate in the subject as in a dead end, since the vital push of the spirit forces him to leave himself to a pure, objective, ideal realm. The human spirit, as a vessel of immortal truths, claims another originary spirit, source of all that is true. Life, certainty and truth are firmly embraced, and through them the Augustinian spirit will ascend to the secure immortal. Man will be a support branch for every flight of thought, as in the modern spirit, and subjectivism will want to rely on the beautiful formulas of Augustinian interiority. But the spirit in Saint Augustine is the ontological lap of truths, anchored in a realm of pure essences and absolute value. The formula so dear to idealism hi interiore homine habitat ventas separates Saint Augustine from the modern spirit s°. But both tendencies, Cartesian and Platonic, unified in Saint Augustine, will endure throughout the efforts of modern thought. There will be a disintegration of the synthesis, to the detriment of philosophy.

Here is the aspiration of a select group of thinkers of our time: the return to Saint Augustine. And with it we also close the introductory pages to the version of his works, which today the Library of Christian Authors presents to Spanish readers. It is now a cliché to call Saint Augustine a modern man and even the first modern man. Cultural philosophers, such as Siebeck, Windelband and Harnack, have honored him with this epithet. And why is Saint Augustine the first modern man, despite belonging to the twilight of antiquity, of which he was an exceptional witness? One reason—the main one without a doubt—is the influence of the Saint on the birth of modernity, understood by this to be the complex cultural movement that began at the end of the 15th century and reaches us. That movement in its origin and development received the impetus of three factors: the Renaissance or literary, the philosophical and the religious. Three names embody him—Petrarch, Descartes and Luther—and none of the three were oblivious to the attraction of the Bishop of Hippo. That is Saint Posidius: a holy brother of Saint Augustine, linked to him not only with the bond of the oldest biography, but also by an exemplary friendship, sustained over forty years of communications, struggles and common victories. In another letter he also says: Hic Sanctus frater et collega noster, Possidius, in quo nostram non parvam praesentiam inventes 2. "This holy brother and friend of mine, Possidius, in whom you will find my own quite expressive portrait." What does this common presence or portrait that the Saint tells us about mean? The expression is inspired by the alter ego, with which the ancients praised the intimacy of friendly relationships. Possidius is the alter ego of Saint Augustine, one of the greatest satellites of his spirit. Saint Augustine, with very fine feelings for friendship, was undoubtedly alluding to friends like his biographer when he wrote: "I gladly throw myself entirely into the hearts of friends, especially when the fatigue of the scandals of the century overwhelms me, and I rest in them with calm abandon. He was undoubtedly African, and probably from Calama or Guelma, whose episcopal see he occupied for many years. With Alypius, Severus and Evodio he belonged to the inner circle of those attracted by the prestige and force of sympathy of Saint Augustine, and he lived with him in the monastery of Hippo, Epist. 104.1: PL 33.388. - Epist. 101.1: PL 33.368. That monastery was a team of seasoned bishops, whose memory endures in these words of the Saint: "I confess to you before the Lord, who scrutinizes the depths of my soul and is a witness of what I say, that since I consecrated myself to his service, just as I have hardly found better men than those trained in the monasteries, I have also seen no worse than those who fell there. And if some slags sadden us, we also have the consolation of finding many precious stones." 4. Possidio is one of the precious pearls, infused with the highest and purest spirit of the Augustinian monasteries. He shone for his culture and holiness, when around 397 he left the convent of San Agustín to succeed Megalio in the episcopal see of Guelma. From the same monastery Alypius left for the see of Tagaste, Profuturo for that of Cirta, Evodio for that of Uzalis, Severus for that of Milevi, Urban for Sicca Veneria, Peregrino for that of Thena, Boniface for that of Catagua. All of them were arms of Saint Augustine in the campaigns for the defense of the Church. Possidius founded a monastery of religious in Guelma to live with them in common life, the same as in Hippo and Tagaste. He understood episcopal zeal in the style of Saint Augustine: as a soldier guarding the City of God. The bishop must be all eyes, all ears and all hands to watch and fight for Christ. He faced the same great enemies that Saint Augustine fought: Donatism, paganism, Pelagianism. Bishop of the Donatist sect in Guelma was Crispin, and Possidius, heir to the irenic spirit of his teacher, worked tirelessly for the peace and unity of the Church. In Hippo he had trained in the use of combative weapons for the anti-Donatist controversy. He was one of the bishops who "had left the monastery and were preaching what they had learned there." Hippo was the royal armory of all the great combatants in the peace campaign. And one of the weapons that Saint Augustine wielded with unsurpassed mastery was public controversy. The enemy had to be sought out and provoked into open combat in a public parliament so that everyone could judge. The Bishop of Hippo, who already had a reputation as a terrible hand-to-hand fighter, was the one who provoked the controversy between the two bishops of Guelma. It was the year 404. But the Donatist shrank from that pride and air of superiority with which they treated those belonging to the Catholic Communion.
Donatism was the pure Church composed of saints, and the Catholic Church, Babylon

of the reprobates. Crispin avoided the controversy, shielding himself with the sentence of the Wise Man: Do not speak in the ears of the fool, who will despise your sensible reasons5. And finally he defined his attitude: "Let the wicked go far from me: I want nothing to do with them." But this response amara et maledica, which Saint Augustine says, provoked the ridicule of the learned and the ignorant. It was an escape for those who did not dare to confront the Frankish enemy, and it brought more than credit and authority to their cause. It undoubtedly also caused irritation in the Donati pars, because not long after a priest, also called Crispin, and apparently a relative of the Donatist bishop, while Possidius was on a pastoral visit, laid an ambush for him using the anarchic group of the circumceliones, ready for any abuse and violation of law. The spiteful priest led a gang of armed fanatics to surprise Possidius on his journey. But he learned about Crispín's plans in time and, changing his route, took refuge in a farm to be safe, thinking that there either they would not dare to carry out their criminal attempts or they would not prevail, or if they did something, they would not be able to deny it in the trial before eyewitnesses. Aware of the change of path and filled with resentment, Crispin and his men went to attack Posidio in his refuge. They surrounded the house, stoned it, surrounded it with flames, and tried to force the door to enter. The settlers who were there put out the fire three times asking for clemency from the Catholic bishop, because a crime was going to be committed, with serious danger to everyone. But the barbarian horde wanted to execute its criminal project. Finally, by throwing stones, the door gave way, and the entire mob broke into the house looking for the prey. They killed the animals housed in the lower part, no doubt as punishment to the owner for having hidden the servant of God, and then, going up to the top, they threw Possidius from there with clubs, amid serious contumelias. At the request of Crispín himself, fearing the notoriety and consequences of the crime, they were not more cruel to him.' Finally, at the repeated urging of Augustine, the conference of the two bishops was held in Guelma, with great participation from both communions and universal expectation of the Church of Africa. The Donatist bishop was convinced of being a heretic, and as such obliged to the pecuniary fine imposed by the imperial law, for Possidius himself had not intervened with his clemency.
But the Donatist appealed to the emperor, who confirmed the proconsular sentence.

They were looking for the bishop and killed a poor monk. These events occurred at the beginning of June of the year 408. Shortly afterwards the Bishop of Hippo passed by, undoubtedly requested by the Bishop of Guelma, to console the afflicted and calm the spirits, which were still very excited. He had an interview with the pagans: Multa a nobis audierunt, tumba etiam ipsi rogaverunt. "I sang good truths to them; they made many supplications to me," says the Saint 5. The same year Possidius undertook a trip to the imperial court of Ravenna, no doubt to obtain sanctions and repress the excesses of the pagans °. In 411 he also participated in the great conference of Carthage. To simplify the course of the conversations, seven representatives were chosen from each group, who bore the brunt of the controversy. Possidius was one of them, although Saint Augustine was the great champion of the Catholic cause, especially in the decisive session, held on June 8, in which the two causes were discussed: the Ecclesiae cause and the Caeciliani cause. Living peeps desecrated by the unbridled horde, creatures lost and abandoned without any help in the world, souls in pain everywhere, misery and desolation everywhere, gave the refugees plenty of material for suffering. But "that man of God did not look like the others at the terrible scourge of the invasion." 13. In everything he saw the fulfillment of merciful justice. With painful sighs and tears we asked the most merciful Father to give us respite and relief in our common misfortune. Around Saint Augustine they prayed, they cried in common, they adored in silence the tremendous mystery of divine Providence. And they also meditated on death, preparing for it. They saw it close, hovering over their heads. It can be conjectured that some sayings and anecdotes that our biographer collected from the lips of the great teacher, who inflamed the refugees of Hippo with his spirit, date back to this time. The saying of a wise man: He will not be magnanimous who is amazed to see the walls and coffered ceilings collapse and mortals die; the words of Saint Ambrose as he died, which seemed so balanced and balanced to our Saint: I do not fear death, because we have a good Lord; those he heard from a bishop who was a very good friend of his, brave and serene in his last moment; the anecdote of another bishop mentioned by Saint Cyprian, who was cowardly towards the Christian military life and cowardly towards death; These and other sayings and actions were, without a doubt, points of meditation on death with which Saint Augustine strengthened everyone for the last battle of life. The doctrine already added his example, with a very serene death that a great medieval artist, Benozzo Goizoli, a disciple of Fra Angelico, has reproduced for us in a wonderful fresco from the convent of Saint Augustine, in San Geminiano (Tuscany). The great fighter of Christ appears serenely lying on his deathbed, surrounded by his family of religious, while two angels take his soul to heaven. Everyone feels the death of the great leader of the holy cause of the Church. At his bedside, a bishop, thin and sad, is reading some prayers; It is the bishop of Guelma, Posidius, who prays for the eternal repose of his soul. He has lived with him for forty years without any dissension and has assisted him in the

last moments. He was moved by his voice, broken by sobs, when from his bed, sick and penitent, he read the psalms of repentance, and he took in his last sigh. He is the best witness of his intimate life, his struggles, his secrets and confidences, and therefore the reliable biographer of Saint Augustine. Following the examples of Sulpicius Severus, who bequeathed us the life of Saint Martin of Tours, and of Paulinus, writer of the life of Saint Ambrose, Possidius, with tender and edifying prose, left us the life of Saint Augustine and a catalog of his works. It comprises 31 chapters, eight of which tell us about his life until the episcopate (1-8), ten his controversies with the heretics (9-18), nine his virtues (19-27) and four the events of his last days and his death (28-31). Possidio is a very informed author, as we have seen: Quae in eodem vidi, ab eoque audivi, minime reticere debeno, he himself tells us. I cannot remain silent about the things I have seen in him and heard about him. He frequently alludes to these personal references of the eyewitness (cc.4, 15, 17, 20, 22, 24, 26, 27, 28, 29, 31). "His Life of Saint Augustine," says Father Cayré, "together with a catalog that he left us of his books, treatises and letters, is one of the most precious documents that we possess on the apostolic activity and virtues of the holy Bishop. It is written, above all, with a purpose of edification, and it shines, more than for the brilliance of the style, for the perfume of piety that is breathed there and the respectful admiration of the disciple and the sincerity of the narrator." BIRTH, CONVERSION AND BAPTISM OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

Saint Augustine was born in an African province, in the city of Tagaste, to Christian and noble parents, belonging to the municipal curia. His son's education was carried out by his care, diligence and diligence, and he was very well educated in all human literature, that is, in what they call liberal arts. He first taught grammar in his city, and then rhetoric in Carthage (capital of Africa), and in subsequent times, overseas, in Rome and Milan, where the court of Valentinian the Lesser was established at the time. In the same city, Ambrose, a highly favored priest of God, the flower of dignity among the most egregious men, then exercised his episcopal office. Mixed with the faithful people, Augustine went to church to listen to the sermons, very frequent in that dispenser of the divine word, and followed him absorbed and pending his word. In Carthage the Manichaeans had infected him with their errors for some time, when he was a teenager; And that is why he followed with greater interest everything related to the pros and cons of that heresy. And the liberating clemency of God was exerted with a gentle touch on the heart of his prelate so that he could resolve all the questions regarding the law with which he struggled; and in this indoctrinated way, with divine help, that heresy gently and gradually faded from his spirit, and was then confirmed

PROGRESS OF THE CATHOLIC CHURCH THROUGH THE WORK OF ST. AUGUSTINE

As the divine doctrine expanded, some servants of God who lived in the monastery under the direction and in the company of Saint Augustine began to be ordained clerics for the Church of Hippo. And later, as the truth of the preaching of the Catholic Church grew and shone day by day, as well as the way of life of the saints and servants of God, their continence and exemplary poverty, the peace and unity of the Church, with great efforts he first began to ask for and receive bishops and clerics of the monastery that had begun to exist and flourished with that distinguished man: and then he achieved it. Well, about ten holy and venerable men, continent and very learned, that I myself knew, Saint Augustine sent at the request of various churches, some of high standing. And they also, following the ideal of those saints, expanded the Church, and founded monasteries; and the desire for edification by the divine word increasingly increased, ordaining new religious, they provided ministers to other churches. Thus the healthy doctrine of faith, hope and charity of the Church spread to many and among many, not only throughout all parts of Africa, but also overseas, and with books published and translated into the Greek language, everything was brought to light through the ministry of one man, and through him to many others with the favor of heaven. A bishop, left his monastery and ordained for the Church, was visiting the diocese of Calama, relevant to his jurisdiction, and was preaching what he had learned in defense of peace against heresy, when in the middle of the road he fell into an ambush, and they attacked him with his entire entourage, stealing animals and luggage, and they showered him with insults, and severely mistreated him. In order not to impede the fruit of peace, the defender of the Church filed a complaint, according to law, before the court. Crispin, Donatist bishop of Calama and that entire region, already known for a long time and considered a learned man, was forced to pay the pecuniary fine that, according to civil laws, heretics had to pay. But he, appearing before the proconsul according to the law, rejected the imputation of the crime of heresy; and the ecclesiastical defender having withdrawn, the Catholic bishop had to confront him, proving to him that he was really what he denied being, and if he cooperated in dissimulation, perhaps in the eyes of the ignorant the Catholic bishop would appear to be a heretic, since Crispin refuted the accusation of heretic, and with this negligence the simple people were given cause for scandal and confusion. At the repeated urging of Augustine so worthy of memory, the two prelates of Calama, in three meetings, held conferences about both communions, with great expectation from the Christians of Carthage and all of Africa, and Crispin, by proconsular sentence, was condemned as a heretic. The Catholic bishop interceded on his behalf before the judge for tizatores Donatistas gestum et perfectum est. Also in Carthage, a procurator of the royal House, named Ursus, a Catholic, managed to discover certain Manichaeans who are called chosen ones, and brought to the Church by him, they were examined before the notaries by the bishops. Among them was present Saint Augustine, of holy memory, who better than anyone knew the execrable sect, and by clarifying all the horrible blasphemies with texts from the books that they themselves accept, he forced them to confess their errors; and the clumsiness and indignities that they used to commit, betraying the chosen women themselves, came to light in the ecclesiastical records. Thus, thanks to the vigilance of the shepherds, the divine flock received increases, being manfully defended against thieves and robbers. He also publicly disputed with a certain Felix, from the number of those chosen, in the church of Hippo, with the participation of the people, preparing a notarial record of what happened; and after the second or third discussion, in which the error and vanity of his sect was refuted, that Manichean converted to our holy faith and Church, as the same minutes show.

DEBATES WITH THE PELAGIANS AND WORK OF SAINT AUGUSTINE IN FAVOR OF THE CHURCH Also against the Pelagians, new heretics of our times, astute in controversy, endowed with a more subtle and harmful art for written propaganda, and who spread their ideas wherever they could, publicly and in homes, Saint Augustine fought for ten years, publishing a multitude of books and very frequently refuting their errors in the Church before the people. And because perverse and ambitious dared to take their perfidy to the Apostolic See itself, the African bishops actively worked in the councils to unmask their errors, first before the Holy Father of Rome, the venerable Innocent, and then before Zosimus, his successor, persuading them how abominable and worthy of condemnation the aforementioned sect was for the Catholic faith. Before dying he wanted to review the books he dictated and published, both those written at the beginning of his conversion, as a layman, and those he composed as a priest and bishop. He himself censured and corrected everything that could be inconsistent with the rule of ecclesiastical faith because he had written it when he was least prepared for it. Necessary and beneficial was the earthly permanence of that man, as the Catholic faith knows well, so strenuously defended by him in word and deed against the Arians. But when a common danger threatens, and there is more to be feared by the suspicion that flight is undertaken out of fear of death and not out of regard for greater goods, and more harm is brought about by the bad example of desertion, than benefit by the alleged obligation to prolong life, then for no reason should one flee. Finally, the holy King David, in order not to expose himself to the danger of battles and disappear by death, extinguishing the torch of Israel, as it is said there, also acted on the advice of his own, not for reasons of his own presumption, otherwise many would have imitated him in that cowardice, believing that he did not look to the benefit and usefulness of others, but obeyed the force of fear. 11. There is also another question that cannot be ignored: if this service is not to be disregarded, with the flight of some ministers, in cases of imminent danger, in order to preserve oneself and serve the survivors of the catastrophe, what should be done when everyone, except the fugitives, is threatened with common ruin? Or when the enemy's rage seeks particularly the ministers of the Church? What will we say to this? Should the Church be abandoned with the flight of the ministers for fear of greater helplessness due to death? But if the laity are not threatened with death, they can somehow hide their bishops and priests with the help of the universal Owner, who can fuerit Ecclesiae, quantumque profuerit, quod vir ille mansit in carne, Catholica fides novit, quae adversus Arianos haereticos ore illius et amore defense est. Sed si laici non quaeruntur ad mortem, possunt occultare quoquo modo episcopos et clericos suos, sicut ille adiuverit, in cuius po50

miraculously preserve the one who refuses flight; However, here we investigate what is lawful to do, without being accused of tempting God, asking Him for miracles. This common risk of priests and faithful people is not like that of a ship in a storm where merchants and sailors are about to get lost. However, it is far from us to value this ship of ours so little that the sailors and, above all, the helmsman have to abandon it in moments of danger, even when they can escape by jumping into a skiff or swimming to safety. What we fear for our faithful is not temporary death, which must come sooner or later, but eternal death, which can come, if not watched, but can also be avoided with pious caution. But in the common danger of this life, why do we believe that where persecution breaks out, all clerics must die and not also all lay people, for whom ecclesiastical service is necessary so that they may die well together? And why don't we expect that, if some lay people survive, the same fate will happen to some clerics, who are in charge of dispensing the divine mysteries to them? 12. How beautiful would be the emulation among the ministers of God to know who has to stay so that the Church is not deserted with the flight of everyone and who has to be saved so that it is not orphaned with the death of everyone! Such will be the emulation in which both are burned by charity and all serve their cause. If this emulation could not be ended in any other way, it would be convenient to cast lots as to who will be the one to whom it falls. Sed ideo quaerimus quid nos faceré debenamus, ne in Ómnibus exspectando divina miracula tentare Dominum iudicemur. Non quidem talis est ista tempestas, quando laicorum et clericorum est commune periculum, sicut in navi una commune periculum est mercatorum atque nautarum. Verum absit ut tanti pendenda sit haec navis nostra, ut debenant eam nautae, et máxime gubernator, periclitantem deserere, etiam si in scapham transiliendo vel etiam natando possint effugere.

13. There are many who say that bishops and priests, when they remain in the midst of these dangers, are a cause of deception for the people, who do not try to flee as long as they see that their shepherds do not move. But it is easy to overcome this objection; There is nothing more to say to the people: Do not use our stay in this place as an excuse not to flee, because not out of concern for our lives, but for your sake, we remain here, because of the need you have for our ministry to save you in Christ. If you flee, we will be free from the ties that bind us to your souls. I believe that this should be spoken to the faithful, when they can take refuge in safer places. If, having heard this, some or all respond: We are under the hand of Him from whose power no one can escape, of Him whose mercy is spread everywhere, even where one wants to remain (sometimes because of some impediment that makes the game difficult, now because there is no desire to painfully seek insecure refuges, where only one can change dangers), then, without a doubt, the ministers of the Lord must remain with them. But if they prefer to leave, following the advice of the bishops, they are not obligated to remain there, because the people whose service subjects them to permanence would be missing. 14. Thus, then, whoever withdraws without depriving the parishioners of the necessary ministry, does what the Lord prescribes or allows; But he who flees, leaving the flock of Christ without the spiritual sustenance it needs, is a mercenary who sees the wolf coming and flees, because he does not love the sheep. 13- Sunt sane qui arbitrantur episcopos et clericos non fugientes in talibus periculis sed manentes, faceré ut plebes decipiantur, cum ideo non fugiunt, quia manere suos praepositos cernunt. Sed facile est hanc reprehensionem vel invidiam devitare, adloquendo easdem plebes, atque saying: Non vos decipiat, quod de loco isto non fugimus. 1. Lives of Saints (Prologue).—Posidius was able to obtain news and receive encouragement for his biography of Saint Augustine from several previous authors. He undoubtedly knew the Vita Sancti Antonii, written by Saint Athanasius (PG 26, 805-976), mentioned in the Confessions (VIII 5: PL 32, 754-755). Also very popular was the Vita Sancti Martini, by Sulpicio Severo, written in the year 397 (PL 20, 157-222), which served as a model for many medieval hagiographers. Saint Jerome is the author of the Vita Sancti Pauli, written around the year 376 (PL 23, 1-28); of the Vita Malchi (PL 23, 53-60), written in 390 or 391, and of the Vita Hilarionis (PL 23, 29-54). Paulinus of Milan wrote the Vita S. Ambrosii Mediolanensis (PL 14, 27-46), surely at the wish of Saint Augustine. Saint Gregory of Nyssa was the author of the Vita Sanctae Macrinae (PG 46, 959-1-000), written around the year 380. Some of this antecedents moved the bishop of Calama to preserve the precious news that he keeps for us in his Vita S. Augustini. 2. The conference of Carthage in the year 411 (c.13).—It marked the legal defeat of Donatism, and its soul was Saint Augustine. The Donatists did not want to meet with the Catholics. "It is unseemly for the children of martyrs to join the race of traitors," Primianus had said. That's why his entire campaign was obstructionist. Despite their bishops having triumphantly entered Carthage, showing off their numbers, they feared the formidable dialectician of the Catholic Church. The sessions lasted from the first to the eighth day of June; The one on the 8th was the decisive session. And at first, the Donatists did not want to take their seats, acceding to the invitation of Marcellinus, who was the judge by imperial appointment. They shielded themselves with the psalm: Non sedi in concilio vanitatis. Saint Augustine, quickly and accurately, shot at them, in turn, another text of the same: "If you do not want to sit with us to obey the psalm: I did not sit in the meeting of fools; then why have you entered here, since the psalm also says: Et cum iniqua gerentibus non introibo: I will not enter with those who do evil? On the second day they demanded the Mandatum Catholicorum, or exposition of the true cause that had to be discussed in the assembly. Saint Augustine replied sharply: "It is clear that they are seeking nothing more than to postpone the discussion": hoc solum constet ipsos rem velle differre. 17. Flavius Marcellinus (el3).—He was commissioned by the emperor Honorius for the ecclesiastical controversy of Carthage. He was a tribune and notary and brother of the proconsul Apringius. Epistles 133, 138 and 139 of Saint Augustine are addressed to him, who held his virtues in great esteem and praises his moral probity, his enthusiasm for religious culture, his fidelity in friendship, his sincere piety, his exemplary married life, his patience and affability, his humility and charity towards all: Quantum decus honestatis, qui splendor gratiae, quae cura pietatis; quae in subveniendo mercy, in ignoscendo benevolentia, in orando fiducial Quanta spes et desiderium bonorum aeternorum! To Marcellin he directed the great work of The City of God, whose first three books he wrote before his death, which occurred in September 413. He died a victim of the hatred of the Donatists and is venerated in the Church as a martyr, whose feast day puts the martyrology on April 6, but Father Noris corrects this date.

"For my part, covered with this protection as with a wall, I await the arrows of your reasonings." Particularly Saint Paul was Augustine's great teacher in this matter. "Let us strive," he says at last, "not to give the label of heretics to those of our brothers who spread such errors, although we can give them that name, but we avoid it. May the Mother bear them with her pious bowels to heal them, to remove them from their error, so as not to mourn their dead. They make too much progress; It is too much, they can barely be tolerated; great patience is needed for this. But do not abuse this long-suffering of the Church; It will be good if they are corrected. As friends we give them this advice: we do not litigate with them as enemies. They murmur about us, we suffer them; but do not contradict the rule of faith, do not contradict the Truth, do not contradict the holy Church, which strives every day to remit original sin in children. This is a fundamental thing. The discussant who errs on things not yet well determined or confirmed with the full authority of the Church must be tolerated; The error must be patiently cured, but it is too much to insist on undermining the foundations of the Church. It is not advisable to go further, and our tolerance is not worthy of rebuke; But let us not make ourselves worthy of censure for our negligence. This is now enough for your charity; Behave with them, with those you know, with friendship, with a fraternal spirit, with sweetness, with love, with pain; deploy your piety with all your resources, because then impiety will have to be hated" '".

22. Controversy with Maximinus (c.17).—He is also a curious adversary of Saint Augustine, very skilled in the swordplay of all the biblical texts. He rejected everything that did not come from divine Scripture. He was an Arian, and when Saint Augustine asked him his faith regarding the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, he responded with a dilatory formula: "I profess the faith that 330 Bishops subscribed to in Rimini." "You have not answered my question," Saint Augustine replies, "say what you believe about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Do not refer me to writings that I do not have at hand and whose authority I do not abide by..." The fencing begins, very skillful on both sides, until Maximinus slips away from the nerve of the cause and extends himself into long explanations about what is not discussed, "talking a lot and not saying anything about the cause," as Saint Augustine reproaches him. ~\ And there was no one to silence him until the evening, when the session had to be adjourned. Finally, Saint Augustine makes a very brief summary of the Catholic faith in response to the Arian accusations. 354.—Born in Tagaste on November 13. 367.—He goes to Madaura to study grammar. 370.—Year of vacation in Tagaste. 371.—Continue studies in Carthage. 373-—Reads Cicero's "Hortensius" and adheres to Manichaeism. 374.—Return to Tagaste and teach rhetoric. 375.—With the help of Romanianus he established himself in Carthage, where he opened a school of rhetoric. 383-—He embarks for Rome as a professor of eloquence. 384.—He went to Milan for the same purpose and began to listen to the sermons of Saint Ambrose. 385.—Pronounces the panegyric of Emperor Valentinian II and Bauton. 386.—Reading of the Neoplatonists and the epistles of Saint Paul, interview with Simplician and Pontician. Conversion in the garden. 386.—He retires to the Verecundo farm, in Casiciaco, with his mother and friends (around September). Write the first books. 387.—He returns to Milan, and receives baptism from Saint Ambrose (April 24-25). He begins his return to Africa with his mother, who dies in Ostia del Tíber. He stayed in Rome for almost a year. 388.—Departs for Africa, stopping in Carthage for some time. He founded the first Augustinian monastery in Tagaste, where he remained for three years. 391.—Valerius, bishop of Hippo, consecrates him a priest. He founded the second monastery in the garden donated by the bishop. 392.—Dispute with Fortunatus, a Manichean, at the baths of Sosio, in Hippo, on August 28. 393.—Synod of Hippo (October 8), where Saint Augustine preaches on faith and symbol. 395.—He is appointed auxiliary bishop of Valerius, and consecrated by Megalio, Primate of Numidia. 397.—Attends a council of Carthage. Saint Valerio dies and Saint Augustine succeeds him in the episcopal see. 398.—Controversy with Fortunio, Donatist bishop of Tibursicum, and with Felix, a Manichean, who converted to the Catholic faith. 399-—Interview with Crispín, Donatist bishop of Calama. 401.—Attends a council of Carthage. Fight with the Donatists. 404.—He goes to the council of Carthage. 410.—Sacking of Rome by the Goths. 411.—Conference in Carthage between Catholics and Donatists (June 1-8). Principles of the anti-Pelagian controversy. 413-—The writing of the "City of God" books begins. Some dates are probable. Those relating to the relics of the Saint are taken from P. E. BELLANDI's monograph Le vicende del corpo di S. Agostifio attraverso quindici secali (Frrenze 1930). Attendance at the councils of Carthage was more frequent than indicated here.

414.—Paul Orosius, a Spanish priest, arrives in Hippo to consult Saint Augustine, who commissions him to go to Palestine (415) on the occasion of the Pelagian question. 416.—Attends the council of Milevi against the Pelagians. 418.—Dispute with Emeritus of Caesarea, Donatist bishop. 419-—Attends the council of Carthage, where the matter of the priest Apiario is discussed. 420.—Obtain the retraction of Leporius, a Gaulish monk. 426.—Finishes the "City of God" and names Heraclius auxiliary bishop. 428.—Conference with Maximinus, Arian bishop. 429-—The Vandals, led by Genseric, invade Numidia. 430.—Genseric besieges Hippo in June. 430.—Saint Augustine dies on August 28 and his body is placed in the Basilica of La Paz. 504.—His remains are transferred to Cagliari, in Sardinia. 722.—By the work of King Luitprando, of Cagliari, they moved to Pavia, to the basilica of San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro. 1832.—The relics are taken to the cathedral of Pavia. 1900.—They are returned to the same St. Peter's Basilica, where they currently rest.

To complete the biographical data of Saint Augustine we will now offer a chronological table of his books, imitating Saint Posidius, who wrote an index or catalog of them. The Bishop of Hippo, at the end of his career, composed the two books of Retractions, carefully pruning everything that seemed unsustainable and incorrect in the expression. And he advises those "who read this not to imitate the one who made mistakes, but rather the one who progressed and improved over time. Because you will see how in the course of my literary career I was advancing the one who read my books in the order in which they were written" l. It is necessary to admit, therefore, a progress or an evolution in the thought of the Saint, and since very erroneous assessments have been made regarding it, I will indicate the main points where some modification can be noticed. Retractions are the best guide for this purpose. Two kinds of opinions can be considered, rectified or modified by him: some philosophical and others theological. In the first writings the traces of Neoplatonism are felt, which were later eliminated. Thus "' alludes to the doctrine of Platonic reminiscence, later rectified 3. The soul does not come to this world endowed with the liberal arts, nor did it have a previous existence, already buried in oblivion. There are experimental arts1

les and arts of pure intelligence. The first two, v. gr., medicine, require learning and are acquired; the latter, like mathematics, are the object of a rational understanding and the help of a higher light 4. In the style of the Neoplatonists, one notices in the first writings an exaggerated tension between the spirit and the flesh, between the sensible and the intelligible. And for this reason he reproves Porphyry's saying: penitus esse ista sensibilia fugienda °. In the same place, there is a veiled allusion to the famous Platonic allegory of the cave, which is, without a doubt, the most profound image excogitated by Antiquity to represent the tragic situation of the human spirit. Similarly, the doctrine of perception and sensible experience does not have the due emphasis that it would later achieve in the books De Trinitate and others, although with less accentuation than in Aristotelian philosophy. But Saint Augustine also admits a domain of knowledge in which sensible experience provides its wealth of data, which cannot be achieved in any other way. The doctrine on the passions, as diseases of the spirit, on the impassibility or apatheia of the wise man, on the happy life and the contemplation of God, accessible in this life, apparently, with a natural dialectical process, also received the critical endorsement of our Saint in the Retractions.' Nor does the happy life consist, as he had said in the first books of Cassiciacus, in living according to pure reason, which is the most excellent portion of man, but according to God, that is, according to reason, illustrated by supernatural faith. Such are the points most worth noting in the philosophical aspect, where Augustinian thought has undergone some variation. In the theological aspect, it is useful to know a short history of the variations, which have been exaggerated in the rationalist field. The main one refers to the mystery of the election of grace. The Semi-Pelagians opposed the first writings to the last, without the Doctor of Grace evading the reproach; He had indeed progressed to a fuller recognition of the sovereignty of God's grace, but his readers did not want to admit this profitable change: non curaverunt proficere mecum. The mystery of Christ as a servant of God and his soteriological mission was presented to him in new light and he began to understand the profound meaning of the Incarnation, the humility of Jesus and the need for faith as a healthy act, in contrast to the gnosis of the philosophers. It must be noted, therefore, a notable variation in the Christological and even Christian ideas of the Saint in the aforementioned period. This opinion is unsustainable. Nor can the categorical statement be accepted: Augustin ist in dieser Zeit immer nocb zu seher Neuplatonisch, um der Menschwerdung, dem Tod, und der Auferstehung Christi eíne wahrhaft erlósende Kraft zuzueignen und sie in das Herz-und Mittelpunk des Christentums zu rücken ls. Saint Augustine was too much of a Neoplatonist to attribute true redemptive virtue to the Incarnation, Death and Resurrection of Christ, placing these mysteries at the heart and center of Christianity. This opinion, defended by K. Adam, forgets two very important factors in the religious formation of Saint Augustine. The first is the ecclesiastical or catechetical, which must include the contact and influence of a teacher as competent as Saint Ambrose. The core of catechetical education was information about the mystery of Christ, his Incarnation, his Death and Resurrection. To be baptized is to be incorporated into Christ, to assimilate with him in death and glorious life. Baptismal symbolism contains these graphically expressed elements, and it cannot be assumed that Saint Augustine, with the enormous assimilative force he possessed at that time, did not encompass such elementary and primary truths of catechesis. Even if a greater depth is admitted into the mystery of Christ, it cannot be denied that he possessed living faith in the value of what he calls in his first writings the sacrosanct mysteries, whose initiation took place in catechesis. The second factor is the scripture, mainly that of the epistles of Saint Paul, which Saint Augustine read on the recommendation of Saint Ambrose. Is it credible that the vigorous Christology of the Apostle, where the human element of Christ, above all his precious blood, acquires so much value, slipped through the spirit of Saint Augustine without leaving a deep mark on him? The Pauline Christ is not a remote and transcendental Christ, a pure archetypal idea of the universe, but an intimate, cordial Christ.

And is it admissible that the living contact of Saint Paul's Christ did not communicate authentically Christian vital force against the coldness of Neoplatonic conceptions? The integral conversion of Saint Augustine—and in it we also include baptism—was the embrace of the Pauline Christ. Epistle to the bishop of Tagaste, Alypius, where he informs him how he put an end to the abuse of the scandalous banquets that the Catholics of Hippo had in the church to celebrate the festivities of the martyrs. I want to tell your charity a fact, so that together with us you can thank God for the benefit received, since you also begged him to grant it to us. When, after your departure, we were informed that some men were in an uproar, saying that the suppression of the so-called festival of joy could not be tolerated, a name with which they vainly try to cover up the intemperance and drunkenness to which they indulge, no doubt by the secret disposition of divine Providence, it occurred to us on Wednesday to comment on that passage from the Gospel: Do not want to give what is holy to dogs nor throw your daisies to swine.' They spoke, then, of the dogs and the pigs, so that those who opposed the precepts of the Lord with their stubborn barking and those given over to the impurities of the flesh would blush; I concluded by pondering how unworthy it was within the sacred precinct of the church and in the name of religion to indulge in such intemperance, which, even when allowed in the homes, were a reason for separating the guilty from the holy and from the heavenly daisies. Although they received my words well, however, as there was little influx of faithful, what was said was not enough for such a serious case. And when the attendees, each according to their ability and commitment, divulged what I had told them in the sermon, contradictors arose. Then, on the fortieth day, a large crowd came to the sermon; The evangelical episode of the expulsion of the merchants from the temple was read, when the Lord overthrew the money-changers' tables and said that his Father's house, a place of prayer, was converted into a den of thieves. Seeing them so intrigued with the question of drunkenness, The event that Saint Augustine refers to here occurred in the year 395, when he was a simple priest. The day took place in three days: Wednesday, Thursday (festival of the Ascension) and Friday, the anniversary of Saint Leontius, patron martyr of the city, in whose honor the faithful celebrated the revels referred to in this epistle. Very close to the church, dedicated to said martyr, the Donatists had their basilica, who also celebrated him with the same excesses in eating and drinking.

From the Catholic church you could clearly hear the singing and shouting of the Donatists. Saint Augustine preached on Wednesday with few people; on Ascension Thursday, with a lot of competition, and on Friday, the feast of San Leoncio, in the morning and afternoon. The suppression of the festival of joy was a great victory for the eloquence and zeal of the Saint. We add it here to enhance his priestly physiognomy. Mt 7,6.

I myself recited this chapter and added a reasoning to show them with much greater reason and force I would banish banquets and drunkenness from the temple of the Lord, with their inseparable procession of frivolities, from which I would throw away permitted businesses because they sold in them what was lawful for the sacrifices of that time. And I asked them themselves: What is a den of thieves more like, those who sell what they need or those who drink immoderately? And as the lessons were offered to me, already prepared for me to declare, I then added that the same carnal people of the Jews, in that temple, where the body and blood of the Lord had not yet been offered, did not celebrate there, I do not say wine-filled banquets, but even sober ones, and that their history does not present other cases of drunkenness with a religious pretext, except those that occurred on the occasion of the adoration of the calf 3. After reading these passages and returning the codex, pondering the sin of drunkenness, with the Epistles of the Apostle Saint Paul, I explained to them what sins it was included, and I read to them that place: What I tell you is that you do not mix with anyone who, bearing the name of brother, is an adulterer, a covetous man, an idolater, a reviler, a drunkard or a thief: with these, do not eat4. Don't be fooled; Neither the fornicators, nor the idolaters, nor the adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor the sodomites, nor the thieves, nor the covetous, nor the drunkards, nor the revilers, nor the rapacious, will possess the kingdom of God. And that was some of you; but you have been washed, you have been justified in the name of the Lord, Jesus Christ, and by the Spirit of our God \ Bringing this reading to a close, I exhorted you to consider how you could hear but have been purified, the faithful who consent to have such filthiness of lust, and close the kingdom of heaven in the very heart, that is, in the inner temple of God. I later reminded them of that chapter: When you come together, it is not to eat the Lord's supper, because each one goes ahead to eat his own supper; and while one is hungry, the other is drunk. I see, don't you have houses to eat and drink? Or do you have the church of God in so little? G With great insistence I recommended to them that in the church they should not even have honest and moderate banquets, because the Apostle did not say: "Do you not have the houses to get drunk"?, as if getting drunk was only illegal in the church; but for

eat and drink, which they can do in moderation, but outside the church, those who have houses to restore their strength with necessary food. I also reminded them of the Gospel that I had told them the day before about the false prophets, of whom it is written: By their fruits you will know them; and how the fruits spoken of there are works. I then asked them what fruits drunkenness included, reciting to them the passage from the Epistle to the Galatians: The works of the flesh are manifest, namely: fornication, impurity, lust, sorcery, hatred, discord, emulations, outbursts of anger, quarrels, arguments, divisions, murders, drunkenness, orgies, and other things like these: of which I warn you that Those who do them will not have the kingdom of God.' Augustine brought a new spirit of culture, which, above all, is the cult of truth, of the elevation of ideas, of the taste for high speculation, ordered to form life. THE PRINCIPLE OF PHILOSOPHY OR INTUITION

In the Dialogues of Casiciaco, philosophical education or culture obtains primacy. And when we talk about Augustinian philosophy, it should not be understood in the strict and precise sense, nor as a dead or merely scholastic system, but, above all, as a vital process ordered to the complete formation of the personality. "Saint Augustine," says Baumgartner, "lived problems one after another, savored their difficulties, looked for solutions and worked them out himself. He had to conquer the kingdom of knowledge inch by inch. That is why his philosophy is the philosophy of a personality: it carries everywhere the mark of the personal and individual. The philosophy of the Dialogues, in its practical and sapiential sense, is like a superior science that souls instructed with

Both lives, the contemplative and the active, stimulated the attention of philosophers and their solution investigated Greek thought. The two brothers Zethus and Amphion were their symbols. The problem has also always worried Christian thinkers. The optimistic conception of philosophy, which is seen in the Dialogues, had been taken by Saint Augustine from the Neoplatonists and from Cicero, who in the Tusculan Questions stamps these praises: Cultura animae philosophia est: philosophy is the culture of the soul; it radically extirpates the vices and prepares the spirits for the sowing, and in season of season, reaps magnificent fruits." 27. Saint Augustine does not share all this optimism of the secular soteriology of Antiquity, since his spirit, tamed by the hand of God, had already opened itself to the supernatural world created by Christ. The moral transmutation of his soul had not been the work of philosophy, but of the imperial force of the grace of Christ: misericordia eius manum porrigente 2". Christ gave him his hand and led him out of the dark forest. In Christ, mediator between God and men, he found the way, the truth and the life. Even in the main operations for integral philosophical formation, such as introversion and supraversion or transcendence, what the Saint calls rediré in semetipsum and respicere in patriam, entering into one's own soul, gradually becoming immaterial, and looking at one's homeland or rising to God, are effects of the awakening of Christ. "So that not only with his precepts, but also with his examples, the souls would be awakened and enabled to enter into themselves and look at the homeland, even without conflict of human arguments" a°.

The philosopher of Casiciaco does not build a radically autonomous science, closed in the realm of pure reason, without connection with higher aspirations. The dialectic of the spirit, as an expression of personality, does not admit splits nor should it dispense with the ultimate goal of the concrete man, which is the fruitive possession of God. That is why "true and, so to speak, genuine philosophy has the mission of teaching us and making known to us the nature of the Beginning of all things, and the greatness of its intelligence, and the goods that without detriment have been derived from there for our salvation; it makes us know the one God, almighty, thrice powerful: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, revealed by the sacred mysteries, whose sincere and unwavering faith saves the people." "Philosophy does not break the connection with the practical and higher truths of a higher order. On the other hand, the moral and religious life, as we will see, turn on its lights in the spirit, just as science must be the moderating principle of action. In the philosophy of the thinker of Casiciaco, as a method of formation and elevation of the personality, the three things that constitute every process can be clearly determined: the beginning, the middle and the end, or in other words: the starting point, the dialectical movement and the goal of speculative activity. The three things—beginning, middle, and end—will help us understand the structure and most of the content of the Dialogues. What, then, is first and foremost the principle of philosophical and rational knowledge with which the cognitive thirst of the spirit is quenched? First of all, it is the desire for happiness, the intimate and profound substratum of the human being, the wheel that sets in motion the dynamism of man. the happy life: Haec una fuet causa philosophandi: here is the only cause of philosophy. And in this the philosophers also agree with the Christians.
Now: knowledge of the truth is necessary to be happy; This is one of the thoughts developed in the anti-academic controversy J \ Knowledge is a necessary natural requirement

for the complete spiritual balance of man, and the desire for happiness entails a secret root of knowledge. The ignorant cannot be happy in the deepest and most real portion of the self. Here the initial germ of philosophy must be sought, since the intimate background of rational life is moved by an inclination towards truth. The Augustinian intellectum valde ama, the passion of knowledge, constitutes a vital stimulus for the vita beataS4. But this natural impulse requires as a second condition the spes inveniendae veritatis, the hope of finding the truth. To search you must have hope of finding: the absolute desperate is the absolute inert, victim of incurable indecision. But absolute inertia, or let's say, absolute skepticism, with the universal denial of the truth, contradicts human nature, all of which is soaked in the spirit of faith, hope and charity. The spes inveniendae veritatis is inserted in the initial impulse of Saint Augustine's philosophy, and has forced him to search for an epistemology, a critical science of the foundations of certainty. One of the first efforts of the thinker Cassiciacus was to unclutter and clear the path of all the obstacles that the skeptics had thrown in his path to obstruct the advance towards the truth. The aforementioned Baumgartner also says: "In the ancient world, Saint Augustine was one of those who most earnestly sought truth. But, strangely enough, in the course of his evolution, truth itself became a problem for him. After a hard struggle, and under the influence of Platonic philosophy, he managed to regain the conviction of the possibility of knowledge. Saint Augustine had the opportunity to fully appreciate the difficulty of the problem of truth. He saw clearly its scope as a door to access to philosophy, as the foundation of all methodical philosophizing. Necessary is, above all, the conviction that the truth can be found, because no one must first dare to seek it. A sign of a truly philosophical and critical spirit is the fact that the early work of Saint Augustine is directed against skepticism, proposing to establish the foundations on which all true knowledge rests" J5. The investigation of the bases and foundations of the certainty of knowledge was a necessity for the spirit of Saint Augustine, because the objections of the probabilists and agnostics of Antiquity took their toll on his spirit.

And how does he solve the critical problem that gives access to his philosophy? Epist. 120.13: PL 33.459. Tu autem, charissime, ora fortiter el jideliter det ubi Dominus intellectum (ibid-, n.14). O. c, p.18-19.

He aspired to a comprehensive science of things, safe from all error and protected from all contradictions of enemies. Certainty, according to him, rests on intuition and, above all, on the apprehension of the immediate data of internal experience. This is not about indirect knowledge, about analysis achieved with difficult dialectical detours, but about the first vital connections of being a thinker with the real, about initial truths that put the spirit in contact with itself and with the world. Breaking these bonds is equivalent to suicide, against which the most powerful instincts of the rational being protest. The starting point of philosophy is not Cartesian doubt, but a core of primary certainties, to which conscience is firmly attached. Saint Augustine, in the fight against academic doubt, starts from a fact or a current connection between the desire for happiness and the knowledge of the truth. If truth is unattainable, so is wisdom. And if man can achieve happiness, he can also achieve wisdom, which is the science of a happy life. Academics, by seeking happiness, but denying any possibility of certain knowledge of the truth, incur a contradiction. Man is an active being, and his main task is the search for happiness; but without certainty, no rational operative activity can develop. To act morally it is necessary to know with certainty even the category of values ​​or goods that are the goal towards which one tends. Therefore, the natural link between the urgency of happiness, which is a confusing love, and the truth, between action and its directive norms, cannot be broken. Saint Augustine takes a path opposite to that of Kant. The German philosopher splits pure reason from practice, making the latter autonomous and independent; but it incurs the same error as the academics, when they granted the wise man the science of good and action that leads to happiness, but denied him the science of truth J. The science of truth and good belong to man, under penalty of introducing a spiritual tear that makes him unhealthily miserable. Thus, for Saint Augustine, as for the best spirits of antiquity, morality and ontology are closely linked. A rational being, disjointed from all knowledge and metaphysical order, is mutilated for life.
This will be one of the first truths of the philosophy of Christianity: we must build the house of the soul, not on the ground.

movement of doubt, like the fool in the parable, but on the immortal rock of eternal truths, on a system of values, which, in turn, rests on a system of absolute rational certainties. Existence and human life are based on solid principles and are not reduced to aimless attitudes and movements. Furthermore, Saint Augustine discovers an intimate contradiction in the academic system. Any radical denial of the truth is contradictory, because the one who denies it affirms the truth of his denial. Strictly speaking, with the myopia of academic doubt one cannot take a step. Skepticism implies an inertia of the rational being. Every movement, that is, every direction, contains a contradiction. Every attempt at a system and defense supposes a collection of statements that destroy doubt. Academics had their own defensive system, that is, a series of affirmations, denials, definitions, arguments. Thus Zeno's definition was classic among them: "Nothing can be the object of true perception." How have you arrived at this point, oh most learned men? "We were moved—they respond—by Zeno's definition." "How! One of two: either that statement is true or false; if true, some truth is admitted by whoever admits it; if false, it should not have moved you, who pride yourself on being very constant" 3S. The skeptic cannot forge a system without contradicting himself. DIALECTIC OF THE SPIRIT

The philosophy of the Dialogues is a dialectic of the spirit in the Platonic sense of gradual ascension to the pure realm of being and ideas. Or, if you want, it is a philosophy of conversion and action. With the religious conversion of Saint Augustine, the entire beam of his energies was fired at one target: the knowledge of God, of the soul and of things. He wanted to train himself and his friends for the investigation of truth, purifying the inner eyes and acclimating them to the inner light. The work and dialectical process by which the spirit is set in motion to investigate the most serious problems of philosophy can be condensed into these three points: having eyes, looking, seeing1'. Having the inner optical apparatus for the vision of absolute truth is the first effort of the African thinker. Saint Augustine has the eyes of an eagle, but still weak and impure. "My business here is to cleanse myself of vain and pernicious opinions." "I am now thirty-three years old and hope to attain wisdom. I despise everything else and dedicate my life to seeking it... But the movement to wisdom is slow and progressive. Before vision, the eyes must be purified and accustomed to the shadows of the divine vestiges, imprinted on created things. From the above it can be deduced what goal the Augustinian thought process aspires to: the contemplation of the truth. Such is the definitive rest and the end of the vita beata. Saint Augustine does not accept the opinion of the academics and agnostics of his time and ours, according to which the end of man is the search for the truth, without ever finding it: semper quaerere et nunquam invenire, which flattered Licentius. As if we said that the end of movement is movement and not the rest of arrival or that the movement of the spirit is that of an endless screw. He who seeks must have faith, hope and charity; Otherwise, it wouldn't move. He who sets out, hopes to get where he wants. The idea of ​​an ultimate reward is also the cause of movement. What, then, is the term or goal of rest of all this laborious searching, the order of which Saint Augustine has described? Ut videat: it is the vision or contemplation of the truth. Quidquid laboras, ad hoc laboras ut videas, he says elsewhere. All your efforts and works are directed towards the achievement of the vision "'. The supreme happiness will also be the supreme vision, which will consist, not only in seeing God, but in seeing him divinely: Divine videbunt, quando Deo pleni erunt 7°. Here the Saint breathes the purest breath of Hellenic antiquity. The greatest riches of the spirit are contained and manifest in the contemplative life. The loving fruition of God will be the eternal Sabbath of man after his dialectical pilgrimage through the world of creatures. The Greeks glimpsed this truth, held so firmly and clearly by Christianity. Sight and contemplation had a singular charm for them. The Greek was very fond of seeing, and therefore, of creating ideal forms of perennial beauty. When Croesus of Sardis asks Solon what the reason for his journey is, he answers: to see the world. Estagirite—says Festugiére—, the tradition has not changed. The union of bios theoretikós with bios politikós constitutes one of the most delicate aporias of the moral world. Religious contemplation was a noble occupation for the Greek spirit. The sculptures of the gods must shine with an august beauty, which well reflects their blissful interior. They must embody ideas, mainly serenity, calm, the intimate calm and balance that accompanies a happy life. Two ideas especially attract the Greeks: agathía and kallos, goodness and beauty, closely linked to each other. Contemplation seeks rest in beauty; and this inner rest, which excludes every disturbing element, and the stillness of all passionate movements is agathía, the supreme enjoyment of the goodness of the gods. Such is, likewise, the supreme Augustinian aspiration, the "theoria" and the possession of an imperturbable restlessness. Here are centered the aspirations of the thinker Casiciacus, strongly influenced by Hellenic and Roman ideas. The wisdom he strives to achieve is the happy consortium of both things: the contemplation of the Beauty of truth and the rest of the spirit, cleansed of passionate disturbances. In the Dialogues, sapiens and sapientia are continually referred to. The theme of the wise man had been studied extensively in Greek and Roman antiquity in pursuit of a secular soteriology. Stoic philosophy also proposed the formation of the wise man—sophós—who lives according to an internal law and enjoys true autonomy and passionate balance. He must be self-sufficient and regulate his life by virtue, which is the supreme good or happy life. Subjectively, this life required an apathetic state, the lack of disordered movements, spiritual immobility, because all movement is stubbornness, effort, fatigue, torment in a word. Man must resemble the gods, numbing all the desires that are the root of discomfort. A radical self-control, with vigorous immobility in the face of all the vicissitudes, misfortunes, reversals of fortune that disturb the serenity of the inner kingdom: this is the ideal of the wisdom and rationalist soteriology of antiquity. Both motifs—theoria and apatheia—, highlighted by Cicero and Seneca in the Roman world, are stirred in the early speculation of Saint Augustine and are forever incorporated into the mysticism of Christianity.

Inner purification is equivalent to the apathetic state for which the ancient sages sighed, since it requires the extinction of disordered desires, the mortification or death of bad passions.
