SOME SPECIAL PROBLEMS With the spirit that moves the speculative process of the Dialogues, it is worth mentioning some special themes, which will always find an echo in his writings. The great problems of European philosophy were those of Saint Augustine: the foundations of certainty, the types and limits of intuition, the knowledge of truth, the essence and origin of error, spiritual catharsis as part of the method, the search for the supreme good, contemplation and action, the unity and harmony of the universe, the origin and cause of evil, the connection between the sensible and intelligible world, the relations between creatures and the Creator, the law of rhythm in force in all things, sensation and ideas, the objectivity and absolute value of our knowledge, the stages of the itinerary to the divine, the problem of the wise man and wisdom, the happy life, its essence and means of achieving it, the meaning of life, the immortality of the soul, eternal laws and truths, the essence of beauty, space and time, matter and spirit, movement and rest, the providential order and the world, free will and prescience, etc., are topics that have attracted since the beginning the speculative activity of Saint Augustine. The first of all is, without a doubt, that of the truth and means of achieving it. "And the truth consists," says the Saint, "in putting these three things in God: the cause of the world, the sovereign good and the fulcrum of reason. The error consists in putting these three things in the world of bodies or in the human spirit." Nothing deeper could be said. Here a totalitarian purpose is already designed, comprehensive of the great problems of God, the soul and the universe. The topic of Truth with its very complex relationships always captured the attention of Saint Augustine, because it was a central point for him. Or if you want, a panorama, a total vision that Sagesie et béatkude p.94.

In fact, the same Saint Justin, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Saint Ambrose, Lactantius, professed the same conviction (HOLTE, ibid., 153ff.). In reality, for Saint Augustine, Christianity is what enables man to achieve his goal, which is the vita beata.

He discovered God, the soul and the world. Thus, v. gr., she made him glimpse the immortality of the soul. In Casiciaco Saint Augustine is seen concerned with the problem of the destiny of man. The Soliloquies", the books De ordine os and the De immortalitate animae, written somewhat later, preserve his reflections on this topic. The knowledge of the immortal destiny of the spirit was like a biological necessity for him, a point of support without which a culture of a spiritual nature is not possible. The investigation of the immortality of the soul occupied the great pagan thinkers, such as Plato and Cicero especially. On the contrary, modern philosophy disdains this argument as unknowable. And this manifests the lack of realism of modern man, crippled by vital certainties and ontological longings. Ancient man and the Christian put temporal life in the perspective of an eternal life, filling our ephemeral existence with profound content. Eternal destiny is the first existential theme of man. We need to know at all times what comes after death, what will become of our soul when the habitat of its body is demolished. The entire process of human life, rationally organized, demands a link with eternity. To hesitate on this point is to move the very foundations of existence, to abandon oneself totally to the brute force of the moment. Thus, the Augustinian man is a radically eschatological man, projected into the future with the passionate demand for a new way of existing, in which his deepest desires are crystallized. A sign of a deeply realistic and human spirit is that Saint Augustine dedicated his first speculations to the solution of the great problem of destiny. The evidence on which he insists to cement his conviction bears the stamp of Platonic inspiration, and is summarized in this principle: What lives attached to the immortal must participate in immortality. The glass of an incorruptible liquor must be incorruptible. Man is a prodigious temporal being who carries within himself eternal truths. It cannot die, because it is the seat of immortal truths. It also appeals to the character of mental operations, since the same experience teaches that for greater penetration of the truth we must abstract from the exercise of the senses: "They are not

material and corporeal are the things for whose understanding the spirit is collected and concentrated, distancing itself from the operation of the senses. They exist and have a more eminent and solid being, because they always remain identical to themselves. For what greater absurdity is there than to say that the objects of sensible perception are real and to deny reality to the objects of intellectual perception, intelligence being clearly superior to the senses? The things embraced with intelligence are always permanent, without alteration in their being, and indicate that the spirit is united to them in a wonderful but spiritual way. Because either he is in them or they are in him." This fact of spirituality and independence of the spiritual operations of the soul and its attachment to eternal things fortifies the belief in the immortal destiny of man. The desire and aspiration for eternity that manifests itself in the entire life of the spirit must also be considered. Saint Augustine admits an instinctus naturalis by which men desire to be immortal and happy, since immortality and happiness attract each other. To be happy you have to be, you have to live, you have to contemplate with the well-founded certainty that contemplation will never be interrupted. We must not forget, therefore, when exposing the Platonic arguments adduced by Saint Augustine, that primary and innate instinct that lies in the innermost core of the spirit yearning for eternal truths. But the Saint himself was not very satisfied with the arguments clustered in his first essays, and later, in the maturity of his thought, he recognized the difficulty of rationally proving the perennity of our being.'" Another of the problems whose solution the Casiciaco thinker seeks refers to the universal order. Saint Augustine cannot get enough of giving formulas to the thought of order in all his writings, especially in his books De ordine and De musica. Order no longer rests merely on itself, as it did in antiquity; but not only in God, and even less in man, where he had to rest according to Kant. It has existence in itself and rests at the same time in the infinitely good spirit of the divine Person.'" Although, delving into Neoplatonic metaphysics, he had reduced the cosmos, its origin and its government to unity, he was still tortured by the presence of evil in the universe, which will be one of the greatest crosses for human intelligence, since evil, particularly in its form of injustice and suffering, offers such darkness that it cannot be completely dispelled by the light of reason. Saint Augustine knew very well that Defense of the Providence or justification of God in the government of the world is one of the most difficult problems of Christian thought. According to him, a singular purity of the inner eye is required to fully encompass the universe, composed of light and shadows. The dialectic of opposites already acquires a very relevant significance in the first Augustinian essays. However, order will be the supreme law of the universe, even when man has the terrible power to attack it through his free will, which is a. power of resistance to God and his commands. But even the rebel to order is not outside of it, since it reaches him in the form of justice and sanction. Even rebellion can be reduced to order by the omnipotence of the Creator, who would not allow any evil in the dominions of his crown if he were not powerful and wise enough to extract good from the same evils. One of the most beautiful and revealing facets of the arcane of infinite mercy shines. Saint Augustine does not consider in its essence and origin the intimate structure of the human being torn by a dissonance and contradiction that makes evil necessary in the world. 8. A.—It's okay; Still, if someone said to you: I will make God known to you as you know Alypius, would you not thank him, saying: I am content with that? A.—I would appreciate it, but I would not be satisfied. A.—Why? A.—Because I do not know God as I do Alypius, nor am I satisfied with my knowledge of him. A.—See, then, whether it won't be insolence to want to know God enough, when you don't know Alypius. A.—The argument is not valid; Well, compared to the stars, what is more vile than my dinner? And yet, I don't know what I'll have for dinner tomorrow, but I do know what lunar phase we'll be in. A.—Et homines sunt, et eos amo, non eo quod animalia, sed eo quod homines sunt, id est, ex eo quod rationales animas habent, quas amo etiam in latronibus. Licet enim mihi in quovis amare rationem, cum illum iure oderim qui male utitur eo quod amo. Itaque both magis amo amicos meos, quanto magis bene utuntur anima rationali, vel certe quantum desiderant ea bene uti.

8. R.—Accipio istud: sed tamen, si quis tibi diceret: faciam te sic Deum nosse quomodo nosti Alypium, nonne granas ageres, et díceres, satis est? A.—Agerem quidem gratias, sed satis esse non dicerem. R.—Cur quaeso? A.—Quia Deum ne sic quidem noví quomodo Alypium, et tamen Alypium non satis novi. A.—Vide ergo ne impudenter velis satis Deum nosse qui Alypium non satis nosti. A.—Non sequitur. Nam, in comparatione siderum, quid est mea coena vilius? Et tamen eras quid sim coenaturus ignoro; quo autem sign future moon sit non impudenter me scire profiteor. See note 6: The knowledge of God and the soul.

R-—Would you be satisfied, then, with knowing God as you know the sign of tomorrow's lunar course? A.—It is not enough, because that belongs to the sphere of sensitive perception, and I do not know if God or some hidden natural thing will change the lunar order and course; and if this happens, all my foresight is destroyed. A.— And do you think that is possible? A.—No, but now I seek knowledge, not faith. And what we know we say well that we believe it; but not everything we believe we know. R-—Do you reject, then, at this point the testimony of the senses? A.—Totally. A.—Well, that friend of yours, still unknown to you, as you say, how do you want to know him: with the senses or with the understanding? A.—What I know about him through the senses—if anything can be known through them—is of little price and is sufficient; But that part for which I love him, that is, the soul, I want to reach with the understanding. R.—Can it be known in another way? Year. A.—And you dare to say that such an affectionate and familiar friend is unknown to you? A.— Why not? I consider it the most just law of friendship

the one that prescribes loving one's friend as oneself. And since I don't know myself either, it is no insult to say that a friend is unknown to me, especially when he doesn't even know himself, I believe. A.—If, then, what you want to investigate now is of an intellectual nature, when I reproached you as presumption for wanting to know God without knowing Alypius, I was not referring to the dinner and the moon as an example, since they are things belonging to the domain of the senses, as you say.

R.—Ergo vel ita Deum nosse tibí satis est, ut nosti quo eras lunar sign cursura sit? A.—Non est satis: nam hoc sensibus approbo. I ignore autem utrum vel Deus, vel aliqua naturae oceulta causa súbito lunae ordinem cursumque commutet. Quod si acciderit, totum illud quod praesumpseram falsum erit. R.—Et credis hoc fieri posse? A.—Non creed. Be ego quid sciam quaero, non quid credam. Omne autem quod scimus, recte fortasse etiam credere dicimur; at non omne quod credimus etiam scire. R.—Respuis igitur in hac causa omne testimonium sensuum? A.—Prorsus responded. R.—Quid illum familiarem tuum, quem te adhucignore dixistí, sensu vis nosse an intellectu? A.—Sensu quidem quod in eo novi, si tamen sensu aliquid noscitur, et vile est, et satis est. Ulam vero partem qua mihi amicus est, id est, ipsum animum intellectu assequi cupio. R.—Potestne aliter nosci? A.—No mode. R.—Amicum igitur tuum et vehementer familiarem audes tibí dicere esse ignotum? A.—Quidne audeam? Illam enim legem amicitiae iustissimam esse

arbitror, qua praescribitur, ut sicut non minus ita nec plus quisque amicum quam seipsum diligat. Itaque cum memetipsum ignorem, qua potest a me affici contumelia, quem mihi esse dixero ignotum, cum praesertim (ut credo) ne ipse quidem se noverit? A.—Si ergo ista quae scire vis ex eo sunt genere quae intellectus assequitur, cum dicerem impudenter te velle Deum scire, cum Alypium nescias, non debuisti mihi coenam tuam et lunam proferre pro simili, si haec, ut dixisti, ad sensum pertinent.

9- A-—But let's leave this alone; Now answer me this: Assuming that what Plato and Plotinus have said about God is true, would their divine science be enough for you? A.—Not because the things they said about God were true does it mean that they possessed them with knowledge. Well, many copiously talk about what they do not know, as I myself have formulated the things that I expressed in the prayer as a wish, which would be irrational if I had knowledge of all that; But maybe that's why I shouldn't have expressed it? I brought to light so many concepts without understanding them, collected from here and there, deposited in memory and harmonizing them with faith, as I was able; but knowledge is something else.

9- R.—Sed quid ad nos? Nunc illud answers: Si ea quae de Deo dixerunt Plato et Plotinus vera sunt, satisne tibi est ita Deum scire, ut illi sciebant? A.—Non continuo, si ea quae dixerunt vera sunt, etiam sciisse illos ea necesse est. Nam multi copióse dicunt quae nesciunt, ut ego ipse omnia quae oravi, me dixi scire cupere, quod non cuperem si iam scirem: num igitur eo minus illa dicere potui? Dixi enim non quae intellectu comprehendi, sed quae undecumque collecta memoriae mandavi, et quibus accommodavi quantum potui fidem: scire autem aliud est.

R-—Tell me, then, do you know in geometry what a line is? A.—I certainly know. A.— Don't you fear academics in this persuasion? A.—Not entirely. Because they don't want the wise man to err, and I don't belong to this category. Let us note, then, confess the science of the things that I know. But if, as I wish, I later attain wisdom, I will do as she advises me. A.—I reject nothing; But to continue our investigation, since you know the line, do you know what the round figure called a sphere is? A.—I know. A.— Do you also know the line and the sphere, or one thing more than the other? A.—Equally both, since I am not deceived in any of them. A.—And have you perceived both with your senses or with your intelligence? A.—The senses at this point have served me as a ship. Well, when they took me to the point where I was going, I left them there; And now, as if settled on solid ground, when I began to think about these things, my feet wavered for a long time. Therefore, I believe that one can navigate on land rather than reach geometric science with the senses, although they provide some help to beginners. R.—Do you not hesitate, then, to call the knowledge you have of these things science? R.—Dec, quaeso, scisne saltem in geometric discipline quid sit linea? A.—Istud plañe scio. R.—Nec in this professione vereris Academics? A.—Non omnino. lili enim sapientem errare noluerunt: ego autem sapiens non sum. Itaque adhuc non vereor earum rerum quas novi scientiam profiteri. Quod si, ut cupio, pervenero ad sapientiam, faciam quod illa monuerit. R.—Nihil renuo; sed, ut quaerere coeperam, ita ut lineam nosti, nosti etiam pilam quam sphaeram nominant? A.—Novi. R.—Aeque utrumque nosti, an aliud alio magis aut minus? A.—Aeque prorsus. Nam in utroque nihil fallar. R.—Quid haec, sensibusne percepisti, an intellectu? A.—Imo sensus in hoc negotio quasi navim sum expertus. Nam cum ipsi me ad locum quo tendebam pervenerint, ubi eos dimisi, et iam velut in solo positus, coepi cogitatione ista returne, diu mihi vestigia titubarunt. Quare citius mihi videtur in tena posse navigari quam geometricam sensibus percipi, quamvis primo discentes aliquantum adiuvare videantur. A.—Ergo istarum rerum disciplinam, si qua tibi est, non dubitas vocari scientiam?

A.—No, as long as the Stoics allow me, according to whom only the wise possess science. I have the perception of these things, that they are combined with stupidity; but I do not fear the Stoics either, and I affirm that I have knowledge of the truths about which you have questioned me. So go ahead and let's see where you take me. A.—Don't hurry, because we have time. Proceed with caution so as not to make rash concessions. I would like to see you enjoy the possession of some certain truths without fear of error, and as if it were little gain, would you spur me to accelerate my march? A.—May God do what you ask and, according to your prudence, correct me sharply if I again commit similar errors. 10. A.— Is it evident to you that the line cannot be divided longitudinally into two? A.—There is no doubt. A.—And can it be cut transversely? A.—A thousand intersections can be made in it. A.— Is it not also evident that not even two equal circles can be drawn from the center of the sphere? A.—I have the same evidence of that truth. A.—And the line and the sphere, are they identical or different things? A.—Very diverse. A.—If, then, you equally know both things and they differ so much from each other, as you affirm, then there is an indifferent science of different things. A.—Non, si Stoici sinant, qui scientiam tribuunt nulli nisi sapienti. Perceptionem sane istorum me habere non denial, quam etiam stultitiae concedunt. Sed nec istos quidquam pertimesco. Prorsus haec quae interrogasti scientia teneo. Perge moda, videam quorsum ista quaeris. A.—Ne propera, otiosi sumus. Intentus tantum accipe, ne quid I will fear you grant. Gaudentem te studeo reddere de rebus quibus nullum casum pertimescas; et, quasi parvum negotium sit, praecipitare iubes. A.—Ita Deus faxit ut dicis. THE EYES OF THE SOUL WITH WHICH GOD IS PERCEIVED 12. A.—Your interest is reasonable. Well, reason promises you, which speaks with you, to show you God as the sun shows itself to the eyes. Because the powers of the soul are like the eyes of the mind; and the axioms of science resemble objects, illustrated by the sun so that they can be seen, such as the earth and everything terrestrial. And God is the sun that bathes them with its light. And I, reason, am to the mind as the ray of vision is to the eyes. Having eyes is not the same as looking, nor looking is the same as seeing. Therefore the soul needs three things: to have eyes, to look, to see. The eye of the soul is the mind pure from all bodily stain, that is, removed and cleansed from the appetite for corruptible things. And this is mainly achieved with faith; because no one will strive to achieve healthy eyes if he does not believe it is essential to see what cannot be shown to him because he is infected and weak. She is a certain ineffable and incomprehensible light of intelligences. Our ordinary light helps us as much as possible to rise to it. There are eyes so healthy and vigorous that, after opening, they can look straight into the light of the sun without blinking. For them, light is healing, without needing teaching, and only some admonition. It is enough for them to believe, hope and love. Others, on the contrary, are dazzled by the same light that they so ardently desire to contemplate, and without getting what they want, they often return to the shadows with delight. To these, even if they improve, until they consider themselves healthy, it is dangerous to show them what they cannot yet see. You have to exercise them first, baking your love with profitable delay. First they will be shown opaque objects, but bathed in light, such as a dress, a wall, something similar. They must then begin to fix their eyes on things that shine with greater beauty not by themselves, but by the reverberation of the sun, such as gold, silver and similar things, whose reflection does not harm the eyes. Non enim casto castitas, sed castitate fit castum; ita etiam, si quid verum est, veritate utique verum est. 28. R.—Quid cum castus aliquis moritur, censes moti etiam castitatem? A.—No mode. A.—Ergo, cum interit aliquid quod verum est, non interit veritas. A.—Quomodo autem interit aliquid verum? Non enim video. i?.—Miror te istud quaerere: nonne ante oculos nostros milia rerum videmus interire? Nisi forte whores have arborem, aut esse arborem, sed veram non esse, aut certe interire non posse. Quamvis enim non credas sensibus, possisque I will respond ignore you prorsus utrum arbor sit, tamen illud non negabis (ut opinor) veram esse arborem, si arbor est. Non enim hoc sensu, sed intelligentia iudicatur. Si enim false arbor est, non est arbor: si autem arbor est, vera sit necesse est. A.—I grant istud.

R.—And what do you answer to this? Do trees belong to the genus of things that are born and die? A.—I can't deny it either. A.—Then it follows that true things can die. A.—I'm not saying the opposite. A.—And don't you think that, even when true things die, the truth does not die, just as with the death of the chaste chastity does not die? A.—I grant you everything; But I'm curious to know where you want to take me around here. A.—Keep listening. A.—I am attentive. 29. A.— Do you accept as true that saying: Everything that exists, must exist somewhere? A.—I find nothing to oppose him. R.—Do you confess, then, that the truth exists? So. A.—Then let us find out where it is; but it is not in any place, since what is not a body does not occupy space, unless it is truly a body. A.—I reject both hypotheses. A.—Where do you think it will be, then? Somewhere is the one we know exists. A.— Ah, if I knew where it was, I wouldn't look for anything else. A.— Can you at least know where it is not?

A.—If you help me with your questions, maybe I will find it. A.—It is certainly not in mortal things. Because what is in a subject cannot subsist if the subject itself does not subsist. Thus we have concluded that the truth subsists, even when true things perish. It is not, therefore, in the things that pass away. The truth exists, and it is not found anywhere. Then there are immortal things. But nothing is true if it is not for the truth. From which it is concluded that only immortal things are true. And every false tree is not a tree, and false log is not log, and false silver is not silver, and whatever is false is not. But everything that is not true is false. Therefore nothing can truly be said to be, except those that are immortal. Consider this brief reasoning carefully, in case it perhaps contains some unsustainable step. For if it were conclusive we would have achieved almost our entire attempt, as will be better seen in the following volume. 30. A.—I thank you; and under the cover of silence, I will diligently and cautiously discuss these arguments with you, and, therefore, with me, although I greatly fear that some darkness may interpose, that it may flatter me with its delight. A.—Believe firmly in God and throw yourself into his arms as soon as you can. Expropriate yourself, come out of your own power and confess that you are a servant of your most merciful and generous Lord. He will draw you to himself and will not cease to shower you with his favors, even without you knowing it.

A.—Quid illud alterum, norme concedis hoc genus rerum esse arborem, quod nascatur et intereat? A.—Negare non possum. A.—Concluditur ergo aliquid quod verum est interire. A.—Non contravention. R.—Quid illud? Nonne tibi videtur, intereuntibus rebus veris, veritatem non interire, ut non morí, casto mortuo, castitatem? A.—Iam et hoc concedo et magnopere quid moliaris expecto. A.—Ergo attende. A.—Isthic sum. 29-—R-—Verane tibi videtur ista sententia: Quidquid est alicubi esse cogitur? A.—Nihil me sic ducit ad consentiendum. R.—Fateris autem esse veritatem? A.—Fateor. A.—Ergo ubi sit necesse est quaeramus, non est enifti in loco, nisi forte aut esse in loco aliquid aliud praeter corpus, aut vetitatem corpus esse arbitraris. A.—Nihil horum puto. R-—Ubinam igitur illam esse credis? Non enim nusquam est quam esse concedimus. A.—Si scirem ubi esset, nihil fortasse amplius quaererem. R.—Saltem ubi non sit potes cognoscere?

A.—Si commemores, fortasse potero. A.-—Non est cene in rebus mortalibus. Quidquid enim est, in aliquo non potest manere, si non manet illud in quo est. Manere autem, etiam rebus veris intereuntibus, veritatem, paulo ante concessum est. Non igitur est veritas in rebus mortalibus. Est autem veritas, et non est nusquam. Sunt igitur res immortales. Nihil autem verum in quo veritas non est. Conficitur itaque non esse vera nisi quae sunt immortalia. Et omnis false arbor non est arbor, et falsum lignum non est lignum, et falsum argentum non est argentum, et omnino quidquid falsum est non est. Omne autem quod verum non est falsum est. Nulla igitur recte dicuntur esse nisi immortalia. Hanc tu tecum ratiunculam diligenterconsider, ne quid tibi concedendum non esse videatur. Si enim rata est, totum negotium penis confecimus, quod in alio fortasse libto melius apparebit. 30. A.—Habeo gratiam, et ista mecum atque adeo tecum, quando in silentio sumus, diligenter cauteque tractabo, si nullae se tenebrae immittant, suique etiam, quod vehementer formedido, mihi faciant delectationem. A.—Constanter Deo crede, eique te totum committe quantum potes. Noli esse velJe quasi proprius, et in tua potestate, sed eius clementissimi et utilissimi Domini te servum esse profitere. Ita enim te ad se rebelle non desinet, nihilque tibi evenire permittet nisi quod tibi prosit, etiam si nescias.

A.—I hear, believe and obey as I can, and I beg you with all my heart to increase my capacity and strength, unless you demand something more from me. A.—I am content with that now; then you will do what He Himself commands once He shows you a. A.—Audio, credo, et quantum possum obtempero, plurimumque ipsum deprecor ut plurimum possim, nisi quid forte amplius a me desideras. A.—Bene habet interim, facies postea quidquid iam visus ipse praeceperit. a See note 16: The truth and the true
OF THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL

1. A.—Our work has been interrupted enough and the desire is fiery, and the tears do not cease until love is given what it asks for; So let's start the second book. A.—Let's get to work, then. A.—And let us trust that God will assist us. A.—Let us trust, if this itself is within our power. A.—Our strength is Himself. A.—Pray, then, with the greatest brevity and perfection that you can. A.— Oh God, always the same!, know me, know you. Here is my prayer. R.—You who want to know yourself, do you know that you exist? A.—I know. A.—Where do you know it from? A.—I don't know. R.—Are you a simple or compound being? A.—I don't know.
BY IMMORTALITATE ANIMAE

1. A.—Satis intermissum est opus nostrum, et impatiens est amor, nec lacrymis modus fit, nisi amori detur quod amatur. Quare aggrediamur librum secundum. R.—Aggrediamur. A.—Credamus Deum adfuturum. A.—Credamus sane, si vel hoc in potestate nostra est. A.—Potestas nostra ipse est. A.—Itaque ora brevissime ac perfectissime quantum potes. A.—Deus semper Idem, noverim me, noverim te. Oratum est. R.—Tu qui vis te nosse, seis esse te? A.—Scio. R.—One six? A.—Nescio. R.—Simplicem, do you feel Anne multiplicem? A.—Nescio.

A.— Do you know that you move? A.—I don't know. R.—Do you know what you think? A.—I know. A.—Then it is true that you think. A.—Certainly. R.—Do you know that you are immortal? A.—I don't know. Rr—Of all these things of which you confess yourself ignorant, which one would you prefer to know first? A.—Yes, I am immortal. A.—Do you love life, then? A.—I confess it. A.—And when you know that you are immortal, will you be satisfied? A.—It will be a great satisfaction, but still insufficient for me. R-—And with this insufficient discovery, how much will your joy be? A.—Without a doubt, very large. R."—Will there be no more room for tears? A.—I think not. R.—And if it turns out from the inquiry that in life you will no longer progress in the knowledge you already possess, will you be able to moderate your tears? A.—I will become a flood of tears and life itself will lose all value for me. R.—Moveri te seis? A.—Nescio. R—Cogitare te seis? A.—Scio. R.—Ergo verum est cogitare te. A.—Verum. R.—Immortalem te &sse seis? A.—Nescio. R-—Horum omnium, quae te nescire dixisti, quid scire prius mavis? A.—Utrum immortalis sim. R.—Vivere igitur arrias? A.—Fateor. R-—Quid, cum te irdmortalem esse didiceris, satisne erit? A.—Erit id quidem inagnum, sed mihi quidem parum. R—Hoc tamen parum est quantum gaudebis? A.—Plurimum. A.—Nihil nosse liceat. A.—Imo tantum fleto ut vita nulla sit.

A.—Then you love life, not for its own sake, but for wisdom. A.—I approve the conclusion. R.—What if science itself serves to make you miserable? A.-—I do not admit in any way what you say; but if it were so, happiness will be a chimera, because ignorance is what makes me miserable now. If, then, science makes one miserable, the misery will be eternal. A.—I see where you are going. Well, since I think that no one is unhappy because of wisdom, it is probably concluded that blessedness is constituted in understanding. But only he who lives is blessed, and no one lives if he does not exist; you want to be, live, understand, and exist to live, and live to understand. Then you know that you exist, you know that you live, you know what you understand. And you still want to expand your knowledge and find out if these things will always survive, or if they will perish, or if some of them will remain forever and some will not, or if they admit of increase and decrease, supposing that they are eternal. A.—That's right. A.—Then, proving that we must always live, it will be concluded that we will be immortal. A.—Logic is your conclusion. A.—There remains, then, the problem of understanding a. A.—Non igitur vivere propter ipsum vivere amas, sed propter scire. A.—I yield conclusioni. A.—What if eadem ipsa rerum scientia miserum faciat? A.—Nullo id quidem pact fieri posse credo. Be, if ita est, nemo esse beatus potest; non enim nunc aliunde sum miser nisi rerum ¡gnorantia. Quod si et rerum scientia miserum facit, sempiterna miseria est. A.—Iam video totum quod cupis: nam quoniam neminem scientia miserum esse credis, ex quo probabile est ut intelligentia efficiat beatum: beatus autem nemo nisi vivirs, et nemo vivit qui non est: esse vis; vivere, et intelli^ere; sed esse ut vivas, vivere ut intelligas. Ergo esse te seis, vivere te seis, intelligere te seis. Sed utrum ista semper future sint, ari nihil horum futurum sit, an maneat aliquid semper, et aliquid intercidat, an minui et augeri haec possint, cum omnia mansura sint, nosse vis. A.—Ita est. A.—Si igitur probaverimus semper nos esse victuros, sequetur etiam semper futures. A.—Sequetur. A.—Restabit quaerere de intelligendo. a See notes 17 and 18: Noverim
me, noverim te and The Cartesian Cogito.

2. A.—It seems to me to be a very clear and brief order. R-—Concentrate your attention, then, and respond cautiously and firmly to my questions. A.—I am willing. A.—If this world lasts forever, is it true that it will always last? A.—Who can doubt that? R'—And if it doesn't last, is it equally true that it won't last? A.—I don't have to object to anything. R-—And if the world must perish, after its ruin, will it not be true that it has perished? While the proposition is true: the world has not perished, it really continues to exist; but there is a contradiction in saying: the world has ended, and it is not true that the world has ended. A-—I grant you everything. R-—And what do you think of this? Can something true exist without truth existing? A.—Not at all. A.—Then the truth will subsist, even if the world is annihilated. A.—I cannot deny it. CAPUT VERITAS

2. A.—Manifestissimum ordinem video atque brevissimum. R-—I did this, therefore, never ask a firm, cautious question that you answer. A.—Isthic sum. A.—Si manebit semper mundus iste, verum est mundum semper mansurum esse? A.—Quis hoc dubitet? R-—Quid si non manebit, nonne ita verum est mundum non esse mansurum? A.—Nihü I resist. R-—Quid, cum interierit, si interiturus est, nonne tune id erit verum, mundum interisse? Nam quandiu verum non est mundum occidisse, non occidit: repugnat igitur ut mundus occiderit, et verum non sit mundum occidisse. A.—Et hoc I grant. R-—Quid illud? Videturne tibí verum aliquid esse posse, ut veritas non sit? A.—No mode. R-—Erit igitur veritas, etiamsi mundus intereat. A.—Negare non possum.

A.—And if the truth perishes, will it not be true that it has perished? A.—The consequence seems legitimate to me. A.—It is thus that there can be no true thing without truth. A.—That has already been granted a little while ago. A.—Then truth cannot die in any way. A.—Keep going, because they are all true consequences.
If THERE WILL ALWAYS BE FALSENESS AND SENSITIVE PERCEPTION, IT FOLLOWS THAT SOME SOUL WILL NEVER CEASE TO EXIST.

3. A-—Now I propose this question to you: in your opinion, does the body or the soul feel? A.—I think the soul. A.—And understanding, do you think it belongs to the soul? A.—Without a doubt. A.—Only to the soul, or perhaps also to something else? A.—Outside the soul I do not see any intelligent subject, except God. A.—Let us now examine this question: if someone told you that this wall was not a wall, but a tree, what would you think? A.—Quid si ipsa veritas occidat, nonne verum erit veritatem disse? A.—Et istud quis negat? A.—Verum autem non potest esse, si veritas non sit. A.—Iam hoc paulo ante concessi. A.—Nullo moda igitur occidet veritas. A.—Perge, ut coepisti, nam ista collectione nihil est verius.
If you FALSITES SEMPER ERIT, ET SINE SENSU ESSE NON POTERIT,
SEQUITUR ANIMAM ALIQUAM SEMPER EXSTITURAM

3. R,—Do you never respond mihi velim, utrum tibi will feel anima video an corpus? A.—Anima videtur. A.—Quid, intellectus videtur tibi ad animam pertinere? A.—Prorsus videtur. R.—Ad solam animam, an ad aliquid aliud? A.—Nihil aliud video praeter animam, nisi Deum ubi intellectum esse credam. A.—Iam illud videamus. Si tibi quispiam istum parietem non esse parietem, sed arborem diceret, quid putares?

A.—Well, either his senses were deceiving him or my senses were deceiving him, or he called what is called a wall a tree. A.—And if the wall is shown to him with the appearance of a tree and to you with the appearance of a wall, could not both things be true? A.—Not at all, because the same thing cannot be a tree and a wall at the same time. And although it is presented to each of us in that unique way, one of us suffers from an error of imagination. A.—What if it is neither a tree nor a wall and you are both deceiving each other? A.—That could also happen. A.—That assumption had not occurred to you. A.—It's true. A.—And if you recognize that it is something different from what it seems, will you be a victim of error? A.—Not certainly. A.—Then there can be a misleading appearance, without causing an error. A.—I admit that possibility. A.—In short, then, not he who sees deceptive appearances errs, but he who assents to them. A.—Agree with what you say. A.—But what is false, why is it false? A.—Because it is different from what appears. A.—There being no one like him, then, there is no falsehood. A.—Aut eius sensum, autem meum fallí, aut hoc nomine ab eo panetera vocari. A.—What if et illi species arboris in eo appareat, et tibí parietis, nonne poterit utrumque verum esse? A.—Nullo manner: quia una eademque res et arbor et paries esse non potest. Quamvis enim singulis nobis singula esse videantur, necesse est unum nostrum imaginationem falsem pati. A.—Quid si nec paries nec arbor, et ambo fallimini? A.—Potest id quidem. A.—Hoc ergo unum superius praetermiseras. A.—Fateor. A.—Quid si agnoscatis aliud vobis videri quam est, numquidnam fallimini? A.—Non. A.—Potest igitur et falsum esse quod videtur, et non fallí cui videtur. A.—Potest. A.—Confitendum est igitur non eum fallí qui falsa videt, sed eum qui assentitur falsis. A,—Plane confitendum. A.—Quid ipsum falsum, quare falsum est? A.—Quod aliter sese habet quam videtur. A.—Si ergo non sint quibus videatur, nihil est falsum,.

A.—You conclude well. A.—Then falsehood is not in things, but in meaning, and he who does not assent to apparent things is not deceived. Therefore, we are one thing and the senses another, because, by deceiving themselves, we can guard against error ourselves. A.—I have nothing to object to you. A.—And perhaps when the soul is deceived, will you dare to say that there is no falsehood in you? A.—How am I going to say such a thing? A.—Now: there are no senses without soul nor falsehood without senses. The soul, then, is the cause or accomplice of falsehood. A.—The previous premises force me to accept the consequence. 4. A.—Now answer me: Does it seem possible to you that there may ever be no falsehood or error? A.— How can it seem to me, when the discovery of the truth is so difficult, that it would be greater nonsense to affirm the impossibility of the false than that of the true? R.—Do you think that someone who does not live can feel? A.—Not at all. A.—Consequently, the soul is immortal. A.—Very soon you introduce me to this joy; Let's go slowly, I beg you. A.—If your concessions are well linked, there is no room for doubt, as I see. A.—Sequitur. A.—Non igitur est in rebus falsitas, sed in sensu: non autem fallitur qui falsis non assentitur. Conficitur ut aliud simus nos, aliud sensus: siquidem, eum ipse fallitur, possumus nos non falli. A.—Nihil habeo quod contradicam. R.—Sed numquid, eum anima fallitur, audes te dicere non esse falsum? A.—What pact istud audeam? A.—At nullus sensus sine anima, nulla falsitas sine sensu. Aut operatur igitur anima, aut cooperatur falsitati. A.—Trahunt praecedentia consensionem. 4. R.—Illud nunc responds, utrum tibi videtur posse fieri ut aliquando falsitas non sit? A.—Quomodo mihi hoc videri potest, eum tanta sit difficultas inveniendae veritatis, ut absurdius dícatur falsitatem quam verítatem esse non posse? R.—Numquidnam arbitraris eum qui non vivit posse will feel? A.—Non potest fieri. A.—Confectum est animam semper vi veré. A.—Nimis cita urges me in gaudia: pedetentim, quaeso. A.—Atqui, si recte illa concessa sunt, nihil de hac re dubitandum video.

A.—It seems very soon to me, I repeat. Therefore I am more inclined to believe that I have been rash in some statements than to profess with certainty the immortality of the soul. However, develop this conclusion and show me the link of all the propositions. A.—You have recognized that there can be no falsehood without the senses and that there will always be falsehood; then there will always be meanings. Thus there can be no senses without a sentient soul; Therefore the soul is immortal, since it cannot feel without living. Therefore, the soul always lives. CHAPTER
CAN THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL BE DEDUCED FROM THE PERPETUITY OF WHAT IS TRUE OR FALSE?

5. A.— What a lead dagger! You could conclude that man is immortal if he had granted you that he is an inseparable part of the world and that the world is everlasting. R.—I see you awake. However, what has been achieved is not a small thing, namely: that the soul cannot but coexist with the nature of things, if falsehood cannot ever be absent from it. A.—In that I do see a legitimate consequence. But it seems to me that we must go back further to secure our positions, without denying that we have taken some steps towards the immortality of the soul. A.—Nimis cita est, inquam. Itaque facilius adducor, ut me fearé aliquid concessisse arbitrer, quam ut iam securus de immortalitate animae fiam. Tamen evolve istam conclusionem, et quomodo id effectum sit ostende. A.—Falsitatem dixisti sine sensu esse non posse, et eam non esse non posse: semper igitur est sensus. At nullus sensus sine anima: anima igitur sempiterna est. Nec valet will feel nisi vivat. Semper igitur anima vivit. CAPUT
EX FALSITATIS SEU VERITATIS PERPETUITATE POSSITNE COLLIGI ANIMAE IMMORTALITAS?

5. A.—O plumbeum pugionem! Posses enim concludere hominem esse immortalem, si tibi concessissem nunquam istum mundum esse posse sine nomine eumque mundum esse sempiternum. R-—Bene quidem vigilas. Sed tamen non parum est quod confecimus: rerum naturam sine anima esse non posse, nisi forte in rerum natura falsitas aliquando non erit. A.—Istud quidem consequens esse confiteor. Sed iam amplius deliberandum censeo utrum superius concessa non nutent. Non enim parvum gradum ad animae immortalitatem factum esse video.

A.— Have you looked at it carefully, in case you have made any concessions lightly? A.—I think so, and I find no statement that could be called reckless. A.—It is, therefore, proven that the universe cannot subsist without living souls. A.—Accordingly, but as long as some can be born and others die. A.—And if we eliminate all falsehood from nature, will not all things be true? A.—You are also consistent in that relationship. R.—Answer me, then: why does that wall seem real to you? A.—Because its appearance doesn't deceive me. A.—Then because it is just as it seems to you. A.—That's right. A.—If, then, a thing is false because it is different from what it seems, the truth of a thing will consist in being what it seems. And once the subject who perceives it is suppressed, there is no truth or falsehood. But if there is no falsehood in the nature of things, they will all be true. Nor can anything appear except to the eyes of the living soul. Therefore the soul is inseparable from the nature of things; Now the falsehood can be removed, sometimes not, it remains there. A.—I see that you have strengthened the conclusion more, but we have not advanced anything with what has been added, because, despite this, an objection bothers me, and that is that souls are born and die, from R.—Satisne considersti ne quid fearé dederis? A.—Satis quidem, sed nihil video quod me arguam temeritatis. A.—Ergo confectum est rerum naturam sine anima viva esse non posse. A.—Confectum hactenus, ut possint vicissim aliae nasci, aliae mori. A.—What if de natura rerum falsitas auferatur, nonne fiet ut vera sinr omnia? A.—Consequi video. A.—Responde unde tibi video paries iste verus esse. A.—Quia eius non fallar adspectu. A.—Ergo quia ita est ut videtur. A.—Etiam. A.—Si igitur aliquid inde falsum est quod aliter videtur atque est, inde verum quod ita ut est videtur, ablato eo qui videtur, nec falsum quidquam nec verum est. At si falsitas in rerum natura non sit, vera sunt omnia. Nec videri quidquam nisi vivirti animae potest. Manet igitur anima in rerum natura, si auferri falsitas non potest; manet, si potest. A.—Video robustius quidem esse factum quod iam conclusum erat, sed nihil hac adiectione promovimus. Nihilominus enim manet illud SAg. 1

luckily their survival in the world does not come from their immortality, but from the succession of one to another. 6. A.—Do you believe that corporeal things can be understood with the understanding? A.—Not certainly. R'—And do you believe that God uses the senses to know things? A.—I do not want to assert anything rashly about this point; but, as I conjecture, he in no way needs senses for what you say. A.—So only souls can feel. A.—Admit that proposition as probable. A.— And what do you say to this? This wall, if it is not true, is it not a wall? A.—Nothing is easier to grant. A.— Do you also grant me that nothing is a body if it is not a true body? A.—I also grant it to you. A.—The true being, then, what really is as it seems, and the corporeal can only be manifested to the senses, and the senses are proper to the soul, since there are, on the other hand, no bodies that are not true, therefore there can be no body if there is no soul. A.—You urge me a lot and I give in to your reasoning. quod plurimum me movet, nasci animas et interne; atque, ut non desint mundo, non earum immortalitate, sed successione provenire. 6. R.—Videnturne tibi quaeque corpórea, id est, sensibilia intellectu posse comprehendi? A.—Non videntur. A.—Quid illud, videtur tibi sensibus uti Deus ad res cognoscendas? A.—Nihil audeo de hac re temeré affirmare, sed, quantum coniicere datur, millo moda Deus utitur sensibus. A.—Ergo concludimus non sentiie posse nisi animam. A.—Conclude interim quantum probabiliter licet. A.—Quid illud, dasne istum parietem, si verus paries non sit, non esse parietem? A,—Nihil hoc facilius dederim. A.—Ñeque quidquam, si verum corpus non sit, corpus esse? A.—Tale etiam hoc est. A.—Ergo si nihil verum est, nisi ita sit ut videtur, nec quidquam corporeum videri nisi sensibus potest, nec will feel nisi anima, nec, si verum corpus non sit, corpus esse; restat ut corpus esse non possit nisi anima fuerit. A.—Nimis urges, et quid resistam non habeo.
Soliloquies CHAPTER WHAT

7. A.—Sharpen your attention now for what is coming. A.—I am at your service. R-—Here you have a stone; and it is true, because it is like us, it would be stone, and it will cease to be when we retire and it can only be perceived with the senses. A.—It's true. A.—Then there will be no stone in the hidden bosoms of the earth nor there where no one can see them; and only if we see it, it would be stone, and it will cease to be when we retire and no one else who is present sees it. And if you close the closets properly, no matter how many things you put in them, they contain nothing. Wood will not be wood in the hidden either, since everything latent in the intimacy of bodies that are not transparent escapes from sensitive perception. All of this, by logical necessity, has no being. Because if it existed, it would be true, and you have defined what is true; what is just as it seems, and all that neither manifests nor appears; therefore it is not true either. Do you have any objections to these conclusions? A.—They are consequences of my statements, and everything is so absurd that I am more willing to deny any of my premises than to maintain the truth of the conclusions. CAPUT VERUM

sing, wherever he is, cannot be subject to death. For although light, entering everywhere, illuminates a place, and due to the wonderful force of opposites it does not admit darkness in itself, it can nevertheless be extinguished, leaving the place in darkness. Thus, what resisted darkness, without somehow admitting it into itself, becoming extinct, gives rise to its opposite, as it could have given it by withdrawing. Therefore I fear that death comes to the body, like darkness to a place, sometimes the soul withdrawing from it like a light or also extinguishing itself there. There is, therefore, no security against bodily death, and a certain kind of death must be desired by which the living soul is separated from the body to go to a place where it cannot die, if this is possible. And if even this cannot happen, because the soul lights up in the same body, like a light, without being able to subsist alone elsewhere, and all death consists in the extinction of the soul or of life in the body, then a type of calm and secure life will have to be chosen, as the human condition allows, which I do not know how it can be achieved, the soul being mortal. Blessed a thousand times are those who achieved the certainty through their own conviction or the authority of others that death should not be feared, even when the soul is mortal. A.—With the premises that you have very cautiously granted me. Conversion (I 1,3).—The word conversion—"epistrophe"—is widely used in the writings of Plotinus, and appears in this prayer of Cassiciacus. In Plotinus, conversion is a turning to God as his beginning to contemplate Him. Christian conversion has a character, above all moral, of repentance of sins and forgiveness of them by the grace of God. "A pagan Neoplatonist and a Christian," says R. Arnou, "both speak of conversion, but, according to the tradition of the ancient prophets and the belief of the Gospel, turning to God is, above all, doing penance for sins, which is the great obstacle to union with God. For a Neoplatonist, on the contrary, to prepare for contemplation is to detach the eye, capable of seeing divine things, freeing it from the matter that obfuscates his insight."' The feeling of guilt permeates the entire Augustinian prayer, "while pagan Neoplatonism has no notion of sin."

It doesn't matter that the dough comes from pagan preparations. The spirit that burns and shines here is personally and personally Christian. Saint Augustine places the intuition of the self, revealed in thought, as the basis of his philosophy. In various places he has brandished the same weapon against skeptics. In Saint Augustine, the perception of one's own existence and thought is linked to the intuition of the intelligible. Simply doubt puts us in connection with the truth, inviscerated in the deepest strata of the self. The intuition of existence and Truth are concomitant and inseparable and have a much richer and more realistic content than the Cartesian "cogito". 19. The concept of truth (II 5-11).—St. Augustine strives here to recover a concept of truth that is objective and immune from all relativistic vices. The ancient sophists, with Protagoras, made man the measure of all things, and therefore, truth, a product of his spiritual activity. In vast sectors of modern thought the same doctrine triumphs. For Saint Augustine, verum est id quod est, the truth is what it is, independently of all subjective appreciation. Prior to man's thought is the being of things, which regulates it. Ancient moral philosophy had striven for the solution of this problem, which is the most interesting chapter in the philosophy of value. Theophrastus wrote a book about the happy life. Substantially it is the theme of Cicero's books: De finibus bonorum et malorum. 2. Well, it seems to me that men who, as navigators, can take advantage of philosophy are distinguished into three classes. The first is of those who, upon reaching the age of rational lucidity, with a small effort and slight help from the oars, change their route closely and take refuge in that peaceful port, where for the other citizens who can, they raise the splendid flag of some work of theirs, so that, warned by it, they may seek the same refuge. The second class, opposite to the previous one, includes those who, deceived by the flattering prosperity, entered the high seas, daring to make a pilgrimage far from their homeland, often forgetting it. If these, I don't know by what secret and ineffable mystery, find the wind in their sails, and taking it as favorable, they plunge into the deepest abysses of misery, conceited and joyful, because everywhere the perfidious serenity of delights and honors smiles upon them, what more favorable grace can be desired for them than some setback and setback in those things, so that, driven by them, they seek escape? And if this is not enough, a fierce storm will break out, contrary winds will blow, returning them, even with pain and groans, to solid and secure joys. But some of this class, because they have not gone far, do not need such strong blows to return. Such are those who, by the tragic vicissitudes of fortune or by the tortures and anxieties of vain affairs, instigated by leisure itself, have been constrained to take refuge in the reading of some very learned and wise books, and in contact with them their spirit has been awakened as in a port, from which no flattery and promise will be extracted from them by the smiling sea. I abandoned them, and crossed this path of the sea, fluctuating in the middle of the waves, I handed over to the academics the governance of my soul, indocile to all the winds. Then I came to this country, and found the north to guide me. Because I learned from our priest's frequent sermons and from some conversations with you that, when one tries to conceive God, every bodily image must be rejected. And let's say the same about the soul, which is one of the realities closest to him. But still, I confess, the attraction of women and the ambition for honors stopped me from giving myself immediately to the study of philosophy. When my aspirations were fulfilled, then, finally, as very happy men had achieved, I could, with unfurled sails, throw myself into its bosom and rest there. I read some—very few—books by Plato, of whom you were also very fond, and comparing with them the authority of the books whose pages declare the divine mysteries, I became so enraged that I would have broken all my anchors had I not been moved by the appreciation of some men. What was missing to shake my indolence and tardiness due to superfluous things but for a storm to favor me, contrary in my opinion? Thus, a very acute chest pain came over me, and then, unable to bear the burden of my profession, for which I sailed towards the sirens, I threw everything overboard to direct my broken and fixed ship to the port of long-awaited rest. 5.
You see, then, in what philosophy I navigate as in a port.

But it is of such vast extension and magnitude, although less dangerous, that it does not absolutely exclude all risk of error. I still don't know where on earth, which, without a doubt, is the only happy place, to enter and tread with my feet. I am not yet on firm ground, for I fluctuate and vacillate in the matter of the soul. Therefore I beg you for your virtue, for your kindness, for the bond and communication of souls, to lend me the help of your hand. I want to tell you to love me, so that I in turn reciprocate you with the same affection. Well, if I succeed, I think I will easily achieve the happy life in which you find yourself, as I presume. For this reason I wanted to write to you and offer you the first fruits of my dissertations, because they seem more religious and worthy of your name, so that you know my occupations and how I gather all my friends in this port, and here you can see the state of my mood, since I can find no other way to make it known to you. This is certainly a very appropriate offering, since we have both disputed about life, and I find nothing else that more justly deserves to be called a divine gift. Do not intimidate me with your eloquence, because the love of a thing drives away all fear, and I will despise the greatness of your fortune, because although great, it is propitious in you and favorably welcomes those it dominates. Now put your eyes on the present that I offer you. 6. November 13 was the day of my birth, and after a frugal meal, which was not to clip the wings of any genius, to all those not only that day, but always are ipse late patet, eiusque magnitudeo quamvis iam minus periculosum, non tamen penitus excludit errorem. Nam cui parti terrae, quae profecto una beata est, me admoveam atque contingam, prorsus Ignoro. Quid enim solidum tenui, cui adhuc de anima quaestio nutat et fluctuat? Quare obsecro te per virtutem tuam, per humanitatem, per animatum Inter se vinculum atque commercium, ut dexteram porrigas, hoc autem est, ut me ames, et a me vicissim te amari credas charumque haberi. Quod si impetravero, ad ipsam beatam vitam, cui te iam haerere praesumo, parvo tonatu facillime accessam.

Aptissime sane; nam de beata vita quaesivimus inter nos, nihílque alíud video quod magis Dei donum vocandum sit. Eloquentia tua territus non sum; quidquid enim amo, quamvis non assequar, tímete non possum: fortunee vero sublimitatem multo minus. Apud te enim veré, quamvis sit magna, secunda est; nam quibus dominatur, eosdem ipsos secundos facit. Sed iam quid afferam, quaeso te, attende. 6. The others doubted and argued among themselves how food could be necessary for the body, when we desired it for life, and life is a thing of the soul. I intervened saying: - Do you think that food is related to that part that grows and develops in us? Everyone agreed except Trigetius, who objected: - Why then haven't I grown in proportion to the appetite I have? “All bodies,” I told him, “have their limits in nature, and they cannot go beyond their limits; But this measure would be less if they lacked food, something that we easily notice in animals, since without eating they all reduce their volume and corpulence. "They grow weaker, they do not decrease," observed Licentius. — It is enough for what I am trying to do, because here we discuss whether food belongs to the body, and there is no doubt about it, because, by suppressing it, it becomes thinner. Everyone agreed with this opinion. 8. And about the soul, what do you say? I asked them. Won't you have your food? Don't you think that science is its delicacy? "Certainly," said the mother, "since I believe the soul is nourished by nothing else but the knowledge and science of things." De qua sententia cum Trygetius dubium is ostenderet:

— Well, haven't you yourself indicated today how and where the soul is nourished? Because shortly after you were eating, you said that you hadn't noticed the glass we were using because you were thinking and distracted by I don't know what things, and yet, you didn't give peace to your hand or your mouth. Where was your spirit then, who ate without paying attention? Believe me, even then the soul feeds on its own delicacies, that is, on its imaginations and thoughts, eager to perceive something. A quarrel broke out with these words, and I said to them: - Do you not grant me that the souls of very wise and learned men are richer and vaster in their kind than those of the ignorant? "It is a clear thing," they responded unanimously. — We rightly say, then, that the souls of the ignorant, horrendous of disciplines and good letters, are as if fasting and starving. "I believe," replied Trigetius, "that their souls are stuffed, but with vices and perversity." "That's the same thing," I told him, "don't doubt it, it's a certain sterility and hunger of souls." For as bodies lacking food often become sick and ulcerous, consequences of hunger, so their souls are full of illnesses, revealing their fasts. Because the ancients called foolishness or evil itself the mother of all vices, because it is nothing. And the virtue contrary to such vice is called frugality. Just as—Hodie—inquit illa—tu ipse nonne docuisti unde aut ubi anima pascatur? Nam post aliquantam prandii partem te dixisti non advertisse quo vasculo uteremur, quod alia nescio quae cogitasses, nec tamen ab ipsa ciborum parte abstinueras manus atque morsus. Ubi ígitur erat animus tuus, quo tempore illud, te vescente, non attcndebat? Inde, mihi crede, et talibus epulis animus pascitur, id est theoriis et cogitationibus suis, si per eas aliquid percipere possit. De qua re cum dubitanter streperent: —Nonne—inquam—conceditis hominum doctissimorum encouragements multo esse quam imperitorum quasi in suo genere pleniores atque maiores?

That word is derived from fruge, that is, from fruit, to signify a certain spiritual fertility, that other, nequitia, comes from sterility, from nothingness, because nothingness is that which flows, that dissolves, that liquefies, and always perishes and is lost. That is why we also call such men lost. On the other hand, it is something when it remains, when it remains firm, when it always is what it is, like virtue, whose main and most noble part is frugality and temperance. But if what I have said seems difficult to understand, you will certainly grant me that if the ignorant have their souls full, both for bodies and souls, there are two kinds of food: some healthy and beneficial and others deadly and harmful. 9. This being so, and finding out that man consists of body and soul, on this day of my birthday it seemed to me that I should not only refresh your bodies with more succulent food, but also gift your souls with some delicacy. What this delicacy is, if you don't lack appetite, I'll tell you. Because it is useless and wasted time to insist on feeding the unappetizing and fed up; and you have to sharpen your appetite to desire the food of the spirit more willingly than the food of the body. This is achieved by having a healthy spirit, because the sick, as well as the body, reject and despise food. From the gestures of their faces and voices I saw the appetite that everyone had to take and devour what had been prepared for them. 10. Threading my speech again, I continued: contrara virtus est, frugalitas nominatur. Ur igitur haec a fruge, id est a fructu propter quamdam animorum fecunditatem, ita illa ab sterilitate, hoc est a nihilo, nequitia nominata est: nihil est enim omne quod fluit, quod solvituti quod liquescit et quasi semper perit. I devise such homines eíiam perditos dicimus. Est autem aliquid, si manet, si constat, si semper tale est, ut est virtus, cuius magna pars est atque pulcherrima, quae temperantia et frugalitas dicitur. Sed si hoc obscurius est quam ut id iam vos videre possitis, certe illud conceditis, quia si animi imperitorum etiam ipsi pleni sunt, ut corporum, ita animorum duo alimentarum genera inveniuntur, unum salubre atque utile, alterum morbidum atque pestiferum. 9.

Quae cum ita sint, arbitror die natali meo, quoniam duo quaedam esse in homine convenir inter nos, id est, corpus atque animam, non me prandium paulo lautius corporibus nostris solum, sed et animís etiam exhíbete debené. Quod autem hoc sit prandium, si esuritis, proferam. Nam si vos invites et nuisances alere conabor, frustrate operam insumam; magisque votes facienda sunt, ut such epulas potius quam illas corporis desideretis. Quod eveniet si sani animi vestri fuerint: aegri enim, sicut in morbis ipsius corporis videmus, cibos suos recusant et respuunt. Omnes se vultu ipso et consentiente voce, quidquid piaeparassem iam sumere ac vorare velle dixerunt. 10. Atque ego rursus exordiens;

—Do we all want to be happy? As soon as he had said this, everyone unanimously approved it. —And do you think he is blessed who does not have what he desires? "No," everyone said. —And will he be happy who has everything he wants? Then the mother answered: •—If you want goods and have them, yes; But if he desires evil, even if he achieves it, he is unfortunate. Smiling and satisfied, I told her: - Mother, you have conquered the very castle of philosophy. You have lacked the words to express yourself like Cicero in the book entitled Hortensias, composed for the defense and panegyric of philosophy: Here everyone, not philosophers precisely, but willing to discuss, say that those who live as they want are happy. Deep mistake! Because desiring what is not convenient is the height of misfortune. It's not so much not getting what you want as it is getting what doesn't suit you. Because the perversity of the will brings greater evils than fortune brings good. She approved these words with such exclamations that, completely forgetting her sex, we believed we were sitting next to a great man, while I considered, as best I could, from what divine source I drank those truths. —Beatos esse nos volumus?—inquam. Vix hoc effuderam, occurrerunt una voce consentientes. —Videturne vobis—inquam—beatus esse qui quod vult non habet? —Negaverunr. -Crux? omnis qui quod vult habet, beatus est? Tum mater: —Si bona—inquit—velit et habeat, beatus est; si autem mala velit, quamvis habeat, miser est. Cui ego arridens atque gestiens. —Ipsam-inquam-prorsus, mater, arcem philosophiae tenuisti. Nam tibi procul dubio verba defuerunt, ut non sicut Tullius te moda panderes, cuius de hac sententia verba ista sunt. Nam in Hortensio, quem de laude ac defensione philosophiae librum fecit 3. Ecce autem, ait, non philosopbi quidem, sed prompti tamen ad disputandum, omnes aiunt esse beatos qui vivtmt ut ipsi velint. Falsum id quidem; velle enim quod non deceat, idem ipsum misemmum. Nec tam miserum est non adipisci quod velis quam adipisci velle quod non oporteat. Plus enim mali pravitas voluntatis affert, quam fortune cuiquam boni. In quibus verbis illa sic exclamabat, ut obliti penitus sexus eius, magnum aliquem virum consider nobiscum crederemus, me interim, quantum poteram, intelligente ex quo illa et quam divino fonte manarent.

"Tell us now, then," said Licentius, "what the aspirant for happiness should desire and in what objects the desire of the aspirant for happiness should be grazed." - On the day of your birth, send me an invitation, if you wish, and everything you present to me I will receive with my love. With the same disposition I want you to sit today at the banquet at my house, without asking for what perhaps has not been prepared. He appearing repentant and embarrassed by the warning, I added: - On one point we all agree: no one can be happy if they lack what they want; but neither is he who brings everything together to the measure of his desire. Isn't that so? They all agreed. 11. Answer me now: is everyone who is not happy unhappy? They all showed their agreement, without hesitation. — Therefore everyone who does not have what they want is unhappy. They all approved. —What, then, must man seek to achieve his happiness? Nor will this delicacy be lacking in our banquet to satisfy Licencio's hunger, since he must achieve, in my opinion, what he can obtain simply by wanting it. This seemed obvious to them. "Then," I said, "it must be something permanent and secure, independent of luck, not subject to the vicissitudes of life." Qua conditione hodie apud me ut epuleris peto, nec flagites quod fortasse non est paratum. Quem cum modestae ac verecundae commonitionis suae poeniteret: —Ergo illud—inquam—convenit inter nos, ñeque quemquam beatum esse posse, qui quod vult non habet; ñeque omnem qui quod vult habet beatum esse? For what is fleeting and mortal we cannot possess at our whim, nor at the time we please. They all made signs of approval, but Trigetius said: - There are many fortunate people who possess abundance and ease of obsolete and perishable things, but very pleasant for this life, without lacking anything that their desire asks for. "And the one who has some fear," I asked him, "do you think he is happy?" - No way. —Then can he who can lose what he loves live free of fear? "You can't," he replied. —It is thus that those assets of fortune can be lost; Therefore he who loves and possesses them cannot in any way be happy. He surrendered to this conclusion. And here my mother observed: - Even though she is sure of not losing those goods, she cannot satisfy herself with them, and she is all the more unhappy as she is more destitute at all times. I answered him: - And what do you think of someone who abounds and has nothing in these goods, but has set a limit and limit to his desires and lives with temperance and contentment with what he has? Won't you think it's happy? "It won't be," she replied, "because of those things, but because of the moderation with which he enjoys them." "Very well," I told him; nor does my question admit another ullis subiectum casibus esse debent. Nam quidquid mortale et caducum est, non potest a nobis quando volumus et quamdiu volumus haberi. Assentiebantur omnes. Sed Trygetius: —Sunt—inquit—multi fortuneti, qui eas ipsas res fragiles casibusque subiectas, tamen iucundas pro hac vita cumúlate largeque possideant, nec quidquam illis eorum quae volunt desit. Cui ego: —Qui timet—inquam—, videturne tibi beatus esse? —Non videtur—inquit. —Ergo quod amat quisque si amittere potest, potestne non timere? —Non potest—inquit. —Amitti autem possunt illa fortuita. Non igitur haec qui amat et possidet, potest ullo moda beatus esse. Nihil repugnavit. Hoc loco autem mater: Etiamsi securus sit—inquit—, ea se omnia non esse amissurum, tamen talibus satiari non poterit. Ergo et eo miser quo semper est indigus.

Cui ego: —Quid—inquam—his ómnibus abundans rebus atque circumfluens, si cupiendi modum sibi statuat eisque contentus decenter iucundeque perfruatur, nonne tibi videtur beatus? —Non ergo—inquit—illis rebus, sed animi sui moderatione beatus est. —Optime—inquam—, nec huic interrogationi aliud nec abs te aliud

answer or you should have answered differently. Let us conclude, then, that whoever wishes to be happy must procure permanent goods, which cannot be taken away by any reverse of fortune. "We have been in possession of that truth for some time now," said Trigetius. —Does God seem eternal and always permanent to you? "That is so true," Licencio observed, "that it is not even worth asking." The others, with pious devotion, agreed. — Therefore he who possesses God is happy. 12. They all joyfully admitted the last idea. — Nothing remains for us — I continued — but to find out who has God in mind, because they are the truly happy ones. Tell me your opinion on this point. "He who lives well has God," Licencio said. "May God possess him who fulfills his will in everything," said Trigetius, to the applause of Lastidianus. The smallest of all said: - God possesses the one whose soul is clean from the impure spirit. The mother applauded everyone, but especially the child. Because the greatest and most deplorable poverty is to lack wisdom, and he who possesses it has everything. 28. — Therefore the misery of the soul — I continued — is stupidity, contrary to wisdom as death is to life, as a happy life is to an unhappy one, since there is no middle ground between the two. No wonder some call frugality the mother of all virtues. I admit this idea, says Cicero in a popular speech: Let everyone stick to what he wants; but I judge that frugality, that is, moderation and temperance, is the most excellent virtue. Very wise and timely sentence. He had his sights set on the fruit, that is, on the fruitfulness of being, contrary to non-being. Since vulgar usage has limited frugality to sobriety or parsimony, he added two more names: moderation and temperance. Let us consider these two names more carefully. 32. Moderation or moderation was said of manner, and temperance, of temperies. Where there is moderation and temperance, there nothing is excess or lack. It, then, understands plenitude, contrary to poverty, much better than abundance, because in the latter a certain affluence and excessive overflow of a thing is suggested. And when this happens, moderation is lacking, and excessive things need measure or mode. Therefore abundance presupposes a certain poverty, while measure excludes the excessive and the defective. Opulence itself, examined well, understands the mode, since it is derived from ope, help. But how can the excessive be of help, if it is often more annoying than the little? Both the excessive and the defective lack measure, and in this sense it is shown

they are destitute and needy. Wisdom is, therefore, the measure of the soul, because it is contrary to stupidity, and stupidity is poverty, and poverty is contrary to plenitude. Conclude that wisdom is plenitude. Thus, in plenitude there is measure. Therefore the measure of the soul is in wisdom. Hence that famous saying, of maximum utility for life: In everything avoid excess. 33- But we agreed at the beginning of our discussion today that if we managed to identify misery and destitution, we would consider the non-destitute as blessed. Well then; We have already reached this result. Therefore to be happy is to not suffer need, to be wise. And if you ask me what wisdom is (a concept to whose exploration and examination reason devotes itself, as best it can, now), I will tell you that it is the moderation of the spirit, by which it maintains a balance, without spilling out too much or shrinking more than plenitude requires. And it is poured out in excess by lust, ambition, pride and other passions of the same kind, with which intemperate and unfortunate men seek for themselves pleasures and power. And it is limited by avarice, fear, sadness, greed and other affections, whatever they may be, and through them men experience and confess their misery. But when the soul, having found wisdom, makes it the object of its contemplation; when, to put it in the words of this child, he remains united to her and, insensitive to the seduction of vain things, does not look at her deceptive appearances, whose weight and attraction he usually pushes away and knocks down.

12. Summus Modus, Ventas (IV 34).—St. Augustine subtly elevates himself to the Trinity through the concepts of modus, sapientia, veritas. The acuity of the catechumen is already manifested, as he struggles to rationally stammer the ineffable mystery, to which he will later dedicate his most profound book. The Truth and Wisdom, which is Christ, come from the Supreme mode or Measure, original and first source of all that exists. There is an essential connection in the Father and the Son. By giving the Father the name of Modus or Sum Measure, he qualifies him as the origin of all proportion and harmony, universal rule, principle and ultimate reason for the very intelligibility of things. Modus and Veritas are coeternal and coexisting. The Measure was never found without the Truth nor the Truth outside the Measure, from which it proceeds by generation (gignitur), and to which it returns by a perfect regression. At the same time, the Truth makes the supreme Measure known to us, because the Son is the revelation, and the word of the Father, and the Medium or Mediator of the return of all things to Him. The Trinitarian and Christological ideas of the greatest Christologist of the West come to light here. One already notices the Augustinian tendency "to build from the beginning something like a metaphysics of Christ," according to E. Przywara. All the great problems that arise between the Creator and the creature find the only solution in Christ. 13. The two books about order were the result of three conversations held about divine Providence on November 16, 17 and 23, 386, and they reveal to us one of the facets of the Augustinian spirit. It is insisted, perhaps too much, that Saint Augustine's speculation is unilaterally inclined towards the probing of interior and spiritual realities. I only want to know God and the soul, which is his mirror. And it is forgotten that the universe is also a vestige of God and reflects the divine excellencies, although with less brilliance and clarity than the image or the created spirit. The books of order constitute the first attempt to probe the problems of the universe, and in them a keen feeling for nature is manifested, which has influenced the education of the sensitivity of the spirit of Europe. Godofredo Quadri says well: "Without a doubt, Saint Augustine, who, according to his book De vera religione', listens in ecstasy to the song of the nightingale, finding vestiges of that harmony that is the law of all things and in the form of vital energy acts in all beings in diverse ways; the one who in the Dialogues of Casiciacus has such joyful accents before the beauty of nature and describes the life of those days in a way that seems like an idyll. terrestrial, as Hans Becker rightly notes, has a very different mentality from that monk of the Thebaid who moves away from the reed field, moved by the wind, in whose whisper he believes he hears the voice of the devil, as read in the Syriac legend. The abbot Antony once visited some monks, who lived next to some reeds, which, swaying by the breath of the wind, rubbed against each other. "They are the reeds moved by the wind," they replied. "Truly I tell you," he replied, "that if the solitary hears nothing more than the chatter of a little bird, he will not be able to achieve the peace of heart he desires. And how will it be possible for you, living here next to that reed field? There is a fundamental difference between the attitude of that monk and that of Augustine, for whom solitude is worthy of praise as a particular position of the spirit above earthly passions, but without exalting it? too much"\

It is a very arduous and very rare thing, friend Cenobius, to achieve knowledge and declare to men the order of things, whether that of each individual, or above all that of the whole or universality with which this world is moderated and governed. Added to this is that, even if one can do it, it is not easy to have a listener worthy and prepared for such divine and dark things, either by the merits of one's life, or by the exercise of erudition. And yet, such is the ideal of the best minds, and even those who already contemplate, as it were, with their heads held high, the pitfalls and storms of life, desire nothing more than to learn and know how, as God governs human affairs, so much perversity spreads everywhere, so that, it seems,

Thus, the spirit, withdrawn into itself, understands the beauty of the universe, which took its name from unity. Therefore, it is not possible to see that beauty in the souls scattered externally, whose greed engenders destitution, which can only be avoided by detachment from the crowd. And I call a multitude, not of men, but of all things that our senses encompass. Don't even wonder that one is poorer the more things one wants to embrace. Because just as in a circle, however large it may be, there is only one point to which the others converge, called the center by geometers, and although all the parts of the circle can be divided infinitely, only the center point is at equal distance from the others, and as if dominating them by a certain right of equality. But if you want to go anywhere from there, the more things you go after, the more they are all lost: thus the spirit, scattered from itself, receives innumerable blows and sees itself exhausted and reduced to the poverty of a mendicant when all its nature drives it to seek unity everywhere and the crowd vetoes it. 4. Quare si tibi molestum non est atque id fieri debenré arbitraris, roga quod vis: defendam, quantum possum, ordinem rerum nihilque praeter ordinem fieri posse asseram. Tantum enim eum animo imbibi atque hausi, ut etiamsi me quisquam in hac disputatione will surpass, etiam hoc nulli fearitati, sed rerum ordini tribuam. Ñeque enim res ipsa, sed Licentius superabitur.
