coughs can reach wisdom. So let's get to work, Licencio; let us confidently foster piety and tread with our feet the pernicious fire of our smoldering passions. 11. Ask me now, I beg you, he said, so that I can explain with your words and mine this I don't know how great I feel. —Answer me first: why does it seem to you that this water does not flow randomly, but in order? That it runs and is carried by wooden aqueducts for our use and employment, well belongs to order, as it is the reasonable work of human industry, which wants to take advantage of its course for cleaning and drinking, and it is right that it should be done this way, according to the needs of the places. But the fact that the leaves fall in the way you say, giving rise to the phenomenon that admires us, how can it be related to order? Isn't it more of a coincidence? "But," he replied, "can he who sees clearly that nothing can be done without sufficient cause think of any other way for the leaves to fall?" So what, do you want me to describe the position of the trees, and their branches, and the weight that nature itself gave to the leaves? Nor is it a matter of pondering now the mobility of the air that drags them, or the smoothness with which they descend, nor the different ways of falling, according to the state of the atmosphere, the weight, the figure, and innumerable other more unknown causes. The power of our senses does not reach this point and these are entirely hidden things; but I do not know how (which is sufficient for our question) it is clear to our eyes that nothing is done without vates sunt quicumque possunt esse sapientes. Ergo aggrediamur, Licenti, freti pietate culturators, et vestigüs nostris ignem perniciosum fumosarum cupiditatum opprimamus. 11. Iam—inquit—interroga, oro te, si possim hoc tantum nescio quid explicare, et tuis verbis et meis. —Hoc ipsum—inquam—mihi responds, primo unde tibi video aqua ista non teréré sic sed ordine influere. Nam quod illa ligneolis canalibus superlabitur et ducitur usque in usus nostros, potest ad ordinem pertinere. Factum est enim ab hominibus ratione utentibus, ut uno eius itinere simul et biberent et lavarent et pro locorum opportunitatibus consequens erat ut ita ieront.

Quod vero illa, ut dicis, folia sic incidenterunt, ut hoc quod admirati sumus eveniret, quo tandem rerum ordine ac non potius casu factum putabimus? —Quasi vero—inquit ille—aliter atque ceciderunt debuisse aut potuisse cadete cuiquam videri potest, serenissime intuenti nihil posse fieri sine causa. Crux? iam vis persequar situs arborum atque ramorum, ipsumque pondus quantum natura foliis imposuit? Quid, aeris vel mobilitatem qua volitant, vel mollitiem qua descendunt, several que lapsus pro affectione caeli, pro onere, pro figuris suis, caeterisque innumerabilibus atque obscurioribus causis, quid me attinet quaerere? reason. An impertinent curious person could continue asking why there are trees there, and I will answer that men have been guided by the fertility of the land. —What if the trees are not fruitful and have been born by chance? —To that I will respond that we know very little and that nature cannot be blamed for having acted without reason by putting them there. What else? Either you convince me that he does something for no reason or you believe that everything follows a certain order of causality.
HE DIRECTS EVERYTHING WITH ORDER

12. I replied to Licentius: - Although you consider me an impertinent curious person, and I certainly must be for you for having interrupted your conversation with Pyramus and Thisbe, I will insist on proposing some questions to you. This nature, which, according to your way of thinking, all shines with order - leaving innumerable other things - can you tell me for what use it created non-fruit trees? When the person questioned was looking for an answer, Trigetius said: - But is the usefulness of trees limited only to the fruit? Don't other things bring its benefit: its very shadow, its wood and, finally, even the leaves? nescio quomodo animum non latet, nihil fieri sine causa. Potcst enim odiosus percontator pergere quaerere: quae causa erat ut ibi arbores poneentur? Respondebo secutos esse nomines uber terrae. —What if fructuosae arbores non sunt ac will fear natae sunt? —Et hic responderbo nos parum videre; nam recklessm, quae illas genuit, nequáquam esse naturam. Quid plural? Aut aliquid sine causa fieri docear aut nihil fieri nisi certo causaum ordine credite. CAPUT

12. Cui ego: —Licet—inquam—me odiosum percontatorem voices (vix enim possum non esse, qui expugnavi ne cum Pyramo et Thysbe colioquereris) pergam tamen quaerere abs te. Natura ista quam vis videri ordinatam, cui bono, ut de caeteris rebus innumerabilibus taceam, istas ipsas arbores quae fructus non afferunt, procreavit? At illo cogitante quid diceret, ait Trygetius: —Numquidnam usus bushrum in solis fructibus praebetur hominibus? Quanta sunt alia, quae umbra, quae lignis, postremo quae ipsis frondibus seu foliis fiant? a See note 5: Bl principle of sufficient reason.

"Do not give this solution to the proposed question," Licencio cut him off. Because innumerable examples can be found of things of no benefit to men or of such little and unknown use that we can hardly defend them. Let him rather tell us if there is anything without a sufficient cause. “We will briefly touch on that point later,” I told him. It is not necessary for me to act as a teacher, because you, who profess the certainty of such a high doctrine, have not yet taught me anything new, and I am so eager to learn that I spend days and nights in that exercise. 13. — In a brave situation, you guys! Is it perhaps because I follow you more lightly than these leaves in the wind, which drags them to the current of the water, so that it is not enough to say that they fall, but rather that they are carried away? Well, what else is it for Licentius to become Augustine's teacher, and nothing less than in the most intimate questions of philosophy? "Don't stoop so low," I replied, "don't exalt myself too much, because in philosophy I'm still a child, I don't even worry, when directing my questions, through whom I am answered by the One Whom I present my laments every day, of whom I predict that you will be a vate one day; and that one day may not be far away. Others also, apart from this kind of studies, can teach us something when they are associated with those who argue with the system of skillful questions. And that something is worth its own. Don't you see how the same leaves — to use your simile —, dragged by the —Noli obsecro—inquit ille—interrogationibus eius haec reddere. Innumerabilia sunt enim quae proferri possunt, ex quibus nulla est hominibus utilitas, aut certe ita latet vcl imbecilla est, ut ab hominibus, praesertim nobis, erui defendive non possit. Ipse potius nos doceat, quomodo aliquid fiat quod non causa praecesserit. —Post-inquam-ista videbimus. Non enim iam me necesse est esse doctorem, cum tu qui iam tantae rei te certum esse professus es, adhuc me nihil docueris nimium discere cupientem et propter hoc solum dies noctesque vigilantem. 13. “What do you mean to me?” he asked. An quia levius te sequor quam ista folia ventos, quibus in profluentem aquam iaciuntur, ut eis cadere parum sit nisi etiam trahantur?

Nam quid aliud erit cum Licentius et Augustinum et ea quae sunt in media philosophia docet? —Noli obsecro—inquam—aut te tantum abiicere aut me extollere. Nam et ego in philosophia puer sum et non nimis curo, cum interrogo, per quem mihi ille responderat, qui me quotidie querulum accipit: cuius te quidem credo quandoque vatem futurum; ñeque hoc quandoque forsitan longum est. Sed tamen alii quoque multum sepositi ab huiusmodi studiis docere aliquid possunt, cum disserentium societati quasi vinculis interrogationum coarctantur. idem autem aliquid non est nihil. An non vides (tuo enim simili utar libentius) illa ipsa folia quae feruntur ventis,

wind and floating on the current, can they offer their resistance to the course of the rushing water, warning men about the order of Nature, if we accept your thesis as valid? 14. Licentius, jumping for joy on his bed, exclaimed: - Who will deny, O great God, that you administer everything in order? How all things are related to each other in the universe and with what orderly succession they are directed to their outcomes! How many and various events have not occurred for us to start this discussion! How many things are done so that we can find you! Where but from the same universal order does this same thing flow and spring, that is, that we were awake and you were attentive to the sound of water and investigating the cause of such an ordinary phenomenon, without finding it? A little mouse also intervened so that I could come out to the scene. Finally, your own speech, perhaps without your intention—no one is the owner of whether any idea comes to mind—I don't know how it flutters around in my mind, inspiring me with the response I should give. Well, I ask you: if you write about the dispute we have here, as you have proposed, and it is spread to some extent, reaching the fame of men, will it not seem like such a serious thing to you, worthy of the answer of some great soothsayer or Chaldean, who, when asked about it, would have answered before it was verified? And if he had answered, it would have been considered such a divine thing; so worthy of being celebrated with universal applause, that no one would dare to ask why a fallen leaf from a tree or a restless mouse was bothersome to a man resting in his bed. For are these predictions of the future the quae undis innatant, resistere aliquantum praecipitanti se flumini et de rerum ordine nomines commonere, si tamen hoc quod abs te defenditur verum est? 14. Hic ille lecto etiam exsiliens prae laetitia: —Quis neget, Deus magne—inquit—, te cuneta ordine administrare? Quam se omnia tenent! quam ratis successionibus in nodes suos urgentur! quanta et quam fines facta sunt ut haec loqueremur! quanta fiunt ut te inveniamus! Unde enim hoc ipsum, nisi ex rerum ordine manat et ducitur, quod evigilavimus, quod illum sonum advertisti, quod quaesisti tecum causam, quod ru causam tantillae rei non invenisti? Sorex etiam prodit, ut ego vigilans prodar.

Postremo tuus etiam ipse sermo, te fortasse id non agent (non enim cuiquam in potestate est quid veniat inmentem), sic nescio quomodo circumagitur ut me ipse doceat quid tibí debenam I will respond. Namque, oro te, si haec quae a nobis dicta sunt, litteris, ut instituisti, mandata pervagentur paulo latius ad hominum famem, nonne ita res magna videbitur ut de illa consultus aliquis vates magnus aut Chaldaeus I will respond debuerit, multo antequam evenit? Quod si respondisset, ita divinus diceretur, ita efferretur laudibus omniuffl, ut tamen ex eo nemo quaerere auderet cur folium ab arbore ceciderit aut utrum mus

Did any of them happen on your own or were you required by the consultant to say them? And if I were to guess that an important book was to be published and I saw that that fact was necessary, because otherwise I would not be able to guess it, then both the fall of the leaves in the field and everything that little animal does at home, everything would be linked to order, the same as this writing. Because with these words we are making arguments that, if such insignificant events had not preceded us, would not have occurred to us nor would they have been exposed or taken into account to bequeath them to posterity. So no one asks me why each of these things happen. It is enough to know that nothing is generated, nothing is made without a sufficient cause, which produces it and brings it to its end. CHAPTER
ORDER UNDERSTANDS EVERYTHING

15. “From what you have said, it is clear,” I told him, “that you have not heard as a teenager how much has been written against divination by serious authors. But answer now, not if something is verified without sufficient reason, because I see that you do not want to respond to this, but if this order whose defense you have taken seems to you good or bad. And he answered loudly: "Have you not proposed the question to me in such a way that I can resoberrans iacenti homini molestus fuerit?" Numquidnam enim taliafutura quisquam illorum aut per se dixit aliquando, aut a consultante coactus est dicere? Atqui, si futurum quemdam librum non ignobílem diceret et id necessario eventurum videret (non enim posset aliter divinare) profecto quidquid volitatio foliorum in agro, quidquid vilissima bestiola in domo facir, tam sunt in rerum ordine necessaria quam illae litterae. His enim verbis fiunt, quae sine illis praecedentibus vüissimis rebus nec inmentem vinore possent, nec ore proceedé posterisque mandari. Quare iam, rogo, nemo ex me quaerat cur quidque fiat. Satis est nihil fieri, nihil gigni quod non aliqua causa genuerit ac moveit.

15. —Hic apparet te—inquam—nescire, adolescens, quam tumba et a qualibus viris contra divinationem dicta sint. Sed respond nunc, non utrum fiat aliquid sine causa (nam id iam video te nolle I will respond) sed ordo iste susceptus tuus bonumne quídquam an malum tibi esse videatur. Et ille submurmurans: —Non—inquit—sic rogasti, ut unum e duobus queam I will respond. a See note 6: Divination among the ancients. S.Ag. 1

consider one of the two things. Because I see a middle ground here. The order does not seem good or bad to me. "What do you think," I urged him, "that at least it is contrary to order?" "Nothing," he said. How can what occupies everything, what reigns everywhere, have an opposite? For what is contrary to order must be found outside of order. And I see nothing placed out of order, nor can it be thought that there is anything contrary to it. "Then isn't error contrary to order?" Trigetius asked him. "Not at all," he replied. Well, I see no one who errs without cause. And the series of causes belongs to the order. And error not only has causes that produce it, but effects that follow it. Consequently, what is not outside of order cannot be contrary to order. 16. When Trigetius fell silent, I was filled with joy seeing how that teenager, the son of a very dear friend of mine, became mine by spiritual filiation; and not only this, but he grew and became greater with his friendship for me; and having distrusted its application even to become mediocre in letters, I now saw it, despising all its wealth, launch itself with all its impetus into the very heart of philosophy. When I was silently marveling at this, burning with the desire to congratulate him, he, as if caught up in some idea, exclaimed: "Oh, if only I could say what I want!" Where, where are you, words? Come to my aid. Goods and evils are within the order. Believe if you want, because I don't know how to explain it. Video hic enim quamdam medietatem. Nam ordo mihi nec bonum nec malum videtur. —Quid saltem censes—inquam—ordini esse contrarium? —Nihil—ait ille—. Nam quomodo esse contrarium quidquam potest ei rei quae totum occupavit, totum obtinuit? Quod enim erit ordini contrarium, necesse erit esse praeter ordinem. Nihíl autem esse praeter ordinem video. Nihil igitur ordini oportet putare esse contrarium. —Ergone—ait Trygetius—contrarius ordini error non est? "No way," he asked. Nam neminem video errare sine causa. Causarum autem series ordine includitur. Et error ipse non solum gignitur causa, sed etiam gignit aliquid cuius causa sit. Quamobrem quo extra ordinem non est, eo non potest ordini esse contrarius. 16.

Et cum tacuisset Trygetius egoque meipsum non caperem gaudio, quod videbam adolescentm charissimi amici filium etiam meum fieri, nec solum, verum in amicum quoque iam mihi arisere atque grandescere, et cuius studium vel in mediocre litteras desperaveram, quasi regard possessione sua toto Impetu in mediam vinore philosophiam. Quod dum tacitus miror et exaestuo in gratulationem, súbito ille quasi mente quadam correptus exclamat: — O si possem dicere quod voló! Rogo, ubi, ubi estis, verba succurrite. Et bona et mala in ordine sunt. Credite, si vultis, nam quomodo id explicem nescio.
God DOES NOT LOVE EVIL, EVEN THOUGH IT BELONGS TO ORDER

17. I, full of astonishment, was silent. Trigetius, when, after the intoxication of his outburst had passed, he saw him more affable and accessible, he urged him: "What you say seems absurd and contrary to the truth to me, Licentius; Have a little patience to put up with me and don't interrupt me with your voices. "Say what you like," he replied; You will not take away from me what I glimpse and is almost at my hands. "I hope," said the other, "you do not deviate from the order you defend or make yourself guilty of neglecting God, to soften my expression." Because is there anything more impious than saying that even evils are within order? For God certainly loves order. "She loves him, no doubt," replied Licentius; from Him it proceeds and with Him it is found. And if something can be said on such a lofty subject with more decorum, you should think about it, because I am not fit to declare these things now. "What am I going to think?" Trigetius asked him. I take your words as they sound, and what I understand is enough for me. Because you have certainly said that evils are within order and that this order comes from the supreme God and loves him. From which it follows that evils come from Him and He wants them. CAPUT
DEUS NON DILIGIT MALA LICET AD ORDINEM PERTINENT

17. Ego mirar et tacebam. Trygetius autem ubi vidit hominem paululum quasi digesta ebrietate affabilem factum redditumque colloquio: —Absurdum—inquit—mihi videtur, Licenti, et plañe alienum a veritate quod dicis; sed queeso patiare me paululum, nec disturbances clamitating. —Díc quod vis—ait ille—; non enim metuo ne me auferas ab eo quod video ac penis teneo. —Utinam—inquit—ab eo quem defendis ordine devius non sis, non tanta in Deum fearis (ut mitius loquar) incuria. Quid enim potuit dici magis impium, quam etiam mala ordine contineri? Certe enim Deus amat ordinem. —I will see amat—ait ille—; ab ipso manat et cum ipso est. Et si quid potest de re tantum alta convenientius dici, cogita, quaeso, ipse tecum. Nec enim sum idoneus qui te ista nuncczam. "Quid cogitem?" asked Trygetius. Accipio prorsus quod dicis satisque mihi est in eo quod intelligo. Certe enim et mala dixisti ordine contineri et ipsum ordinem manare a summo Deo atque ab eo diligi. Ex quo sequitur ut et mala sint a summo Deo et mala Deus diligat.

18. In this conclusion Licentius feared. But he, lamenting the difficulty of the words, without seeking an adequate response, but rather embarrassed by the form of the response, said: - God does not want evils, because they do not belong to the order that God loves them. That is why He loves order very much, because He does not love evils, which, how can they not be within order when God does not want them? See, this very thing belongs to the order of evil, not being loved by God. Does it seem little order to you that God loves the good and does not love the evil? Thus, even evils are not outside the order, because God does not want them, and loves, instead, order. He wants to love good things and hate evil, which is a complete order and of a divine disposition. Order and disposition that preserve the harmony of all things through different elements, making the same evils necessary in a certain way. In this way, as with certain antitheses, by the combination of contrary things, which in oratory please so much, the universal beauty of the world is produced. 19- There was a brief pause of silence; but, suddenly standing up on the side where Trigetius had his bed, he urged him: "Tell me, please, if God is just." The other was silent, because, as he later confessed, he admired and feared another sudden speech inflamed with new inspiration from his fellow student and friend. Seeing him silent, Licentius continued: - Because if you answer me that God is not just, you will see what you are doing, since not long ago you criticized me for impiety. And yes, 18. In qua conclusione timui Licentio. At ille ingemiscens difficiúltate verborum nec omnino quaerens quid responderet, sed quemadmodum quod responderdum erat promeret: —Non diligit Deus mala—inquit—•; nec ob aliud, nisi quia ordinis non est ut Deus mala diligat. Et ordinem ideo multum diligit, quia per eum non diligit mala. At vero ipsa mala qui possunt non esse in ordine, cum Deus illa non diligat? Nam iste ipse est malorum ordo ut non diligantur a Deo. An parvus rerum ordo tibi videtur, ut et bona Deus diligat et non diligat mala?

Ita nec praeter ordinem sunt mala, quae non diligit Deus, et ipsum tamen ordinem diligit: hoc ipsum enim diligit diligere bona, et non diligere mala, quod est magni ordinis, et divinae dispositionis. Who ordo atque dispositio quia universitatis congruentiam ipsa distinctione custodit, fit ut mala etiam esse necesse sit. Ita quasi ex antithetis quodammodo, quod nobis etiam in oratione iucundum est, id est ex contrariis, omnium simul rerum pulchritudo figuratur. 19- Post hoc intersiluit rnodice. Et suddenly sese erigens qua Trygetius lectum habebat: —Nam quaero ex te, quaeso—inquit—, iustusne sit Deus? Tacebat ille, nimis, ut postea retulit, admirans et horrens, súbito condiscipuli et familiaris sui afflatum nova inspiratione sermonem. Quo tácente, ille ita secutus est: Si enim Deum iustum non esse responderis, tu videris quid agas, qui me dudum impietatis arguebas. Si autem, ut nobis traditur, nosque ipsius

According to the doctrine that we receive and the feeling of the need for order persuades us, God is just, without a doubt he is, because he gives to each what is his. And what distribution fits where there is no distinction? And what distinction, if everything is good? And what can be out of order, if God's justice treats good and bad according to what they deserve? But we all affirm that God is just. Then everything is enclosed within order. Having finished this speech, he jumped out of bed, and with the softest voice, because no one answered him, he said to me: - Are you saying anything to me either, who has provoked this discussion? I answered: 20. —; Hey! I see that a new enthusiasm takes over you now. But I will express my opinion during the day, which already seems to be approaching, unless the glare from the window is from the moon. At the same time, we must make an effort, Licencio, so that oblivion does not take away things as beautiful as those you have said. Our literary occupation demands that everything be remembered. I will tell you carefully what I think, disputing against you according to my strength, because my greatest triumph will be to be defeated by you. But if perhaps your weakness, still insufficiently strengthened with the erudition of the arts to support the cause of such a great God, yields to cunning and acute reasoning in favor of human errors, whose defense I will take charge of, that same will teach you the lack of new strength you have to climb up to Him with more ordinis necessitate sentimus, iustus est Deus, sua cuique distribuendo utique iustus est. Quae autem distributio dici potest, ubi distinctio mile est? Aut quae distinctio, si bona sunt omnia? Quidve praeter ordinem reperiri potest, si Dei iustitia bonorum malorumque meritis sua cuique redduntur? Iustum autem Deum omnes fatemur. Totum igitur ordine includitur. Quibus dictis resilit e strato, et iam lenior voce, cum ei verbum nemo faceret: —Nihilne mihi—inquit—vel tu qui compulisti ad ista, answer? Cui ego: 20. —Nova nunc religio isthaec in te incessit cedo *—inquam—. Sed quod videbitur, per diem respondero, qui mihi iam videtur rediré, nisi lunae est ille qui fenestris fulgor inducitur. But as for this lower part through which he uses the bodily senses—which I believe should not be taken into account when speaking of the wise man—I confess that I do not know it nor can I conjecture what it is. 6. "Then you deny," I told him, "that the wise man not only consists of soul and body, but even of the entire soul, since it would be madness to deny that the portion that he uses of the senses also belongs to it. And if we do not put the same faculty of feeling in the intellectual power, it will not be necessary to put it anywhere in the soul either. "It's not an easy thing to refuse what you say," I told him. ORDERED THEY CONTRIBUTE TO THE DECORUM OF THE UNIVERSE 11. But let us return to order, so that Licencio may someday be restored to us. Now, then, I ask you if everything that a fool does is also done in order. Notice the trap in the question. An affirmative answer destroys your definition: the order is by which God does all things, if the fool also works with the same order in everything he does. And if order is lacking in things done foolishly, there is, without a doubt, something outside of order and this is not universal; and neither of the two things pleases you. Be careful, I beg you, not to confuse everything under the pretext of defending order. As Licentius was still absent, Trigetius took his turn, answering: - It seems easy to me to defeat your objection, but no simile occurs to me now to illustrate my thoughts with more force and clarity. I will present my ideas and you will complete them with the light of your ingenuity. For great service has been provided by the comparison of darkness to declare what I had obscurely formulated. Although the inconstant life of fools is not ordered by themselves, yet divine Providence fits it within an order and settles it as in certain places arranged by its ineffable and eternal law, without allowing it to be where

should not. And thus considered in itself with a narrow spirit, it offends and disgusts us with its ugliness. But if we lift and extend the eyes of the mind to the universality of things, we will find nothing that is not ordered and occupying a distinct and arranged place. 12. "How many sublime ideas," I replied, "how many admirable truths our God communicates to me through your mouth, and I don't know what hidden order of things, as I am increasingly inclined to believe!" Nor more truculent and fierce than his spirit? And yet, it has a necessary place in the laws and is incorporated into the order with which a well-governed society must be governed. TWO MEANS TO LEARN: AUTHORITY AND REASON 26. What remains now is to expose the rules with which those who have already learned to live well must be instructed. There are two paths that lead us to knowledge: authority and reason. Authority precedes in the order of time, but in reality reason takes precedence. Because one thing is what is preferred in the executive order and another is what is more appreciated in the order of intention. Thus, although the authority of the good seems healthier to the ignorant multitude, reason is preferred by the learned. But since every man undoubtedly becomes learned from the unlearned and no unlearned knows the disposition and docility of life with which he must place himself under the direction of the teachers, it turns out that for all those who wish to gain knowledge of the great and hidden questions, authority opens the door. And once he entered without any hesitation, he observes the best moral precepts, and trained by them, he will finally see how reasonable are the things that he embraced without even understanding; and what is reason, which it follows with firmness and security after leaving the cradle of authority; and that the understanding, where all things are, or rather, he is all of them; and what is the beginning of all things, and how it is superior to the universe. Few achieve this knowledge in this life, and in the next one cannot aspire to better ones.

From here, passing into the domain of the eyes and traveling through heaven and earth, he realized that nothing pleased him but beauty, and in beauty the figures, and in the figures the dimensions, and in the dimensions the numbers; and he inquired whether lines and spheres or any other form and figure are in reality, as they are contained in intelligence. And he found the advantage in favor of this, pointing out the difference between the bodily figures and the ideals of the mind. He called the science that distinguishes and orders this knowledge geometry. And he greatly admired the movements of the sky, and he began to study them diligently; and he found that dimensions and numbers also predominated there in the regular vicissitudes of times, in the fixed and concerted movements of the stars, in the moderate intervals of distances. He ordered all the results with definitions and divisions, and invented astronomy, a great spectacle for religious souls, hard work for the curious. 43. In all these disciplines, numerical proportions were encountered everywhere, which shone with more evidence and brilliance of absolute truths in the realm of thought and inner intuition than in the sensible world, where they appeared rather as shadows and vestiges of them. 20. "Auctoritas" and "ratio" (II 5,16).—The book On Order had a primary importance in the scholastic organization of the Middle Ages. The trivium and quatrivium comprised the seven liberal arts, essentially ordered to a better possession of divine Truth. On the other hand, the means of learning were authority and reason; That is to say, the doctrine of the Church, of divine Scripture and Holy Fathers, agreed with the rational data of human culture. In this way, the two pitfalls were avoided: rationalism, the pure dialectical and profane sport, which leads to the sterility of science, and blind fideism, which despises intellectual cultivation to enable man to know the Christian mysteries. The fides quaerens intellectum summarizes the entire Augustinian spirit of medieval culture. Saint Augustine, with his intellectum valde ama, was always present in the rational effort of that age and in the process of penetration and harmonization of the revealed and rational elements. 21. 22. The end of philosophy (II 5,16).-—In this passage, which has received various comments, Saint Augustine includes the knowledge of the Trinity in the scope of authentic philosophy. This Trinity includes the Beginning of all things, which is the Father, the understanding or Word, and the Holy Spirit, to whom other passages of the Dialogues attribute the impulses of the return of creatures to God. This is undoubtedly the Christian Trinity and not the Plotinian Trinity, which includes the Beginning of everything, or One, the Understanding or the Nous, and the universal Soul. The Trinity that Saint Augustine speaks of is the one revealed by the holy mysteries (veneranda mysteria) in which he was imbuing himself to receive baptism. She is the one who saves the people with sincere and indisputable faith "\ 23. The first says, speaking of God: Perfectus super perfections, tripotens in unalitate spiritus, perfectus et supra spiritum. Icarus soared so high that the sun melted the wax that held his wings, and he fell to the ground, dying instantly. The second was a young Trojan, companion of Aeneas, of extraordinary beauty, and linked to Nisus with an endearing friendship. Both were immortalized by Virgil in the Aeneid (1. IX, vv. 314-466). There he also celebrates his mother's cry. 33. Forms, measures, numbers (II 15,42).-—£; in pulchritudine figures, in figuris dimensions, in dimensionibus numbers. Saint Augustine points out here three very important elements of beauty, namely: form, proportion and number. The form is the external, the accessible portion of beauty; and in it the measure, the proportion, as well as the number must shine. This implies plurality, but reduced to unity and ordered for a reason. These elements are continually alluded to in the aesthetics of the books On Order, which is considered St. Augustine's second aesthetic, after missing his first essay De apt et pulchro. Usefulness and beauty are two categories that reign in the universe, but that of beauty is superior, which has an end in itself, as a matter of pure disinterested and beatifying contemplation. That is why in the body of the resurrected all the organs will be returned, even if they are devoid of use, to enhance beauty." 34. To think is to reduce to unity the dissimilar and complex elements of the real. The universe receives its name from the Unity.

Its cohesion was a guarantee of strength and victory, just as its dissolution was an indication of defeat or failure. 37. The principle of totality (II 19,51).—In the books On Order, to solve the problem of evil, Saint Augustine insists on the need for a complete vision of the universe. This is what I have called elsewhere the principle of totality. You cannot have a perfect idea of ​​a part without embracing its connection to the whole. In the Dialogues of Casiciaco, in De vera religione and in De Música he has repeated this principle: "If one remains like a statue in the corner of a sumptuous palace, one cannot fully encompass the architectural beauty of the work. A soldier standing in ranks cannot appreciate the total order of the formation. Likewise, the syllables of a poem, if they lived and felt, while they sound, could not contemplate the harmony and beauty of the whole" 50. Man is like a living and sentient syllable of a great poem, and it is a mystery to him what has happened, and a mystery what is missing or what follows. The beginning and the end are hidden from their end. He only perceives an aliquot part of what is present, of what belongs to him. How in these conditions can "integral beauty" be encompassed? Only God, in quo lotum est, a quo totum est, suh quo totum est', offers a universal perspective, and only by relying on Him can we glimpse the beauty of the world and the reason for evil and disorder. 38. He is, above all, "filius lacrymarum", as the unknown bishop who consoled Saint Monica beautifully defined him.
